What This Story Is About

Immigration activists filed a lawsuit on Friday challenging a new rule from the Tennessee Department of Safety and Homeland Security (TDOS).

Why It Matters

Immigration activist organizations said the TDOS’s new rule that the TIRRC said “blocks many non-U.S. citizens from getting temporary driver’s licenses, even when they have authorization from the federal government to be present in the U.S.”

What Happens Next

The TIRRC said their lawsuit is asking the court to block the new rule and to make the TDOS reinstate its previous process for issuing temporary driver’s licenses.

For Context

The TIRRC said Tennesseans who could prove they had permission from the federal government to be in the U.S. have been able to obtain driver’s licenses for many years, adding that they routinely accepted work permits and other federal documents as proof of legality in the U.S. for a period of time.

Catch Up

Among the new laws that went into effect in Tennessee on January 1 is one that mandates lawful permanent residents receive a different form of ID or driver’s license than those who are U.S. citizens.

NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV) - Immigration activists filed a lawsuit on Friday challenging a new rule from the Tennessee Department of Safety and Homeland Security (TDOS).

The National Immigration Law Center, the Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition (TIRRC) and Bass Berry and Sims, LLC, said the lawsuit is in response to the TDOS’s new rule that the TIRRC said “blocks many non-U.S. citizens from getting temporary driver’s licenses, even when they have authorization from the federal government to be present in the U.S.”

Old policy vs. new rule

The TIRRC said Tennesseans who could prove they had permission from the federal government to be in the U.S. have been able to obtain driver’s licenses for many years, adding that they routinely accepted work permits and other federal documents as proof of legality in the U.S. for a period of time.

In recent weeks, however, the TIRRC said the TDOS abruptly changed this policy, and now only issues driver’s licenses to certain non-citizens who can present a valid visa, I-94,I94W or temporary green card.

“The new rule excludes thousands of people living in Tennessee with federal authorization who have relied for decades on the agency’s prior practice,” the TIRRC said.

Following the implementation of the new rule, the TIRRC said many people, such as Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) recipients, have been denied a Tennessee driver’s license. The organization also said many of those denied did not learn about the new policy until they were at the Driver Services Center.

What the lawsuit argues

The TIRRC said their lawsuit argues that the policy change was made without following legal steps, that the TDOS overstepped its authority and failed to give the public a chance to give their input.

“Tennessee’s denial of driver’s licenses to immigrants is unlawful and infringes on Tennesseans’ right to have a say in matters affecting their communities,” said Peter McGraw, legal deputy director of the National Immigration Law Center. “TDOS issued its new driver’s license policies without first seeking community input or approval, and a state agency must consult the public before implementing extreme policies that affect all of us. Tennesseans should be able to drive safely and freely, and we look forward to putting driver’s licenses back in the hands of people who depend on them.”

The TIRRC said their lawsuit is asking the court to block the new rule and to make the TDOS reinstate its previous process for issuing temporary driver’s licenses.

“Regardless of where they were born, Tennesseans rely on the ability to drive in order to work, care for their families, and access the basic needs of life - groceries, medical appointments, their children’s education. The plaintiffs in this action, like so many others across the state, have found their lives upended by the state’s abrupt rule change, which was implemented without warning or explanation” stated Spring Miller, senior legal strategy director at TIRRC. “This is why we are taking legal action. All Tennesseans expect to be treated fairly before the law, and expect their own government to follow it too.”

WSMV reached out to the TDOS for comment on the lawsuit. Spokesperson Jason Pack shared this statement, “Longstanding policy prohibits the department from publicly discussing pending litigation outside of court filings or hearings.”

text:
Reading Time: 3 minutes

Federal immigration authorities asked the U.S. Supreme Court on Wednesday to hear the case of a Mexican national whom agents arrested last year in Racine. The petition is the latest escalation in a legal fight over the Trump administration’s mandatory detention policy for immigrants facing deportation.

The justices’ decision will determine whether tens of thousands of immigrants currently in federal detention can seek release on bond.

“The question of mandatory detention thus boils down to one question: Can we lock up noncitizens without giving them a day in court first?” said Jenifer Bizzotto, the Wisconsin attorney representing Jaciel Cirrus Rojas, the man at the center of the case. “The stakes could hardly be higher.”

Arrested as ‘collateral’

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents turned up at then-24-year-old Cirrus Rojas’ apartment in June 2025 in search of a prior tenant. They instead arrested Cirrus Rojas, who entered the U.S. in 2018 without a visa, as “collateral.” Wisconsin court records show no criminal convictions under his name.

He spent most of the next nine months in custody at the Dodge County Detention Center in Juneau, entangled in a new White House policy barring ICE detainees from posting bond — a departure from decades of precedent.

The 1996 Immigration Reform Act requires immigration authorities to detain — without bond — anyone found crossing the U.S. border without authorization. Prior administrations applied that rule narrowly, allowing many immigrants arrested in the country’s interior to seek a bond hearing in immigration court.

The Trump administration bucked that approach in July 2025, when ICE Director Todd Lyons issued a new legal interpretation requiring detention without bond regardless of where immigrants are arrested.

The Board of Immigration Appeals, a panel of judges who set the rules for the federal immigration court system, later signed off on the interpretation.

With bond off the table, tens of thousands of immigrants in ICE custody turned to a backup option: filing habeas corpus petitions in federal district courts to challenge their detention.

Unlike immigration courts, which are part of the U.S. Department of Justice, federal district courts belong to the judicial branch and, therefore, are technically independent of the White House. When a federal district court grants a habeas petition, it generally orders an immigration court judge to hold a bond hearing.

Wisconsin’s Western and Eastern District courts have received more than 100 habeas petitions over the past year.

A federal appeals court split

The 7th Circuit ruled 2-1 in Cirrus Rojas’ favor in July, joining appellate courts based in New York, Cincinnati, Denver, Atlanta and San Francisco in rejecting the policy.“If Congress had indeed demanded — but not funded — no-bond detention for all unlawful entrants, that may well have thrown the nation’s immigration system into chaos,” Judge Joshua Kolar, whom Joe Biden appointed to the court, wrote in the court’s majority opinion. “Immigration authorities might have found themselves quickly overwhelmed by a colossal unfunded mandate to arrest and detain millions.” Judge Diane Sykes, a George W. Bush appointee, dissented alone.

“At this point, only the Supreme Court can bring uniformity and settle this question once and for all,” she wrote. “I anticipate that it will do so soon.”

Cirrus Rojas left custody earlier this year after a federal district court judge in California vacated the mandatory detention rule. The San Francisco-based 9th Circuit Court of Appeals stayed that decision less than a month later.

The 7th Circuit allowed his case to move forward because federal authorities plan to re-detain him.

Supreme Court could have final say

“Nothing, absent our intervention, stops the government from making good on its promise,” Kolar wrote.The U.S. Department of Homeland Security, ICE’s parent agency, is now asking the Supreme Court to step in.

The court agreed to take up another mandatory detention dispute earlier this month. That case involves a Brazilian national arrested during a traffic stop in Massachusetts last September.

DHS asked the justices to hold Cirrus Rojas’ case until they decide the Massachusetts case.

In Bizzotto’s view, both cases “offer the Supreme Court the opportunity to affirm that the Constitution means what it says.”

A ruling against the mandatory detention policy would open the door for thousands of ICE detainees — at least those within circuits that side with the Trump administration — to request bond hearings in immigration court. It would not require immigration court judges to grant their bond requests.

The Supreme Court also quietly declined this week to revive a Biden-era policy that allowed immigration court judges to pause deportation proceedings for immigrants seeking humanitarian visas or other forms of legal status.

text:
The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals has ruled that State Department is not required to open the FY 2027 Diversity Visa (DV) program registration period while litigation challenging the halt of the program continues. The appeals court has issued an emergency stay of an October 14 district court preliminary injunction that required the State Department to open this fiscal year’s DV registration and conduct the program according to a specified timeline.

In issuing the stay, the Ninth Circuit says that the court does not endorse the State Department’s failure to open the FY 2027 registration period, but that the plaintiff, a law firm that represents DV applicants, did not show that it met the legal requirements for a preliminary injunction. The court determined that the firm is not within the zone of interests to be protected or regulated and does not have a cause of action, as required under the preliminary injunction legal standard. The case is Red Eagle Law, L.C. v. Rubio, No. 26-6943 (9th Cir., case filed Oct 20, 2026; order issued Oct 29, 2026).

After making an announcement in November 2025 that changes were underway for the FY 2027 DV entry period, the State Department paused the program entirely in December 2025. The agency simultaneously paused immigrant visa processing under the FY 2026 DV program. Several groups sued to reinstate the DV programs underway or in the planning stages at the time of the pauses; the litigants challenging actions affecting the FY 2026 DV program had some limited success.

In August 2026, law firm Red Eagle Law, L.C. sued in a California district court to reinstate the FY 2027 DV program. On October 14, the Red Eagle court issued a preliminary injunction ordering the State Department to open the FY 2027 DV program by midnight ET, November 1, 2026 for a period of 30 days; to make an advance public announcement with all registration details on the State Department website by midnight ET, October 29, 2026; and then after DV registration closes, to notify selected foreign nationals of their selection by midnight ET on December 3, 2026. The preliminary injunction order also required the State Department to timely process any submitted FY 2027 DV immigrant visa applications in accordance with the agency’s usual procedures. The district court case is Red Eagle Law, L.C. v. Rubio, Docket No. 3:26-cv-04738 (S.D. Cal., case filed Aug 19, 2026).

The State Department quickly appealed the preliminary injunction to the Ninth Circuit, resulting in the above emergency stay of the district court order.

text:
Rio Grande Valley, Texas – Leaning over plates of tamales, pan dulce, and sugar skulls, community organisers and local residents in the border city of Brownsville remembered the dead.

This year’s Dia de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, vigil honoured victims of state violence, including those killed in immigration enforcement and detention. Just days before the US midterm election on November 3, the event reverberated in a region long subject to Washington, DC’s shifting political winds.

Recommended Stories

list of 3 items

list 1 of 3Who is leading the US midterm polls as Trump and Harris campaign?

list 2 of 3Pentagon says Iran war has cost US taxpayers $47bn: What that means

list 3 of 3What does bourbon have to do with the US midterms?

end of list

“The atmosphere here in the Rio Grande Valley when it comes to ICE detentions and the ICE raids, there’s just the overall feeling amongst folks that there’s no real due process to this,” said Mark Anthony Vasquez, a 52-year-old community organiser.

“What is it that we can do to move together and build together to try to make it past this, and make that change that we seek?”

Down the block, at a bookstore panel on border and immigration policy, 24-year-old Juliana Garcia raised her hand to ask advice on how to find a lawyer able to navigate the aggressively shifting policies of the administration of US President Donald Trump, which has used both an increase in physical enforcement, as well as a reinterpretation of administrative policies, to fuel its mass deportation campaign.

Garcia’s aunt, a well-known member of the community in the nearby border town of Progreso, was deported just weeks ago, after being called to a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) hearing. There she learned she had missed a court date related to her immigration status.

In the stress of the moment, she signed a voluntary deportation form.

“Within 36 hours, she was deported,” Garcia told Al Jazeera, tucked between bookshelves. “People are waking up, and they’re remembering that politics, regardless of what branch you’re in, it’s going to impact you every day.”

Shifting dynamics

Views on immigration are complex in the Rio Grande Valley, a geographic and cultural region located in subtropical southeast Texas with about 1.5 million residents. That complexity has only increased in recent years as border policy and immigration enforcement have become increasingly partisan, leading, reformers say, to dramatic policy swings that prevent more sustainable solutions.

It is not difficult to find Latino – or Tejano, the local term for Texans of Latino descent – residents wary of the years preceding Trump’s return to office. After the restrictive policies of Trump’s first term, border crossings increased dramatically under US President Joe Biden, fuelled in part by the end of a COVID-era policy that made asylum seekers wait for their cases to be processed in Mexico.

Some felt the border region was left to deal with the fallout from the influx. That discontent has been credited, in part, with Trump’s success in the once-reliably Democratic region in the 2024 presidential election.

In Hidalgo County, home to the city of McAllen, Trump won 51 percent of the vote in 2024, a three-point margin over Kamala Harris. In 2020, Biden beat Trump in the county by 17 percentage points.

In neighbouring Cameron County, Trump won by about five percentage points in 2024, despite a 13-point loss in 2020.

Voter Jose Arizpe, a 40-year-old resident of Brownsville, assessed the two years since Trump took office as a “positive change”, with fewer asylum seekers waiting in the US for their cases to be processed.

Upon taking office, Trump declared a state of emergency at the border, staunching asylum claims in what rights groups say runs counter to US law. The US Supreme Court has since ruled that US border agents can physically block asylum seekers from reaching US soil to claim asylum.

“A lot of people claim that they support illegals and want to let them in,” said Arizpe, a regular Republican voter, “but then, I say ‘well let them in your house’. And they don’t want to do it, right?”

On border policy, “at first, I supported Trump,” said Martin Torres, a 55-year-old who cast his ballot for Democrats at a public library in Brownsville as part of the state’s early voting.

But domestic enforcement, and its impact on the local workforce, soured his views.

“Now he changes everything,” he said.

A report from the Caminos Institute has estimated the region has lost $180.6m in economic activity due to the Trump administration’s immigration policies, including in construction and restaurants.

Other voters saw Trump’s approach as fuelling bigotry. Last year, the US Supreme Court lifted a lower-court order barring immigration officials from considering “apparent race or ethnicity”, as well as language spoken, when on patrol. Rights groups say the decision effectively allows racial profiling.

In Texas, a state law also lets local officials stop individuals they suspect entered the country illegally.

“I just see a lot of discrimination going on,” said George Castorena, a 46-year-old department of education worker, who said he was voting for change.

To be sure, midterm elections can only offer incremental change on an issue as entrenched as immigration enforcement and border policy.

Democratic control of the House of Representatives would at best serve as a bulwark against the Trump administration legislating more immigration enforcement funding and policy, while opening the door to investigations into the administration’s approach.

Control of the Senate, which could be determined by the contest between Texas Republican Ken Paxton and Democratic challenger James Talarico, could further increase the party’s leverage.

A change in the governor’s office, meanwhile, could end Texas Governor Greg Abbott’s myriad uses of state agencies to support federal immigration enforcement. But Democrat Gina Hinojosa, if she were to pull off an upset, would be largely constrained by a likely Republican-dominated state legislature and a mountain of pre-existing law.

A galvanising moment?

Although a more lasting transformation remains far off, evidence suggests the local dismay runs deep.

A poll conducted by the American Civil Liberties Union of Texas found that only 34 percent of respondents from the area felt that immigration enforcement by both local and state officials had made their communities safer. Fifty-three percent said it made their lives harder without improving safety.

Meanwhile, 64 percent felt ICE tactics have gone too far. The numbers broadly align with polls showing Democratic challenger Bobby Pulido leading Republican incumbent Monica De La Cruz and Democratic incumbent Vicente Gonzalez leading Republican challenger Eric Flores in two Rio Grande Valley congressional districts.

Republicans, eyeing Trump’s success in 2024, viewed the races as strong prospects early in the election season.

“What this survey conveys is: people along the border in the Rio Grande Valley are not in alignment with what they probably voted for back in 2024,” Osvaldo Grimaldo, a policy strategist at ACLU of Texas, told Al Jazeera.

Even prominent community figures who support Trump’s policies acknowledge a broader change in sentiment.

Eli Lara, the lead pastor at the non-denominational New Life Family Church in McAllen, Texas, said locals have been dismayed by the wide scope with which the administration has targeted undocumented individuals.

“The immigration issue is bigger because [the community] is seeing people being taken,” he told Al Jazeera. “I don’t like the separation of families, but here’s the thing: there are consequences for choices.”

That view held even for a congregant who had recently been deported in connection with a past drug possession conviction.

“He’s been faithful [to the church] for two, three years, but they picked him up,” Lara said. “Why? Because he had a bad criminal record in the past. God forgives, but the government doesn’t.”

Voter Garcia, who volunteers with the Hidalgo County Young Democrats, was among those who believed the current situation could galvanise the Rio Grande Valley.

She pointed to several instances that have recently shaken the region, including the assault of a 17-year-old by immigration agents in the town of Alamo in the Rio Grande Valley, and the fatal ICE shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in July 2026 in the Texas city of Houston.

“I’ve had a lot of people tell me, ‘Why do I care about politics? Politics doesn’t affect me,'” she said. “And with all of these ICE raids, they realise politics does affect them, and it sucks that it took a lot of trauma to really bring that to people.”

text:
A federal immigration agent who drove into and seriously injured a Texas man on 10 October after a botched traffic stop was indicted Friday on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.

Mario Alberto Morales, 33, an agent with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), deliberately veered his SUV into Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, causing multiple leg fractures and a hip injury, journalists at a news conference in Houston were told.

In announcing the charge against Morales, Harris county district attorney Sean Teare questioned the training that Morales, a recent appointment by ICE, had received – and denounced the activities and conduct of the agency in support of the frequently violent immigration crackdown during Donald Trump’s second presidency.

His office is also investigating the fatal shooting by ICE in Houston in July of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, an immigrant who, like Parra Hernandez, was not the intended target of an enforcement operation.

Friday’s indictment came little more than five months after Christian Castro, an ICE officer who shot and wounded a Venezuelan man in an operation in Minnesota in January, was charged with assault and falsely reporting a crime.

“Their behavior and the fear that’s being instilled in such a big, vibrant group of people, of Harris county residents, is objectively making us all less safe,” Teare told reporters, citing what he said was a documented drop-off in reports of domestic violence, aggravated robberies and sexual assaults by victims who feared deportation.

“One of the most insidious things about these tactics and the way that ICE is behaving in our community is the fear that a large percentage of our population has right now. An ICE badge does not give you free rein to injure, kill, or violate the constitutional rights of anyone.”

A grand jury empanelled to investigate the case involving Morales returned the indictment on Friday morning after hearing evidence that Teare said was “as clear as any that I’ve ever prosecuted or investigated”.

Morales was driving an unmarked Jeep Cherokee and attempted to stop a pickup truck containing two men who jumped out and fled. Surveillance video played at the news conference showed Parra Hernandez, a Mexican construction worker with no criminal record or active deportation order, running across a restaurant parking lot when the pursuing SUV swerved into him and ran him over.

In an audio recording of a 911 call Morales made requesting the assistance of paramedics and the Harris county sheriff’s office, he is heard telling the dispatcher that Parra Hernandez ran in front of his vehicle and was hit, an assertion repeated in an official ICE account of the case released the following day.

In a statement on Friday, an ICE spokesperson said: “Allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra Hernandez intentionally are reckless and false. The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct.”

The spokesperson said the indictment was “nothing more than a political stunt by Houston sanctuary politicians”, using a term meant to describe local officials who don’t cooperate with federal immigration authorities.

“Federal officers acting in the course of their duties can only be investigated by other federal agencies,” the spokesperson also said. “Local governments do not have the authority to run such an investigation.”

Harris county sheriff Ed Gonzalez told the press conference his investigators later found out that, at the time it struck Parra Hernandez, Morales’s SUV also contained two handcuffed detainees from a previous, unrelated operation.

“I know of no law enforcement agency that would deem that to be acceptable,” he said. “To the contrary, it’s very unsafe. If some other crash could have occurred with them being handcuffed and shackled inside the vehicle it would have been a maybe even worse situation because they were very limited in their movement and in the backseat of the vehicle.”

Teare said that ICE deported at least two “material witnesses” within a week of Parra being struck over the prosecutor’s objection and with no opportunity to interview them. Parra Hernandez, he said, “is not even able to leave the rehab facility, and they are having court dates to try to deport him”.

The district attorney said he had collected “a significant amount of information” on Morales’s background – and said he was hired by ICE in August 2025 as part of the agency’s aggressive immigration “surge” into a number of US cities.

He declined to give details of any previous employers and said he had not received any of Morales’s training records.

“Whether or not he has those, we don’t know, but I can unequivocally tell you that I’ve reviewed thousands of job applications and resumes for law enforcement officers from around this state, and I’m not familiar with a single agency that would have hired this person based on his past,” Teare said.

Lawyers for Parra Hernandez, who remains in ICE custody, have said he would need numerous operations to recover from his injuries.

The whereabouts of the person that ICE said it was pursuing when Parra Hernandez was hurt are unknown. The agency identified a man named Jose Mendoza-Cervantes as their target, and released an image of someone they said was him.

text:
A grand jury in Texas has indicted a United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer accused of deliberately running over a Mexican construction worker during an operation in Houston this month.

ICE officer Mario Alberto Morales faces charges of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon for the October 10 incident, Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare announced on Friday.

Recommended Stories

list of 3 items

list 1 of 3Will ICE agents play a role in the 2026 US midterm elections?

list 2 of 3On the US border in Texas, Trump deportation drive galvanises midterm vote

list 3 of 3Trump administration attempts to take down leak of ICE personnel data

end of list

Criminal charges against federal immigration officers have been rare during President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, although several encounters involving officers have prompted investigations.

Morales is accused of striking 48-year-old Miguel Parra-Hernandez, an immigrant who has lived in Harris County for more than 30 years. Teare said that Parra-Hernandez had no criminal record.

Parra-Hernandez was running away from federal agents when an unmarked black Jeep Cherokee struck him in a car park near Clay Road and Highway 6, according to investigators. He suffered multiple fractures to his right leg and an ankle injury which required surgery.

The indictment follows a dispute between local prosecutors and federal authorities over what happened. ICE has maintained that Parra-Hernandez ran in front of the vehicle, dismissing the allegations that the officer intentionally struck him as “reckless and false.”

But Teare has said surveillance video contradicts the agency’s account.

It shows the SUV crossing a median and pursuing Parra-Hernandez as he runs away. Although another vehicle obscures the moment of impact, the video shows the man on the ground moments later.

Authorities also released body-camera footage on Friday. In the recording, Morales can be heard acknowledging that he struck Parra-Hernandez with his vehicle.

Teare also accused federal authorities of failing to cooperate with the investigation, including by removing the Jeep before local investigators could examine it for potential evidence.

A search warrant obtained by local media shows investigators had not been granted access to the vehicle as of October 23.

SAN ANTONIO – Federal prosecutors in the Western District of Texas filed 256 new immigration and immigration-related criminal cases from Oct. 23 through Oct. 30, announced U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons. Charges were brought against alien smugglers and illegal aliens with past convictions for violent crimes, numerous DWIs, thefts, and multiple prior removals. The new batch of immigration cases brings the total number across the district’s seven offices to nearly 1,000 in October, averaging approximately 250 cases filed per week.

Among the new cases, prosecutors charged Miguel Malo Poggio with transportation of illegal aliens. Supporting an investigation led by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), U.S. Border Patrol agents conducted a traffic stop on a tractor-trailer traveling north on Interstate 25 north of Las Cruces, New Mexico. The driver was identified as Malo Poggio. As alleged in a criminal complaint affidavit, agents located a black backpack containing numerous cellular devices in a storage compartment of the truck’s cab. When questioned about the devices, Malo Poggio allegedly handed an agent a set of keys from his pocket, indicating that the keys were for the cargo trailer, which was secured with a red tamper-evident seal.

According to the affidavit, agents discovered 42 illegal aliens inside the trailer, including three unaccompanied minors. The aliens were unrestrained and seated on the floor in rows and columns without an apparent means of exit. The affidavit alleges that at least one of the aliens stated they had illegally crossed into the United States less than a week prior, was taken to a stash house where their phone was confiscated and eventually loaded into the tractor-trailer where they were told to sit, remain quiet and stay hidden. This case remains under investigation and is being prosecuted in El Paso.

Also in El Paso, Omar Lorenzo Olivas-Chavez, an illegal alien from Mexico, was charged with illegal re-entry after he allegedly attempted to enter the U.S. with false information. A criminal complaint alleges Olivas-Chavez applied for admission via the pedestrian lane at the Bridge of the Americas Port of Entry on Oct. 23, stating to a U.S. Customs and Border Protection officer that he was a U.S. Citizen and had lost his entry documents. The complaint alleges Olivas-Chavez wrote down a name and date of birth for the officer, which, after further inspection, was determined to be fictitious. A fingerprint scan revealed Olivas-Chaves has been previously removed from the U.S. to Mexico six times and has been convicted of burglary of habitation twice. He’s also been previously convicted of criminal trespass, evading arrest, assault on a public servant, and escape while arrested.

Alvaro Lopez Ayala, an illegal alien from Mexico, was transferred to ICE custody and charged with illegal entry in San Antonio. Lopez was arrested in New Braunfels in May and transferred to the Travis County Jail in July to serve time pending a rape charge, according to a criminal complaint. On Oct. 21, Lopez was convicted of indecent assault in Travis County and sentenced to 300 days confinement. Lopez was previously removed from the U.S. in 2014. In addition to the indecent assault conviction, he has been previously convicted of cred card abuse, aggravated assault causing serious bodily injury, and evading arrest.

Roberto Espinoza-Ponce, also an illegal alien from Mexico, was arrested by a deportation officer in Del Valle on Tuesday. Espinoza-Ponce has been previously removed from the U.S. three times and convicted for two DWIs, a hit-and-run, and failure to ID. If convicted, this will be his second for illegal re-entry.

Selvin Noe Santos-Umana, an illegal alien from Honduras, was arrested by U.S. Border Patrol agents near Eagle Pass and charged with illegal re-entry. Santos-Umana was deported for the first time in April. He was convicted in 2024 for robbery using force, and has also been previously convicted of domestic battery, use and possession of drug paraphernalia, and interfering with a law enforcement officer.

Jose Elmer Argueta-Argueta, an illegal alien from El Salvador, was also arrested near Eagle Pass and charged with illegal re-entry. He was just deported in August for the eighth time. Argueta-Argueta has been previously convicted of two illegal re-entry charges, a DWI, forging public documents, and destruction of property with malicious wounding.

These cases were referred or supported by federal law enforcement partners, including ICE, U.S. Border Patrol, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), the FBI, the U.S. Marshals Service (USMS), and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), with additional assistance from state and local law enforcement partners.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Texas comprises 68 counties located in the central and western areas of Texas, encompasses nearly 93,000 square miles and an estimated population of 7.6 million people. The district includes three of the five largest cities in Texas—San Antonio, Austin and El Paso—and shares 660 miles of common border with the Republic of Mexico.

Indictments and criminal complaints are merely allegations and all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

These cases are part of Operation Take Back America a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.

Surveillance video shows a Jeep Cherokee speed over a median and drive toward Parra Hernandez as he runs away.
The video then shows Parra Hernandez on the ground and grabbing his leg, yelling in pain.

text:
HOUSTON (AP) — A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer accused of intentionally ramming his car into a Mexican construction worker in Houston was indicted by a grand jury Friday on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, prosecutors said.

The officer, Mario Alberto Morales, was driving an unmarked SUV on Oct. 10 when he struck and ran over Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, who was running away during a pursuit through a parking lot, the Harris County District Attorney's Office said. Parra Hernandez broke his leg and remains in federal custody at a rehabilitation facility, District Attorney Sean Teare said.

READ MORE: ICE officer appeared to intentionally hit a man with a vehicle in Houston, Texas prosecutor says

ICE has asserted that Parra Hernandez ran in front of the vehicle, an account that Teare said is contradicted by video.

"The evidence we have in this case is as clear as any that I've ever prosecuted or investigated," Teare said.

Morales, 33, of Brownsville, Texas, is one of just a few federal officers who have faced criminal charges over their actions on the job during President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown, although other encounters have come under investigation, including a fatal shooting by an ICE officer this summer in Houston.

Morales' attorney, David Lindenmuth, said his client didn't commit a crime and he accused Teare of indicting Morales "for political gain." Morales had worked as an ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations officer for a little more than a year, Lindenmuth said.

"Mr. Morales is truly a good man, a former member of our military, that has given his entire life to public service either for his country or in or adjacent to law enforcement," Lindenmuth told The Associated Press. "To have him charged for what was so clearly just an accident — the DA's office, the DA himself, has invented a crime out of thin air."

WATCH: ICE shooting of man in New York with child in his car sparks outrage

Teare hinted at concerns over Morales' background but would not provide details.

Morales, who is charged with a second-degree felony, was not in custody Friday and a warrant will be issued for his arrest, according to Teare.

ICE asserted that local officials do not have the authority to investigate federal officers acting in the course of their duties.

"Allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE," the agency said in a statement.

The district attorney played Morales' body camera footage

Teare has said video clearly contradicts the ICE account. Surveillance video shows a Jeep Cherokee speed over a median and drive toward Parra Hernandez as he runs away. During a news conference Friday, he played Morales' body camera footage, which shows him driving and talking about pursuing someone.

The video shows Morales making a few sharp moves with the steering wheel before the SUV shakes. Morales stops the vehicle, then gets out and turns toward Parra Hernandez, who is several feet away. The video then shows Parra Hernandez on the ground and grabbing his leg, yelling in pain.

Morales is heard saying, "He got hit with a car, bro." It is not clear to whom he is talking.

"I was coming in and I hit him with the car," Morales says.

Family says ICE was looking for a dead person during operation

Parra Hernandez has lived in Harris County for more than 30 years and did not have a deportation order or criminal background, according to Teare.

Other aspects of ICE's account have also been called into question.

READ MORE: New ICE guidance bans high-speed car chases and sets tighter rules for traffic stops, memo shows

After Parra Hernandez was taken into custody, ICE released a photo of another man, Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, and said he was the target of the operation that day. ICE said he was seen entering a vehicle with Parra Hernandez. Family members of Parra Hernandez said they had never heard of him. FIEL, an immigrant rights group in Houston that has been working with the family, said Mendoza-Cervantes' daughter told them her father has been dead since 2017.

Teare's office has previously said its investigation has not found that Parra Hernandez and the man ICE identified as Mendoza-Cervantes were in a vehicle together, contrary to ICE's statement.

ICE has not responded to claims that the suspect they were looking for has been dead for years.

Fatal summer Houston shooting also under investigation

Teare has said the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, has not cooperated with his investigators and accused ICE of destroying evidence "either intentionally or through gross negligence." He has said Morales left the scene before the vehicle could be impounded.

In July, Teare said DHS also ignored his requests for information after an ICE officer fatally shot 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in his van. DHS has said Salgado Araujo had "weaponized his vehicle" before the shooting and that an officer fired in self-defense. Other passengers in the van have disputed that account.

Wilder reported from Austin, Texas.

Wilder is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

ICE vehicles were reported near the Monterey County Jail and Salinas Regional Soccer Complex on Thursday, prompting the complex to update the community about activity in the area.

The county also said ICE vehicles had recently been seen on a dirt road near the jail on Thursday.

The Solidarity Network Monterey County Rapid Response said legal observers saw four ICE vehicles, two SUVs and two other vehicles, at or near the jail as of 1 p.m. Thursday.

The complex later closed its gate and asked the agent to leave.

The County of Monterey also confirmed to KSBW 8 that three vehicles carrying ICE officers had been on county-owned property at the soccer complex, were asked to leave and had done so.

However, Monterey County Supervisor Luis Alejo posted that vehicles returned shortly after leaving at around 11 a.m. and that two ICE vehicles were parked outside the entrance.

ICE agents are seemingly there for targeted operations for certain individuals leaving the jail. No detentions have been reported at this time.

In an update posted at 1 p.m. Thursday, the soccer complex said it had seen increased immigration enforcement activity nearby, including across the street.

The complex said ICE had not entered its property and there had been no reported enforcement incidents there.

A source familiar with jail operations told KSBW 8 that 15 people who the source said qualified for protections under California’s SB 54 had been released to ICE, most recently on Oct. 7.

KSBW 8 has not independently verified the source’s account or the number of people involved.

text:
A liberal-majority appeals court in California handed the Trump administration a victory by blocking a lower court's ruling that ordered the State Department to open its application pool for the 2027 Diversity Visa lottery, which admits roughly 55,000 immigrants from low-immigration countries each year.

In a 2-1 ruling, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals blocked a preliminary injunction issued by U.S. District Judge Jinsook Ohta requiring the lottery pool to be opened after Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued a notice in November delaying the program's acceptance of new applications in order to "implement certain changes," but the application period never opened.

A month later, the State Department ordered an indefinite pause on issuing diversity visas after a Portuguese national who was issued a lottery visa in 2017 committed a mass shooting at Brown University, killing two people and injuring nine others. The shooter, Claudio Manuel Neves Valente, was also tied to the murder of a Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) professor two days after the Brown University shooting.

FBI REVEALS BROWN UNIVERSITY MASS SHOOTER BEGAN PLOTTING MASSACRE AS EARLY AS 2022, BLAMED VICTIMS

The Ninth Circuit has been a perennial thorn in the side of President Donald Trump, having ruled against key portions of Trump's 2017 executive order restricting travel from predominantly Muslim countries and blocked a policy barring immigrants from being eligible for asylum if they crossed the southern border between ports of entry.

However, the appeals court ruled that the lower court's preliminary injunction could not be enforced, finding that the immigration law firm Red Eagle, which represents individuals going through the visa lottery process, did not have standing to sue the federal government. The appeals court ruled that the program was intended to "encourage immigration, not generate revenue for law firms."

LIBERAL COURT STUNS WITH RULING THAT HANDS TRUMP MAJOR IMMIGRATION WIN

The court wrote, "If Red Eagle Law were allowed to allege standing based upon its hypothetical or conjectural collateral injury, we would be opening the floodgates, allowing all lawyers to ‘roam the country in search of governmental wrongdoing.’"

However, the court made clear that its ruling was based on procedural grounds and did not weigh whether the State Department failed to follow the law.

"We do not endorse the Department’s failure to open the lottery registration period," the court wrote.

Abhishek Kambli, a former federal prosecutor and partner at Holtzman Vogel, said the decision by the liberal court was a "very easy call" in a post on X.

"Here, the plaintiff was a law firm not bringing a claim on behalf of someone in the diversity visa lottery but on behalf of the firm itself," Kambli wrote. "The district court should have never gone beyond standing but CA9 corrected this one."

TRUMP ADMIN ANNOUNCES EXPANSION OF VISA RESTRICTION POLICY IN WESTERN HEMISPHERE

President Donald Trump has been vocal about his opposition to the Visa Lottery Program for years. During his January 2018 State of the Union address, he called for ending the program, arguing that visas should be issued based on merit.

Earlier that same month, Trump said during a bipartisan meeting with lawmakers at the White House that lottery visas allow the "worst of the worst" to come into the country.

"They call it ‘visa lottery,’ I just call it ‘lottery.’ But countries come in and they put names in a hopper," Trump said. "They’re not giving you their best names; common sense means they’re not giving you their best names."

text:
Very early on Wednesday morning, Dover, N.J., Councilwoman Sandra Wittner started getting messages about immigration agents. A dozen or more were gathering outside a Walgreens, according to the messages she was getting. Throughout the day, neighbors in north New Jersey saw a spike in Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity.

And New Jersey is not alone. In the weeks ahead of the midterms, various cities and states across the country are reporting a notable rise in ICE activity, according to reports gathered by NPR and its member stations.

"The tactics that the administration has been deploying in communities really appear to be designed to try to intimidate voters," says Wendy Weiser of the Brennan Center for Justice at NYU Law School. Despite that, early turnout is surging.

"There was definitely a lot of apprehension and fear," Wittner recalls. "We just really weren't sure if something huge was about to happen. People were not feeling very comfortable or safe."

Wittner is not sure who was detained or where, which is unsurprising: these days it's difficult to report on ICE crackdowns as they happen, because the Department of Homeland Security no longer publicly shares timely information on its operations.

NPR wrote to the agency to ask if there has been a recent surge. It responded: "ICE agents uphold our nation's immigration laws in all 50 states, seven days a week, 24 hours a day."

And yet NPR and its member stations have received tips from rural Illinois,Oregon,Detroit andCalifornia about surges in ICE enforcement, throughout October.

An official within New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani's office who was not authorized to speak publicly confirmed that they have noted a surge in ICE activity in the city.

"We're certainly witnessing an uptick in activity, and have been since the summer," says a member of a volunteer group of neighbors in New York. She asked that NPR not use her name, as she is worried about retaliation. Her group goes to the scene where an ICE operation is happening, documents it, reminds those being detained of their rights, and alerts neighbors.

"In the past few weeks we've seen numerous large operations, or what we call cluster raids, multiple agents going to one spot and then the next," she said.

On the other side of the country, Oregon Public Broadcasting reporter Troy Brynelson has reported on a similar trend. "What we were seeing in early October and what we've seen continue, at least anecdotally throughout this month, is that ICE activity has really picked up in Portland." Brynelson says it seems to be concentrated in commercial areas. "I'd say it's a noticeable uptick compared to what we've seen over the summer."

Juan Proaño of the League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC), a civil rights organization says he's concerned because this is happening so close to the midterm elections. "It's not about ICE at the actual polling station, it's ICE at the perimeter of the polling station," he says.

"Mass enforcement actions could be away from the polls, but with social media and the news, it could be enough to dissuade somebody from actually going out to vote."

Weiser of the Brennan Center says there's no indication the raids are affecting turnout. On the contrary, she says there has been a surge in early voting in minority communities across the country. "The good news is: it isn't working. Americans are tuning this out and we are not seeing a significant impact on participation. And we are actually seeing huge surges in participation in communities of color, and in Latino communities, and in all the communities that have been targeted by ICE and DHS."

text:
Elia smiles as she speaks, moving her scrunchie-laden wrists to describe two things that bring her joy: math and basketball. She pauses a moment to ask her foster mom how to say volleyball in English.

The 17-year-old from Central America is a recipient of Special Immigrant Juvenile Status, a humanitarian protection for immigrant children who survived neglect, abuse or abandonment from one or both parents. She’s had nearly two years of stability here in the U.S.. But now, that’s in jeopardy.

“My attorney called and said I have to be at the court hearing, so I went, but my attorney did the speaking to the judge,” Elia said in a video interview, tugging at the pink rose on her purple sweater. GBH News is using a pseudonym for Elia since she is a minor.

“I’m afraid I’m going to lose the opportunity to study. I’m just really confused,” she said.

In April, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services rescinded a Biden-era policy that deferred deportation proceedings for youth who are current and future Special Immigrant Juvenile petitioners for green cards.

Elia is one of many immigrant youth and children who have been ordered removed from the country as a result, despite having already gained humanitarian relief to be in the U.S. legally. Other youth and children who have the same immigration status, or are in the process of getting it, fear they will be ordered to a court hearing and told to leave the country.

An hour before getting the life-changing call from her attorney, Elia was talking about college majors with Stacey, her foster mother. Right after the call, Stacey, connected with Elia’s therapist to get her additional emotional support. GBH News is not using Stacey’s real name due to concerns of repercussions on Elia from the Trump administration.

Federal immigration authorities ordered Elia to appear in court earlier this month, where she joined many children at a room in an Ascentria Care Alliance location in Worcester for a virtual immigration court hearing. Immigration Judge Omar Karram ordered her deported, but that’s on hold while she appeals the decision.

Worcester-based Ascentria is the only foster care service provider for the state’s Unaccompanied Refugees Minors Program. Staff there are used to representing children in routine immigration hearings. Recently, staff there say more children are being forced to miss school to attend hearings.

“These are children who are victims of extreme abuse, abandonment, neglect, trafficking, all kinds of things. And their escape to the United States was quite frankly the only option, and it is not an option that comes easily for them, “ Angela Snyder, supervising attorney at the Immigration Legal Assistance program at Ascentria. “There has been a systematic attack on the rights for these youth through the immigration system.”

The Trump administration cut funding to support unaccompanied minors’ legal representation with the organization in 2025. Some of the immigration policy changes have also caused adult Special Immigrant Juvenile visa recipients to have their work permits cancelled.

So far, no one in the program has been deported, but they’re concerned that could change, and more children have been ordered to hearings.

From immigrant to foster care

To gain that status, there are many requirements, including an order from a state court that children can’t return and live safely in their county of origin in order to get the status.

When unaccompanied immigrant children arrive in the U.S., they’re held at facilities run by the Office of Refugee Resettlement, which works with local provides to establish state guardianship and bring them into the specific state’s foster care system.

Two agencies co-administer the program, the state Department of Children and Families and the federal Office of Refugees and Immigrants. The Executive Office of Health and Human Services, which houses both DCF and ORI, told GBH News that the Office of Refugees and Immigrants has opened its help desk services for children with SIJs.

“Since the 1990s, Massachusetts has hosted children in foster care on behalf of the federal government’s Unaccompanied Refugee Minor program,” said a spokesperson for DCF. “The federal government has long held the responsibility to provide legal services for unaccompanied immigrant children, including those in the federal URM program. But the Trump Administration has cut that funding and rolled back longstanding protections against deportation, leaving vulnerable young people across the country without legal representation.”

The office said that for decades, immigration enforcement action against SIJ holders was deferred and Judges regularly cancelled deportation hearings for those children and young adults with SIJS, who were on a lawful pathway to a green card.

“Simultaneously, Immigration Court Judges have been ordering these children deported, when in previous years their hearings would be delayed while they await their green card process,” said the spokesperson. “In Massachusetts, we are working to provide access to legal services for unaccompanied immigrant children and DCF-involved young adults through the Massachusetts Access to Counsel Initiative, the ORI Help Desk, and our contracted partners. This includes those in the care of the Department of Children and Families and other unaccompanied youth who hold Special Immigrant Juvenile Status.”

Elia spent a month at a federal facility in Texas for minors who arrived in the U.S. without parents. Then she was connected with her foster parents.

Stacey says of Elia, “she’s just pure joy and innocence.” She said Elia had an education gap, but has been able to make up at least four grade levels in less than two years. She’s now hoping to go to college after high school, and the family is supporting that dream with extra tutoring. Stacey proudly mentioned an award Elia recently got at school, and says the family was already planning her next birthday with a prom theme.

“We want to make sure she has that experience because we don’t know what’s going to happen. She has this deportation order. We don’t know if that means that it’s going to be appealed or there’ll be some legislation that stops it or that she’ll have to leave,” said Stacey.

Ascentia Care Alliance has 30 days to appeal her order of removal. Then the Board of Immigration Appeals, the highest court in immigration court system, must issue a timeline with deadlines for parties to file arguments.

Change affects older immigrants, too

People over 18 who have Special Immigration Juvenile status are nervous about what the changing policies can mean for them as adults, and their foster families are trying to be preemptive in supporting them.

One of those is Juan, a 20-year-old student from Central America who is studying to be an HVAC technician. GBH News isn’t using his real name because he’s afraid of being detained. He’s been in Central Massachusetts living with a foster parent since he was 15.

“I’ve done everything that has been asked of me, all of my responsibilities,” said Juan. He said he’s nervous about an upcoming court hearing in December, and doesn’t understand if it’s routine or not.

“I really don’t want to leave my studies, my dreams. My foster mom is my family,” he said. Juan is hoping to one day own his own business, and is working at a restaurant until he can finish the degree. “We’re here to work hard, build a future, and not hurt anyone, or take anything from anyone,” said Juan.

Grace, his foster mother, launched a change.org petition with over 1,200 views. GBH News is not using her last name due to her concerns of retribution of the Trump administration on Juan, and repercussions as a state employee. She wants to see the deferred action policy reinstated by the federal government, and accountability in the immigration courts.

The petition urges Gov. Maura Healey, the Department of Children and Families, and state legislators to take action to protect the youth from deportation. It is unclear what can be done on a state level, however. The Governor’s office referred to Health and Human Services’ comment to GBH News. A spokesperson said the administration had spoken with the petition creator and spoke to her again on Friday.

“I’m hoping that they’ll be able to either connect me with the right contacts in order to find procedural safeguards for these kids or get the word out there to people to know that this is happening right here in Massachusetts,” said Grace.

text:
A Harris County grand jury on Friday indicted an U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon in connection with an Oct. 10 crash in northwest Houston that left an immigrant wailing in pain from a broken leg after he was hit by the agent’s SUV, according to the Harris County District Attorney's Office.

Mario Alberto Morales, 33, is believed to be the first federal agent to be charged in Texas over an incident related to the agency’s recent ramped up enforcement actions during the Trump administration. It represents a rare instance of a state prosecutor pursuing charges against immigration authorities.

During a news conference announcing the charge, Teare said Morales "aggressively" steered his vehicle into Miguel Parra Hernandez, seriously injuring him. Parra Hernandez, 48, who hails from Mexico, is a construction worker who had been in Houston for decades without a criminal record or deportation order.

Teare, a former vehicular crimes prosecutor, said "the case is as clear as any that I've ever prosecuted or investigated.

"As long as I am district attorney, this office will prosecute any law enforcement officer who violates the law," Teare said. "An ICE badge does not give you free reign to injure, kill, or violate the constitutional rights of anyone.”

David Lindenmuth, a McAllen-based attorney representing Morales, criticized the indictment as a rushed "political prosecution" and defended the agent's actions during the chase.

Lindenmuth called the crash an accident and contended Morales had swerved in Parra Hernandez’s direction to avoid an idling truck in front of him. He accused Teare's office of guiding the investigation to the indictment.

Teare “basically told the investigators where he wanted them to go -- and they went there," Lindenmuth said.

MORE ON THIS CASE:Who is Mario Alberto Morales? What to know about ICE agent accused of hitting Houston immigrant with car

Lindenmuth said Morales, whom he described as a military veteran and pastor, is in the Houston area and is expected to surrender himself once the case is assigned to a court. He was placed on administrative leave from ICE following the incident.

Lindenmuth expects proceedings that could remove Morales' state prosecution to federal court as the agent is a federal employee. Similar legal maneuvers have taken place in prosecutions involving other federal law enforcement officers.

Following the indictment, U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz in Houston mirrored Lindenmuth's sentiment that Teare targeted the agent.

"The Harris County District Attorney now appears determined to put a different federal agent's scalp on the wall," Reitz said in a statement. "This time he's pursuing what looks like a political prosecution of an ICE agent for doing his job — exactly what his allies have been agitating for."

Reitz said he conducted his own review of the evidence and declined to pursue federal charges.

An unidentified ICE spokesman called the indictment a "political stunt by Houston sanctuary politicians" and called the allegations that Morales intentionally hit Parra Hernandez "reckless and false."

Morales is accused of severely injuring the 48-year-old Parra Hernandez, a Mexican immigrant who worked as a construction worker in Houston, during a chase around 7:30 a.m. on Oct. 10 through a strip mall parking lot at the intersection of Texas 6 and Clay Road.

Morales is alleged to have driven his Jeep Grand Cherokee into Parra Hernandez, who has been recovering at a rehabilitation facility under the watch of ICE agents since the crash.

The crash was investigated by the Harris County Sheriff's Office, which responded to the scene after ICE called an ambulance for Parra Hernandez.

MORE ON THIS CASE: Search warrant details Harris County investigation into ICE agent for crash that injured Houston immigrant

Harris County Sheriff Ed Gonzalez, who joined Teare at the news conference, said the indictment was an example of holding law enforcement officers responsible for upholding their "extraordinary authority."

“Our responsibility is not to be guided by politics or public pressure," Gonzalez said. "Our responsibility is to follow the facts, uphold the law, and do what is right.”

ICE agent was wearing body camera

The indictment coincided with an unusual step by Teare's office to make public evidence in the case before a trial or other court proceedings. The office shared portions of a 911 call that Morales made following the crash, as well as footage from his body-worn camera.

Teare credited the use of the body-worn camera for allowing the investigation to progress sooner for a grand jury to issue an indictment in less than a month.

The agent's body-worn camera footage, as well as security video from a nearby business, showed Morales' vehicle going after the occupants of a white pick-up truck that came to a stop on the wrong side of the road. The two men inside then got out of the driver's side door and bolted.

Moments later, Morales jumped the elevated median of Clay Road and turned into a parking lot they ran into.

RELATED: Texas leaders react to ICE agent's indictment in crash that injured immigrant

The surveillance footage from a nearby bakery appeared to show Morales turn into Parra Hernandez as he ran, though a view of the actual collision was obscured by another vehicle that authorities believe isn't connected to the incident.

A former law enforcement official, Bryan Corb, who now works in private investigations, estimated the agent was going anywhere from 20 to 25 mph at the time of the impact after reviewing the surveillance footage.

The body-worn camera showed a closer look at Morales' actions not seen from the surveillance footage, such as Morales notifying other ICE agents that the the two men inside the vehicle were running away on foot. Less than five seconds later, Morales can be seen veering to the left in the direction of Parra Hernandez just moments before striking him.

After the collision, Morales stepped out of the Jeep and in Spanish asked Parra Hernandez, who was on the ground and crying out in pain, “where’s the other one” before telling him to show him his hand.

Parra Hernandez then turned on his back and said, “You ran over me.” Parra Hernandez later screamed in pain “my foot.”

"He got hit with a car, bro," Morales told another ICE agent. "I was coming in and I hit him with the car."

The other man Morales sought managed to escape as other authorities rushed to the scene. He remains in the country and not in ICE custody, Teare said.

'He hit my car'

During Friday's press conference, Teare also played parts of Morales' 911 call that he made seeking an ambulance for Parra Hernandez's injuries.

“I tried to get around him and he hit my car,” Morales told the dispatcher. “He’s fine, he’s just complaining of the pain”

As Parra Hernandez’s screams can be heard in the background, Morales told the dispatcher that he wanted to move the injured man to his government vehicle. The dispatcher told Morales not to move him and to wait for paramedics to arrive.

Representatives with FIEL Houston, an immigrant rights group, reported that Parra Hernandez's leg was broken in three places and required surgery in the days after the crash.

MORE COVERAGE: Man struck by ICE vehicle lived in Houston more than 30 years

Throughout the chase, Morales had two detainees in the back of his Jeep that have since been deported. The video doesn't make clear that the men are there, and they're never heard in the footage shared by Teare's office.

Investigators went to Port Isabel to interview one of the men, José Presa Cañada, before they were removed from the country, Teare said.

The other detainee was identified by NBC News and Telemundo as Luis Delfin Martinez. They were arrested earlier that morning before Parra Hernandez was hit.

Teare previously said it would be against most law enforcement agency protocols for a police officer to participate in a vehicle chase with detained individuals aboard.

Rare indictment of federal agent

Morales’ indictment is a rare case of state prosecutors seeking charges against federal agents who injure, or even kill, people in the line of duty.

However, the charges aren’t without precedent.

Earlier this year, prosecutors in Minneapolis charged an ICE agent, Christian Castro, with assault and making a false statement after he allegedly fired a gun through a home’s front door and shot a man in the leg. He was also indicted on charges of lying to the FBI.

In February, after Cameron County prosecutors in South Texas presented evidence, a grand jury declined to indict federal agents over the March 2025 killing of Ruben Ray Martinez. He was fatally shot by agents with a Department of Homeland Security subagency near a traffic accident scene in South Padre Island.

Investigation into ICE shooting of Salgado continues

Morales’ indictment comes as Teare’s office continues to investigate ICE agents who were involved in the July shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo.

Salgado was shot at the end of a chase through Houston’s East End. In the immediate aftermath of the shooting, DHS claimed Salgado “weaponized” his vehicle against the agents pursuing him. That claim was disputed by three men who were in Salgado’s van when he was shot.

The men, including Salgado’s brother, were held in ICE custody for days before being ordered released from custody by federal judges. All three men were later spotted entering a grand jury area of Houston’s downtown courthouse in September, but weeks have passed with no news of an indictment.

The grand jury that is believed to have heard evidence about the Salgado shooting had been scheduled to end its term on Friday, but a district court judge granted their request to extend their term for 90 days.

Teare expects evidence gathering and evaluation of the Sagaldo shooting to end before Thanksgiving.

text:
The U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement flights that have been happening almost daily in recent months at Akron-Canton Airport are soon coming to an end.

The private contractor handling Homeland Security deportation flights at the Akron-Canton Airport has announced its intentions to stop servicing those flights at the end of November, airport officials said Oct. 28.

For nearly six months, prison buses have been arriving almost daily at the Avflight hangars on West Airport Drive to transfer Immigration and Customs Enforcement detainees to Eastern Air Express, Air Wisconsin and Global X jets usually headed to Alexandria, Louisiana. Alexandria is the site of a major immigration detention facility and serves as a primary hub for deportations out of the country.

The flights have drawn protesters, who hold signs like “Ice out,” “Immigrants are welcome here,” and “Stop ICE flights.”

“Akron-Canton Airport (CAK) has been made aware that Avflight has notified the ICE flight operator, AEG Fuels, of its decision to discontinue providing ground-handling services at CAK effective November 30, 2026. ICE flights will cease from CAK beyond that date,” airport Vice President Lisa Dalpiaz said in an email Oct. 28.

Avflight, based in Ann Arbor, Michigan, and the private contractor that manages ICE flights, AEG Fuels based in Miami, did not respond immediately to questions.

Avflight is a major operator at the airport with additional hangars on the east side servicing dozens of private planes daily.

Deportation flights began at Akron-Canton at the end of April when Youngstown Warren Regional Airport closed a portion of its longest runway and tarmac for repairs.

Flights were expected to return there when work was completed in August, but that did not happen until a Sept. 29 collision of two Eastern Air Express planes outside the Avflight facility at the Akron-Canton Airport.

The tip of one wing scraped a stabilizer wing on the rear of the other and both planes had to be sidelined for inspection and repairs.

For two weeks, deportation flights were moved to Youngstown Warren until both 737s were repaired and removed from Akron-Canton. On the day before President Donald Trump was to arrive at Youngstown Warren for a campaign rally Oct. 12, planes were transferred from Youngstown Warren to Akron-Canton, as were daily flights.

Since then, at least 20 Eastern Air Express Boeing 737s and Air Wisconsin CRJ200s have landed at the airport in the city of Green, according to the fight-tracking application FlightAware.

The Western Reserve Port Authority, which manages the Youngstown Warren airport, said it was not aware of the Akron-Canton developments and referred questions to the private operator at the airport that serviced ICE flights in the past. The private contractor, JetsFBO, did not respond immediately, nor has it responded to any previous requests of the last two months.

Meanwhile, Akron-Canton officials learned that the bills for landing fees sent to the three charter companies will not be paid. The airport had accumulated more than $46,000 in landing fees through September.

The Federal Aviation Administration in a memo released in early 2026 said that private contractors working for the government would not be required to pay landing fees.

Airport officials said that the loss is insignificant.

The Akron-Canton airport authority has been the only organization forthcoming with information since news coverage began in July, though officials have maintained an arms length from the deportation activity.

Officials said that as a public agency and partly funded by the federal government the airport cannot obstruct any legal business activity that fits with the airport’s purposes. However, they said that they had no intention of trying to convince deportation contractors to stay at the airport because it did not fit their long-term business model.

Doug Oplinger is a retired Akron Beacon Journal reporter and editor. He can be emailed at oplingerdoug@gmail.com

text:
When Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents killed Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis, thousands of people nationwide took action. Many took to the streets to protest. Others posted on social media, or called or wrote to their elected officials.

The First Amendment protects all these activities, and no one who engages in these nonviolent forms of protest should face fear, intimidation, or consequences for exercising their right to speak out.

That’s why two New Yorkers who expressed their anger over ICE’s killings were shocked when federal agents tracked them down and gave them official warnings that what they did was potentially illegal.

It’s also why we sued for all records relating to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) investigation into one of these New Yorker’s social media posts.

DHS’ actions make clear that going after these individuals was not about protecting federal agents. It was an effort to scare them into shutting their mouths. These scare tactics from the Trump administration are unlawful and undermine our most basic freedoms.

A Post, an Email – Then a Knock at the Door

On January 8, the day after ICE agents shot and killed Renee Good in Minneapolis, Syracuse-based activist Paigelynne Gonyea posted a photo of the officer who killed Good. She added the following caption: “The ICE agent who shot and killed Renee Good in broad daylight has been identified as Jonathan Ross by the Minnesota Star Tribune. I think today is a great day for Jonathan to be indicted!” She had every right to publish the post, which constitutes protected speech under the First Amendment.

More than five months later, Gonyea was working at a polling site when she received a voicemail from a DHS agent who said he was at her home. He had come to talk to her about a post she made that he said “doxxed” a federal agent. A group of agents then arrived at the polling site to speak with Gonyea. They produced a copy of her post and a document labeled “WARNING NOTICE” that explained it is illegal to make “restricted personal information” about a federal official “publicly available.” The agents asked Gonyea to sign the document. She refused.

DHS later claimed that in a different post, a copy of which only they have produced, Gonyea shared Jonathan Ross’ address. Gonyea denies having made such a post and the post could not be found on her account. And because no media outlet found the post, and agents did not show Gonyea the post when they confronted her, we have serious questions about whether DHS may have fabricated it.

That’s why we’ve filed our lawsuit. We want to understand the basis for DHS’ assertion that Gonyea’s social media activity constituted “a federal crime,” and we want to prevent them from chilling protected speech by coming after people just for speaking out against ICE’s violence.

What happened to Gonyea is not an isolated incident. On the same day agents confronted Gonyea at the polling site, they came looking for David Streever at his Rochester home. Five months earlier, Streever had written an email to acting ICE director Todd Lyons in which he warns Lyons will be “tormented” by having protected murderous agents and “will never know peace.”

Like Gonyea, Streever wasn’t home when agents arrived with a warning similar to the one Gonyea received. He was returning from vacation with his 7-year-old daughter. Another agent later tracked Streever down at the hotel where he and his daughter were staying and left a business card at the front desk.

Fighting to Protect the Freedom of Speech

The impact of these threats extends far beyond one email or one Instagram post. Left unchecked, these won’t be the last times DHS threatens people who speak out against ICE’s killings. Countless others will be scared into silence.

At a moment when ICE agents are flooding our streets and shooting people in broad daylight, we must fight back against any effort to muffle protest.
