text:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia must adopt a more comprehensive approach to tackle illegal immigration, as repatriating undocumented foreign nationals alone will not provide a lasting solution, says Tan Sri Lee Lam Thye.

The Alliance for a Safe Community chairman said repatriating 45,597 foreign nationals in the first nine months of this year was a significant step that would help ease overcrowding at immigration detention depots.

However, he said the focus must also be on preventing the problem from recurring by dismantling human smuggling syndicates and taking action against those who facilitate and profit from illegal immigration.

"If the syndicates, middlemen, unscrupulous recruitment agents and employers who facilitate and profit from illegal immigration are not effectively dealt with, undocumented migrants will continue finding ways to enter and remain in the country," he said when contacted on Friday (Oct 30).

Lee said Malaysia needed an integrated strategy involving stronger enforcement, improved border security, better detention depot management, a review of foreign worker recruitment practices and greater regional cooperation.

He said enforcement efforts should focus on the masterminds behind illegal immigration, including networks involved in human smuggling and trafficking, providing fake documents, facilitating illegal border crossings and arranging unlawful employment.

He also stressed that employers who knowingly hired undocumented workers must be held accountable, rather than allowing action to focus solely on the migrants.

On border security, Lee called for greater use of modern surveillance technology, intelligence-sharing and coordinated operations involving the Immigration Department, police, Malaysian Maritime Enforcement Agency and other relevant agencies.

He said vulnerable entry points, particularly along coastal areas and land borders, required greater attention.

Lee also called for improvements to immigration detention depot management, stressing that the welfare, safety, health and human dignity of detainees must not be overlooked.

"Overcrowding, inadequate sanitation, insufficient medical attention and prolonged detention are matters requiring urgent attention.

"Every detainee should receive proper medical screening, timely healthcare, adequate food and clean living conditions," he said.

He proposed a more efficient digital case management system to monitor detainees' identities, legal status, documentation and repatriation arrangements.

Independent monitoring and greater transparency should also be encouraged to ensure accountability and prevent misconduct, he added.

Lee said the Government should also review the foreign worker recruitment and employment system by addressing weaknesses in existing channels, improving accountability among recruitment agencies and reducing opportunities for exploitation.

A properly regulated foreign worker system, he said, would help reduce demand for undocumented labour.

He further called for stronger cooperation with neighbouring countries, particularly in intelligence-sharing, border surveillance, identification and repatriation arrangements, noting that illegal immigration and human smuggling were transnational issues.

Lee emphasised that firm immigration enforcement and respect for human rights were not mutually exclusive.

"Malaysia has every right and responsibility to protect its national sovereignty, security and the integrity of its immigration system.

"At the same time, all individuals in detention must be treated humanely and with dignity, regardless of their immigration status," he said.

He said the success of the country's immigration policy should not be measured solely by the number of undocumented migrants arrested or repatriated, but by how effectively illegal entry was prevented, smuggling networks dismantled and opportunities for illegal employment eliminated.

"Malaysia needs a sustainable solution, not merely a temporary reduction in the number of undocumented migrants in the country," he added.

text:
SCOTT DETROW, HOST:

A new term at the Supreme Court is just getting started, but one theme is already clear. Immigration will dominate the justices' time. NPR's Carrie Johnson reports.

CARRIE JOHNSON, BYLINE: University of Virginia law professor Amanda Frost counts a half dozen immigration cases on the high court calendar, with more on the way.

AMANDA FROST: It's looking to be a blockbuster term for immigration law.

JOHNSON: She says the Trump administration has been pushing the envelope to stretch old laws to do drastic new things.

FROST: This administration is trying to rewrite immigration law without actually getting Congress to do so.

JOHNSON: Congress has failed to act on immigration for decades. So presidents from both parties have used executive action to advance their agenda. Chad Maisel, a former official in the Trump Justice Department, says immigration has been top of mind for the president since his first political campaign.

CHAD MAISEL: Part of the reason why we're seeing so much of this is that that was Trump's promise to the American people that he was going to take border enforcement seriously.

JOHNSON: A Justice Department spokesman says the administration's approach is, quote, "grounded in common sense measures that uphold both the law and the integrity of our borders." Chad Maisel says if history is a guide, the president and his policies are in line for some significant victories.

MAISEL: The president has an unprecedented track record of success at the Supreme Court and nowhere is that more true than when we're talking about the immigration docket and the immigration cases.

JOHNSON: But civil liberties and immigrant rights groups say the human cost of Trump's tough enforcement could be devastating. Trina Realmuto is executive director at the National Immigration Litigation Alliance. She's been fighting for migrants at risk of being deported to third countries where they have no prior ties.

TRINA REALMUTO: They have families, they have jobs, and under this policy, they are being abruptly and suddenly ripped from their communities and their loved ones and being sent to third countries.

JOHNSON: A lower court judge has ruled the migrants need a chance to argue they could face torture or persecution before they're deported. But the Supreme Court has repeatedly bigfooted that judge in Massachusetts and allowed those deportations to proceed for now. The administration says it won assurances from third countries that the migrants will not be abused. But Trina Realmuto says her class members have routinely described being detained abroad by armed guards in what she calls horrendous living conditions.

REALMUTO: What we know is that those so-called assurances aren't worth the piece of paper that they're written on.

JOHNSON: The justices are set to hear the case about third country removals in December. Legal experts say a separate immigration case will be among the most important of the term. That case revolves around the president's effort to use mandatory detention for migrants without giving them access to a bond hearing. Michael Tan of the American Civil Liberties Union explains.

MICHAEL TAN: The policy at issue in these cases is truly a radical break with the law. For decades, it's been universally understood, including by the first Trump administration, that immigrants who are living in the country and detained for a deportation proceeding generally have the right to seek release at a bond hearing before an immigration judge.

JOHNSON: Last July, Tan says, the Trump administration declared those immigrants would be locked up even if they were in the process of seeking legal status.

TAN: If allowed, this rule would literally subject millions of immigrants to mandatory detention, amounting to the largest mandatory detention regime in U.S. history.

JOHNSON: Meanwhile the solicitor general has asked the justices to accept another set of immigration cases about an effort to revoke visas for scholars at Georgetown and Columbia University. The administration says their presence in the U.S. compromises the nation's foreign policy. They say they were being targeted for their speech, which should be protected by the First Amendment. Former Columbia student Mahmoud Khalil put it this way recently.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

MAHMOUD KHALIL: Our question is simple. Can the government weaponize immigration laws to punish someone's speech, then tell federal court that they have no power to step in?

JOHNSON: The high court could weigh whether to hear the case sometime next year. Carrie Johnson, NPR News.

(SOUNDBITE OF EMOTIONAL ORANGES SONG, "TALK ABOUT US") Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.

text:
A deported immigrant who was profiled in a CalMatters story earlier this week failed to disclose his criminal record and deportation history to the news organization.

CalMatters learned of his background through a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement social media post attacking the news organization Thursday.

ICE’s X (Twitter) account said Luis Arreguin had been deported five times and had “a criminal history including aggravated assault with a weapon, firearms offenses, and DUI,” and said that CalMatters failed to include that context in its story published Wednesday.

CalMatters editor in chief Kristen Go said the nonprofit news outlet’s reporter tried, twice, to reach ICE’s media team over a period of six days, with no response. The reporter also looked into Arreguin’s background in a court database and a public records database, neither of which turned up the records ICE described.

“We always want to believe what our sources tell us, but as journalists, we also take steps to verify that information,” Go said. “In this case, we did a background check and reached out to ICE two times. It wasn’t until after our story ran that ICE decided to provide the information we had requested.

“We believe in transparency from the people we cover and extend that standard to our reporting as well.”

Arreguin was arrested on an assault charge in Fresno County one year ago. The District Attorney’s Office declined to prosecute him and did not press charges, a spokesperson said.

The reporter, Wendy Fry, sent ICE’s media team seven questions about Arreguin’s immigration history on the evening of Oct. 21 seeking the legal basis for Arreguin’s deportation and the basic facts of his detention.

“We did not find any recent criminal history for Mr. Arreguin, did ICE or the federal government consider him a threat to public safety. If so, why?” Fry asked in the email.

The rest of the questions sought to confirm elements of Arreguin’s account of his detention and deportation flight.

Fry sent a follow-up email to ICE the following Tuesday “Circling this back on top. Our story is publishing tomorrow.”

Go said Fry received no response to those questions.

In her story, Fry quoted Arreguin family members, who repeated his account. CalMatters has reached out to them, and to Arreguin, for comment but has received no response.

Reached Thursday, Arreguin’s daughter said her father was focused on describing his ordeal in his interview with the reporter and did not intend to conceal his deportation and criminal history.

On Thursday, a day after Fry’s story published, a Fox News reporter wrote on social media that he was told by sources in the federal government that Arreguin has been deported five times.

Exactly 30 minutes later, ICE quoted the Fox News reporter’s message in its own social media post.

“We’d like to believe that government agencies operate in good faith — but there is a valid question as to why ICE waited until after publication and even so, (did) not contact the reporter directly,” Go said.

ICE did not immediately respond to questions about its response from CalMatters, or whether the social media team has access to records that are unavailable to the media team responding to reporter requests.

The agency has still not responded to Fry’s initial questions.

Edward Wasserman, a journalism professor and former dean of UC Berkeley Graduate School of Journalism, said it’s impossible to know whether an agency as large as ICE “deliberately stonewalled.”

“It’s dangerous to speculate whether they had a motive,” Wasserman said.

From a “hard-nosed PR perspective,” Wasserman said, the strategy of releasing information after a story published doesn’t help an agency’s cause.

“It doesn’t really serve their own purposes,” he said.

text:
By Dan Israel/Hudson County View

On July 24th, Jersey City resident Raul Raagas, 62, was pulled over for a traffic violation in Palisades Park before being arrested and transferred to the Hudson County Correctional Facility (HCCF) in Kearny on an outstanding warrant for failing to pay child support.

While Raagas was later released the same day after a virtual court hearing, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detained him shortly afterwards. He was taken to an ICE processing center before being transferred to the CoreCivic Elizabeth Detention Center in Elizabeth.

On August 21st, Raagas was transferred to the Adams County Correctional Center in Mississippi.

After 10 weeks in ICE custody, Raagas was eventually granted bond on September 30th, and is now back home in Jersey City.

Hudson County Executive Craig Guy told HCV he was first notified back in September that an inmate at the Hudson County Correctional Facility was improperly transferred by Correctional Center staff to the custody of ICE agents.

Guy said he subsequently requested a thorough investigation of the incident, to be conducted by both the Hudson County Law Department and the Department of Corrections.

According to Guy, the investigation confirmed Corrections Department personnel notified ICE and facilitated the transfer of the inmate to ICE.

Guy underscored not only that this was in violation of the State of New Jersey’s Immigrant Trust Directive, but also his executive order banning federal immigration authorities from county-owned property, as HCV first reported.

As for the corrections officers involved? Their discipline is still pending but they have been reassigned, Guy said.

“We are currently exploring disciplinary actions for the personnel involved in this investigation and have taken immediate corrective action in assigning the personnel in question to a new post. I take the results of this investigation very seriously,” Guy said in a statement.

“Hudson County has been at the forefront of protecting the most vulnerable members of our community, from developing Executive Orders to keep our communities safe from unlawful federal immigration tactics to bolstering the county budget with funding for constituent legal services, rental assistance, and food security programs.”

Guy touted actions his administration has taken against ICE, including forming two committees on the topic- the Safe Communities Committee and the Immigrant Community Safety Committee, as well as adopting a $1.3 million budget amendment which was approved by the board and pushed by Guy after advocates rallied for $2 million to provide rental assistance, legal services, and food security programs.

According to Guy, as a result of this investigation the Corrections Department has strengthened its procedures and begun additional training.

He said the department also established new policy guidelines such as supervisory review, senior leadership approval, documentation requirements, and controls over ICE access to the facility.

Additionally, Guy said he has ordered an investigation into all of ICE’s interactions with the Corrections Department since the implementation of his executive order banning federal immigration authorities from county-owned property.

“We are committed to full transparency and reinforcing our policies to ensure federal immigration authorities follow the law when conducting operations,” he added.

title: When The Government Loses In Court, It Should Not Get Unlimited Do-Overs
description:

text:
Now imagine that you want to engage in the very same conduct as your neighbor, inside the same judicial district where the government’s prohibition was just enjoined. The government would rely on the same law and the same legal arguments to prevent you from doing so.

You might reasonably think the government has already had its chance in court and lost — and that the matter has therefore been resolved in your favor.

Under current Supreme Court precedent, however, the federal government gets another chance. In fact, it gets a new chance each and every time someone wants to vindicate the same right under the same unconstitutional law.

Our firm, the Texas Public Policy Foundation’s Center for the American Future, represents two Texans, David McCann and Kirk Launius, in a case challenging that extraordinary privilege.

The underlying dispute involves whether law-abiding citizens may carry otherwise lawful firearms with them when they visit a post office. Federal law and Postal Service regulations prohibit carrying firearms on postal property, including by people lawfully carrying them for self-defense — a recognized constitutional right.

In 2025, several plaintiffs challenged those restrictions in the Northern District of Texas. They succeeded, and a federal judge held that the government could not enforce the restrictions upon ordinary, lawful firearm possession at post offices.

Regardless of what one thinks about the specific ruling on firearms, the matter exposed a broader unfair procedural problem. Under current case law, that judgment only protected those specific plaintiffs who brought that specific lawsuit. Even though the Northern District of Texas had stated and applied its opinion on the unconstitutionality of the restrictions, others in the same district still faced the same prohibitions.

Regardless of what one thinks of the specific firearms ruling, the case exposed a broader procedural problem. Under current case law, the judgment protected only the plaintiffs who brought that particular lawsuit. So even after the Northern District of Texas held the challenged rules unconstitutional, others in the very same district still faced the same restrictions.

McCann and Launius were among those still affected. So, we filed a second lawsuit on their behalf in the same federal district. We raised a question far beyond firearms: How many times should the federal government get to litigate the same issue after it loses?

Ordinarily, our legal system has an answer. The doctrine of collateral estoppel, also called issue preclusion, prevents a party from repeatedly litigating an issue that has already been fully and fairly decided against it.

The principle is straightforward: litigation must eventually end. A losing party generally cannot keep demanding a new adjudication of the same issue in hopes that a different judge will give it a better answer.

But in 1984, the Supreme Court created a special exception to this doctrine for the federal government.

In United States v. Mendoza, the Court held that the federal government generally cannot be subjected to what lawyers, in a mouthful, call “nonmutual offensive collateral estoppel.” In other words, someone who was not a party to the first case normally cannot use the government’s previous loss to prevent it from relitigating the same issue against him or her.

The Court offered practical reasons for creating this exception for the federal government. Federal litigation occurs across the country, and important legal questions should be allowed to develop as the government defends its position in multiple courts. The government also should not feel compelled, the Court thought, to appeal every adverse district-court ruling for fear that one loss will bind it forever nationwide.

Those concerns may explain the Court’s reasoning, but they come at a real cost: they allow the federal government to keep relitigating issues it has already lost, forcing Americans into the uphill battle of perennially fighting for the same recognized rights. In this way, the federal government effectively holds a Sword of Damocles over the nation even after judges rule against it.

The Supreme Court’s recent decision in Trump v. CASA makes that problem even more consequential. Whereas Mendoza was a case about avoiding duplicative litigation, CASA was a case about remedies after litigation. The Court in CASA held that, in general, one judge may not simply block a federal policy throughout the whole country. Relief usually extends only to the parties who actually brought the case. So one person can win, while everyone else remains subject to the same government action.

That problem has become more serious after the Supreme Court’s recent decision in Trump v. CASA. Whereas Mendoza limits a plaintiff’s ability to avoid redundant litigation, CASA limits the relief a plaintiff can obtain after winning it. In CASA, the Court held that, in general, one judge may not simply block a federal policy throughout the whole country, because relief usually extends only to the parties who actually brought the case. The result is that one person can defeat an unlawful government action, and yet everyone else remains subject to its force — and under Mendoza, if prosecuted, must litigate the same issue in its entirety.

Our case is about whether Mendoza should really require that result for everyone else within the same federal district.

McCann and Launius are not trying to take one district judge’s decision and impose it nationwide. They sued in the very same federal district in which the government had already litigated and lost the issue. Yet the district court concluded that Mendoza categorically foreclosed our collateral-estoppel argument.

McCann and Launius are not trying to take one district judge’s decision and impose it nationwide. They brought suit to vindicate their rights before the same federal district court that had already ruled against the government on the same issue. Yet the district court concluded that under Mendoza, that didn’t matter; McCann and Launius must bear the burden of litigating the entire issue again.

We are appealing that ruling to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit.

And events since these cases were filed have made the problem even clearer.

The government has since dropped its appeal of the original post office ruling, leaving that decision in place. And the Trump administration’s own Office of Legal Counsel has concluded that the challenged restrictions are indeed unlawful as applied.

So the government lost the underlying issue in court, abandoned its appeal, and has now itself concluded that the challenged regulatory prohibition violates the law. Yet under the district court’s reading of Mendoza, another citizen in the same district still cannot invoke that earlier judgment to protect himself from litigating the issue all over again.

That result is not necessary to preserve healthy disagreement among courts. It is disorder within the same court system.

And after CASA, the problem extends far beyond this case. If judicial relief ordinarily protects only the parties who sue, while Mendoza permits the federal government to relitigate the same issue against every new plaintiff, then constitutional rights are effectively dispensed by the government at sufferance — even within the same federal district.

The alternative does not have to mean that one district judge dictates federal law to the entire country. Different courts may remain free to disagree, legal questions may develop through the judicial system, and appellate courts may establish binding precedent for broader jurisdictions, as CASA contemplated.

But there is a vast difference between allowing different courts to disagree and requiring the same court system to reconsider the same issue every time a new citizen walks through the courthouse door.

Mendoza described itself as protecting the legitimate development of federal law. In the post-CASA world, it should not become a rule of perpetual relitigation.

When the government loses, it should have the same basic choices other litigants have: accept the result or appeal it.

It should not have an endless supply of second chances.

text:
As the sun dipped low outside the Otay Mesa Detention Center, Pedro Rios and Adriana Jasso laid out the cempasúchil flowers carefully, the brilliant orange petals staining their fingertips.

Nearby, organizers and artists had built a ceremonial altar decorated with candles, calaveras and monarch butterflies.

“We’re breaking up the cempasúchil flower, the marigolds and creating a path,” Rios said, cradling the flowers in his arms. “To the ceremonial altar that recognizes them as human beings.”

On Wednesday evening, a little over a dozen people gathered for a vigil outside the U.S. Customs and Immigration Enforcement (ICE) facility, which sits along the southern edge of San Diego County.

Vigil participants were there to celebrate Día de Muertos, the traditional holiday with deep roots throughout Mexico and Central America — and to honor the dozens of people that ICE agents have shot or who have died in the agency’s custody this year.

The event came just days after a 43-year-old immigrant from Guatemala named Guillermo Pascual Verganza died on Saturday in a cell at Otay Mesa.

Verganza was the 60th person to die in ICE detention since President Donald Trump took office again and launched a deadly mass deportation campaign. That’s according to Austin Kocher, a Syracuse University professor who tracks deaths in ICE custody.

In a statement earlier this week, ICE said it is investigating Verganza’s death. (The agency incorrectly identified Verganza as “Roberto Jimenez Gutierrez.”)

San Diego County officials have demanded an independent investigation into Verganza’s death.

Wednesday’s vigil was organized by several immigrants’ rights groups, including the American Friends Service Committee, the nonprofit human rights organization where Rios and Jasso work.

Since 2020, the organization has held an annual Día de Muertos gathering outside the detention center on Oct. 28. Traditionally, that date is reserved for honoring people who have died from sudden accidents, tragic events or violence.

Jasso said they wanted to call particular attention to CoreCivic, the private prison contractor that runs day-to-day operations at Otay Mesa. It’s one of several companies that make money by detaining immigrants on behalf of the U.S. government.

“CoreCivic has the profits of billions of dollars a year from the cruelty of holding people,” Jasso said. “It is important for us to be here and to make sure that CoreCivic knows that we know — and that ICE also understands — that they are responsible for the lives.”

Verganza is the first person that ICE has reported dying at Otay Mesa since the beginning of Trump’s second term. Two other immigrants, Huabing Xie and Luis Beltrán Yañez-Cruz, died while being held at the Imperial Regional Detention Facility in neighboring Imperial County.

Jasso said ICE has tried to criminalize Verganza in its public statements.

Earlier this week, the agency alleged that he was arrested multiple times for charges including child abuse and battery against a spouse. ICE said he was also convicted for selling liquor to a minor. (Verganza’s family has denied those allegations.)

“The agency seems to make a clear effort to … present people as criminal, alien rather than human beings,” Jasso said. “We didn't hear about the fact that, from what we understand now, he was a father of five children — that he had a life, dreams and aspirations just like many other people.”

Through their vigils, she said, they hope to humanize Verganza and others who have died in ICE custody.

May, another attendee who did not share her last name, pointed out that Verganza’s death was the second in the span of just five days. Last week, 48-year-old Luis Sandoval died amid an ongoing hunger strike at a detention center in Georgia.

“We can’t become desensitized,” May said. “We can't let at least that part of our humanity be taken away.”

text:
A transgender woman in New York says Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents wrongly arrested her at an airport and held her in a men’s detention facility. She says she was released after government officials were satisfied with an inspection of her bottom surgery.

Clara Tan said in a Facebook post on Tuesday that four men identifying themselves as ICE agents approached her as she headed toward the taxi stand after landing at Frederick Douglass Greater Rochester International Airport around midnight.

“As I was exiting the terminal and heading towards the taxi stand, I was accosted by four men who called me by my name. I turned, and did not recognize a single one of them. The tallest, a pipe-cleaner looking fellow with a mildly Snidely Whiplash-esque mustache and some of the deadest eyes I’d ever seen, tells me ‘We’re with ICE and we have a warrant for your arrest,’” Tan posted.

Related: Queer trans ICE protester recounts pepper-spraying, jailing by agents

“Mind you, it’s 12 am, I’ve just been on a cumulative 8 hours of flight and I just want to go home and sleep. So I do what any red blooded American would and say, ‘Can I see the warrant? Do you have any identification?’ Pipely Whiplash says, ‘We can show it to you in the car, just come peacefully.’ Meanwhile, one of his compatriots flashes a wallet, far too quick for anybody to actually confirm its veracity, and they all converge on me.”

Tan said she tried to make a phone call, but the agents tackled her to the asphalt, threw her into the back of a black SUV and drove her to a detention facility in Batavia at speeds she estimated reached 90 mph.

According to Tan, ICE declared she was in the U.S. illegally and not studying at the American Musical and Dramatic Academy, as her visa required. She disputed parts of the agency’s account, including its claim that she entered the country on an unknown date through an unknown entry point. Tan said she had records showing that she flew into New York City on June 18, 2019. She also said she had studied at the academy and that her graduation photos were publicly available online.

Related: Transgender woman alleges abuse inside Arizona ICE detention

Tan, a cosplayer, had been returning home from a trip to Los Angeles to attend an anime concert series that had been canceled because of delays in securing U.S. visas for performers.

Tan said she was taken to an ICE facility and placed in a metal cage, where she spent the night curled up in a rough hemp blanket provided to her, listening to agents make racist jokes. She said she was kept separate from male detainees but eventually concluded she was in a men’s facility because she appeared to be the only woman there.

Tan said she told an agent she was a woman and asked why she was being held in a men’s facility.

“Well, do you have your junk?” the agent asked, according to Tan.

“Not last I checked,” she replied.

Related: Trump administration stops abuse protection for transgender detainees in ICE custody

Tan said the exchange led to a medical examination. She said she was subsequently released from custody with an ankle monitor and a December 8 court date after the examination confirmed she had undergone gender-affirming genital surgery. She said she spent about 18 hours in custody.

“Pre-op trans women are housed there, but not anybody with a vagina,” Tan wrote. “My decision to pursue bottom surgery is why I’m now sitting here, in the emergency room of Strong Memorial Hospital, 90% sure that my left foot is fractured and regaling you all with this tale of weft and woe, instead of living it up on bread and water, seatless toilets and no sinks to wash your hands.”

Representatives for the Department of Homeland Security did not respond to reporters’ questions when Rochester NPR station WXXI requested comment. The Advocate contacted ICE for comment.

Tan said she was sharing her story to put a face to the Trump administration’s mass deportation policies.

“If any of you met me and enjoyed our time together, know that this administration and their policy goals are targeting me specifically,” Tan posted. “I am a part of every single group they’ve singled out to hate. If you need a face to put to this issue, maybe it can be mine. It’s always easier to make sense of something when you have a personal connection to it.”

text:
BUFFALO, N.Y. — With Election Day less than a week away, New York Attorney General Letitia James is warning voters about potential intimidation at polling places, but Republicans are questioning whether her warning is creating unnecessary fear.

James issued a statement Tuesday reminding New Yorkers that armed federal agents, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers, are prohibited from policing polling places under federal law.

"No eligible New Yorker should stay home on Election Day because of fear," James said. "I want New York voters to know the law is on their side. Armed federal agents are not allowed at polling places, and no one can use a badge, a weapon, or a threat to stop you from voting."

But the Department of Homeland Security has already said ICE is not planning operations targeting polling locations.

That has not stopped the political disagreement over whether New York should be preparing for potential interference.

Erie County Republican Committee Chairman Michael Kracker accused James of using her office to unnecessarily alarm voters.

"I think she’s trying to scare voters. Frankly, if she weren’t the attorney general, she’d probably be investigating herself for voter intimidation," Kracker said.

Kracker argued the warning could have the opposite effect of what James intends, potentially discouraging people from casting their ballots.

He also accused Democrats of turning the issue into a political fight ahead of the Nov. 3 election.

Democratic Rep. Tim Kennedy sees it differently.

Kennedy, who has already clashed with Homeland Security over plans to expand the ICE detention facility in Batavia, questioned whether the Trump administration’s assurances can be trusted.

"The fact of the matter is, there is no place for ICE at the ballot box," Kennedy said. "And so the fact that the Justice Department is not planning on sending them there is at least a positive message. But, you know, we have no trust in their word."

Kennedy expressed confidence in James’ ability to protect voters and ensure ballots are counted.

Despite DHS saying ICE has no plans to target polling places, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has said federal agents could still appear under certain circumstances, including serving a warrant or responding to a specific threat. Whether such actions would be permissible at polling places remains a legal question.

James said her office is coordinating with state and local election officials and law enforcement to address potential intimidation or interference.

There has been no publicly confirmed plan to deploy ICE agents to New York polling places for the election.

The attorney general also noted that the Department of Justice may send federal election monitors to New York. Those monitors are permitted to observe elections but cannot interfere with voters, challenge their eligibility, or direct poll workers.

Under New York law, local government employees are also prohibited from granting immigration enforcement officers access to polling locations for immigration enforcement purposes without a valid judicial warrant or court order.

Early voting continues through Sunday, Nov. 1, with Election Day scheduled for Tuesday, Nov. 3.

Voters who experience or witness intimidation, harassment, or interference can contact the New York Attorney General’s Election Protection Hotline at 866-390-2992 or file a complaint at electionhotline.ag.ny.gov.

Anyone witnessing an immediate safety threat should contact local law enforcement.

text:
HILLSBORO Ore. (KPTV) - The ACLU of Oregon has filed video with a complaint against the Department of Homeland Security that the group says shows an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent stabbing the tires on a couple’s car after a pursuit that began at a Hillsboro Safeway.

“Our clients were simply trying to get away,” said Kelly Simon, ACLU of Oregon legal director.

According to the ACLU filing, the incident began just before 7 a.m. on Oct. 7. The couple saw what they believed to be an ICE vehicle in their Beaverton neighborhood. Keeping a distance, they followed the vehicle into the parking lot of the Safeway in Hillsboro’s Tanasbourne Village, according to the filing.

Simon said cameras in the couple’s car recorded the events. The couple is staying anonymous out of fear of retaliation.

RELATED:

The couple saw masked officers in vests labeled “ICE” meeting with two other cars in the lot, according to the filing. They yelled “This is ICE” and blew whistles to alert shoppers.

“When they saw that the federal agents took notice of their recording and began to engage them, they tried to disengage, in fact,” Simon said.

The ACLU video shows an agent running after the couple’s car with a shopping cart. Simon said the couple was never given instructions but grew afraid and left.

The car’s video shows the couple being followed out of the parking lot. On Stucki Avenue, lights turn on and one car boxes them in. An agent can be seen from behind stabbing the Tesla’s tire multiple times until it pops. The agents then leave.

The couple pulled over and called 911.

“People are afraid that what they’ve seen on the news is going to happen to them. And understandably so. It’s a quite chilling experience to have a federal officer wearing a mask coming towards you physically. You don’t know what that officer is going to do,” Simon said.

title: Lawsuit seeks to block ICE from hiding locations of detainees with final removal orders
authors: Ryan J. Foley, The Associated Press
description:
Groups that provide legal services to immigrants filed a lawsuit Wednesday seeking to stop the Trump administration's new policy of hiding the locations of tens of thousands of detainees with final deportation orders.
The lawsuit challenges U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's decision, first reported by The Associated Press, to remove the locations of people facing final removal orders from its Online Detainee Locator System and to instruct staff not to reveal their whereabouts.
As of last month, the move affected more than 16,000 of the nearly 69,000 detainees who were in ICE custody.
ICE and its parent agency, the Department of Homeland Security, have not publicly confirmed the change but have said they are prioritizing people with final removal orders for deportation.
Approximately 1.4 million people living in the U.S. are subject to final orders of removal, which means an immigration judge has ruled they should be deported and the decision has been upheld on appeal or not appealed.
text:
Groups that provide legal services to immigrants filed a lawsuit Wednesday seeking to stop the Trump administration's new policy of hiding the locations of tens of thousands of detainees with final deportation orders.

The policy, adopted suddenly last month to expedite deportations, interferes with immigration lawyers’ rights by making it difficult, and sometimes impossible, to locate their clients, according to the lawsuit filed in federal court in Boston. It asks a judge to issue an order blocking the “unlawful and inhumane” change.

“No one should be denied a meaningful opportunity to defend their rights because the government has made it impossible for their lawyer to find them,” said Jacquelynne Bowman, executive director of Greater Boston Legal Services, one of the four groups listed as plaintiffs. “This arbitrary new administrative change leaves hundreds of thousands of people at risk of potentially life-altering consequences without essential legal help."

The lawsuit challenges U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's decision, first reported by The Associated Press, to remove the locations of people facing final removal orders from its Online Detainee Locator System and to instruct staff not to reveal their whereabouts. As of last month, the move affected more than 16,000 of the nearly 69,000 detainees who were in ICE custody.

ICE and its parent agency, the Department of Homeland Security, have not publicly confirmed the change but have said they are prioritizing people with final removal orders for deportation. They have also said they are facing a “historic number of injunctions” from courts blocking their efforts. The agencies have denied that they are disappearing detainees, saying they remain free to make phone calls.

“Illegal aliens in detention have several ways to communicate with their family members and lawyers,” DHS said in a statement responding to the lawsuit. “The appropriate process due to an illegal alien with final deportation orders is removal, plain and simple.”

Since 2010, lawyers and family members have used ICE's online system to track detainees as they get moved from facility to facility through ICE's sprawling detention network.

Approximately 1.4 million people living in the U.S. are subject to final orders of removal, which means an immigration judge has ruled they should be deported and the decision has been upheld on appeal or not appealed.

Those individuals still have several options to challenge the conditions of their detention and looming deportations, including asking to reopen proceedings, seeking relief from removal to third countries and challenging violations of their rights. Federal judges have ruled thousands of times that detainees should be released or granted bond hearings.

Since the change went into effect, lawyers have been unable to find clients and potential clients and have spent “significantly more time” tracking down others, the lawsuit says. Calls to ICE, including to its Detention and Removal Information Line, “lead to long wait times on hold, sudden hang-ups, a general lack of information or no answer at all,” it says.

As a workaround, some lawyers have tried to find their clients through an ICE program that schedules legal calls, but only a small percentage of detention centers use it, the lawsuit says. The result has been delayed or missed legal filings and fewer cases taken, according to the organizations.

The lawsuit argues the change violates the Administrative Procedure Act because it was adopted without explanation and the First Amendment, which protects lawyers' ability to advise people of their legal rights and seek prospective clients.

text:
Immigration detainees held at Indiana’s Miami Correctional Facility are suing state and federal agencies for what they say are inhumane and unconstitutional conditions.

The 72-page court filing details medical neglect, cells flooded with human waste, and abusive punishments detainees claim to have experienced at the maximum security prison used by the Trump administration for its immigration enforcement policies.

The lawsuit also alleges conditions at the facility violate the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendment due process clauses because the detainees are civil detainees, not under criminal convictions, and are facing punitive punishments like lockdowns and solitary confinement.

The ACLU of Indiana and Illinois filed a class action lawsuit Thursday, Oct. 29, in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Indiana. The lawsuit covers the three named plaintiffs and all other detainees at the correctional facility north of Kokomo.

"Frankly, they are experiencing physical decline, potential long-term medical consequences, and, like, severe emotional distress and suffering,” said Katie Hickey, an attorney with the ACLU of Illinois representing the plaintiffs.

Officials with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, ICE and Indiana Department of Correction are listed as plaintiffs. Representatives for the agencies did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The lawsuit comes after continued reports from detainees, lawyers and advocates about the conditions at the prison. This summer Gov. Mike Braun called for an audit to review the private healthcare provider the state contracts to work in the facilities after reports from the IndyStar on delays in medical care for detainees.

Indiana began housing Immigration and Customs Enforcement detainees at Miami Correctional in October 2025 through a two-year contract with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. Miami Correctional is a maximum security facility for men.

Since detainees began to arrive, there have been two reported deaths.

In the lawsuit, plaintiff Cynthia Acevedo said healthcare providers at the facility switched her to a different seizure medication that is ineffective at preventing seizures. Even then, Acevedo, a transgender woman, does not regularly receive the medication and has multiple seizures a week. When she goes to get medical treatment, no Spanish translator is made available.

Sergei Vasenin and Kemoye Muslar, the other plaintiffs, share their experiences of slow and limited medical care and regular solitary confinement and lockdowns.

During a 10-day lockdown, Muslar said his cell flooded over with sewage for three days. He was not provided cleaning supplies or hygiene products.

The detainees also allege guards call them racial slurs, threaten death and physically beat them without any reason.

The lawsuit details a case of a recent suicide attempt by a detainee. It alleges, staff were notified of concerns for the man’s mental health. It goes on to say that guards locked him alone in his cell where he went on to use a cable and hang himself according to witnesses. The lawsuit says the condition and whereabouts of the detainee remain unconfirmed.

The plaintiffs are asking for the court to declare the facility’s medical and mental health care and conditions inadequate and in violation of the the Fifth Amendment and Fourteenth Amendment due process clause.

‘Further litigation forthcoming’

Hickey said she hopes this lawsuit forces changes but also gets answers to what has occurred at Miami Correctional Facility.

“The people who have died, the recent suicide attempt. There’s been no transparency from the government about all of that, so we hope that we can learn a lot more about all of these things in Miami over the next; over the coming months,” Hickey said.

For more than a year religious leaders have gathered monthly at or near the prison to pray for the detainees being held there and their families. André Carson visited Miami Correctional in April demanding answers to the deaths in the facility. After speaking with people held at the prison he said the state needed to end its holding of ICE detainees there.

Other groups including the Indiana Organizing Project have held events across the state calling on the governor to end the contract with ICE or at least not renew it.

Indiana Organizing Project Executive Director Stuart Mora said nothing in the lawsuit surprised him and it comes as conditions fail to improve.

“I think that there will be further litigation forthcoming,” said Mora. “Our team has not seen significant changes in Miami Correctional, since the governor called for an investigation several months ago.”

The ACLU was joined by the National Immigrant Justice Center, Macarthur Justice Center and law firm Dunn Issaacson Rhee in filing the lawsuit on behalf of the detainees.

text:
Image: DHS

Immigration enforcement at churches, synagogues and mosques is back before the courts after a federal appeals court revived a religious freedom lawsuit against the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS). In January 2025, the department scrapped the sensitive locations policy, which for more than thirty years had limited immigration operations at places of worship, schools and funerals. Twenty-seven Judeo-Christian organisations, representing millions of worshippers, sued under the First Amendment, the Religious Freedom Restoration Act and the Administrative Procedure Act. Their congregations serve undocumented immigrants through worship, food pantries, legal advice and job training, now with enforcement left to office-level supervisors’ case-by-case discretion.

From strict approval rules to supervisor discretion: what changed for places of worship

The safeguard dates to 1993, when the government directed immigration authorities to avoid arrests and tightly control investigations at schools, places of worship, funerals and religious ceremonies. According to the appeals court opinion published by Justia, the latest version arrived in 2021 under then-Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas. It told officers to avoid action at or near such places to the fullest extent possible and demanded prior approval from agency headquarters or its delegates. It allowed exceptions only in emergencies such as national security threats, imminent violence, destruction of evidence or hot pursuit of a public safety threat. Acting Secretary Benjamine Huffman replaced it with an instruction to use discretion and common sense. Eleven days later, Acting Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Director Caleb Vitello rejected fixed rules, leaving office-level supervisors to decide case by case, verbally or in writing. The DHS said in a press release that immigrants it classed as criminals could no longer shelter in schools and churches to avoid arrest.

Raids, surveillance and falling attendance: the evidence the faith groups put before the court

The plaintiffs comprise sixteen national or regional denominational bodies and eleven associations, among them the Union for Reform Judaism, the Latino Christian National Network and the Rabbinical Assembly. Their traditions range from Quakers and Mennonites to Catholics, Evangelicals, Pentecostals and United Methodists. Leaders and congregants filed declarations, and members of all but one plaintiff reported falling attendance at services and community events as worshippers feared enforcement. The court record also lists specific incidents after the rescission: a raid at a church linked to a plaintiff, a raid next door to another, a raid at a church outside the lawsuit, and surveillance at or near three plaintiff-linked churches. The North Georgia Conference of the United Methodist Church said in a declaration that agents entered a church daycare office looking for a staff member they believed to be undocumented. The Episcopal Church said agents photographed people queuing at a food pantry hosted by a California congregation.

Why the appeals court rejected a gun-case test and saw a credible threat to worshippers

The district court refused the groups’ request for a temporary order, known as a preliminary injunction, ruling their fears too speculative. Its reasoning turned on standing, the legal right to sue, which requires a harm that is imminent, linked to the policy and fixable by a court. It borrowed a test from firearms cases that asks whether plaintiffs were singled out for enforcement. Bloomberg Law reported that the Justice Department made a similar argument on appeal, saying the groups needed specific information that a particular church was about to be raided. Two judges appeared sceptical at oral argument in early February, with one asking how churches could possibly have such insider knowledge of upcoming operations. Circuit Judge Florence Pan, joined by Circuit Judge Robert Wilkins, wrote for the appeals court that the firearms test does not suit a challenge to an agency policy that burdens religious expression. Applying the Supreme Court’s credible threat standard instead, she wrote that the government had not disavowed enforcement at such places. The government’s own statements said agents believed the rescission would free them to pursue more undocumented immigrants, and operations had begun near plaintiffs’ congregations as a direct result of the change. Reinstating the old guidance, she wrote, need only prevent a single operation at a single congregation. A judicial warrant requirement would force agents to show a judge probable cause, slowing and deterring operations.

Judge Rao’s dissent: The argument that restoring the old memo would not change enforcement

Circuit Judge Neomi Rao argued that the 2021 guidance never limited the government’s legal authority or enforcement discretion, so predicting its effect is speculation. She described its rescission as one relatively minor part of a broader policy of increasing immigration enforcement. The dissent noted that the district court found only one enforcement action at the hundreds of member congregations, and three instances at or near any place of worship nationwide in the first ten weeks. It added that courts cannot direct how the executive branch prioritises enforcement. It also said a judicial warrant requirement would exceed judicial powers and is barred by a federal law limiting lower courts’ power to restrain parts of the immigration code. Pan answered that the dissent rested on a mistaken belief that the old memo was non-binding. Courts generally assume agencies follow their announced policies, she wrote, and otherwise the administration would not have needed to rescind it. The majority added that the lawsuit was filed less than three weeks after the rescission, so even a few incidents point to increased enforcement.

What happens next as the case returns to the district court, and what the ruling leaves open

The split decision, handed down on 20 October 2026, reverses the denial of the temporary order and sends the motion back to the district court for further consideration. It does not decide whether the policy is lawful. The panel rested on a single theory of harm, the threat of immigration enforcement at congregations. It left the groups’ claims about falling attendance, moral dilemmas and security costs undecided. It also declined to say whether a judicial warrant requirement is permissible, because neither side had argued that point.

Maryland and Massachusetts cases test the same policy as scrutiny of immigration tactics grows

Bloomberg Law reported that the ruling arrives amid heightened scrutiny of ICE tactics. Two Americans were fatally shot in Minnesota during an enforcement surge, and congressional gridlock over Democrats’ demands to rein in the agency caused a partial government shutdown and a funding lapse for the DHS earlier this year. Kelsi Brown Corkran of Georgetown Law’s Institute for Constitutional Advocacy and Protection, lead counsel for the religious associations, told the publication by email that the decision was “an important victory for the millions of people of faith” in the coalition. A Justice Department spokesperson declined to comment. Other organisations are challenging the same change in federal courts in Maryland and Massachusetts. In August, six months after oral argument in the Washington case, the United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit upheld a ruling barring federal immigration operations at certain houses of worship. That case was brought by the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting of the Religious Society of Friends, and the order requires the DHS to revert to the 2021 guidance at those plaintiffs’ houses of worship. In February, a Massachusetts federal judge temporarily blocked enforcement, absent emergencies, in or around certain houses of worship that sued, and that case is pending on appeal. The dissent noted that courts hearing similar cases have found plaintiffs likely to succeed on the merits yet refused to order judicial warrants.

Continue Reading

End of Article

text:
A reported archive called "Icepick," published by transparency collective Distributed Denial of Secrets, allegedly contains indexed entries for 41,191 DHS personnel across seven component agencies and 55,603 internal groups. Those figures come from a Help Net Security analysis of the dataset and have not been independently confirmed by DHS. Knowing someone's supervisor, their agency group memberships, and the investigative tools associated with their account is a different order of exposure than a name and work email alone.

Who Shows Up in the Records

Customs and Border Protection dominates the archive, but the reach extends across nearly every major DHS component.

CBP accounts for more than half the indexed entries, according to WIRED's analysis. ICE contributes approximately 10,000 records by WIRED's count, with roughly one-third tied to Homeland Security Investigations; a separate UPI analysis placed the ICE figure closer to 6,600, a discrepancy likely reflecting different inclusion criteria or dataset scope. USCIS adds about 6,200 records, while CISA accounts for nearly 1,000, with more than half of those belonging to contractors.

Why the Group Memberships Are the Sensitive Part

Permission-group labels can suggest access to specific tools or operations, even when membership alone does not confirm participation.

In an identity management system, groups do more than organize people: they can indicate what tools, platforms, or operational programs a person is provisioned to use. WIRED reported that 39 HSI employees appeared in groups whose labels court filings associate with certified undercover operations. Other group names in the archive reportedly reference Title III wiretap programs, communications interception, and a reported Illicit Sensor Intercept Program, though group membership does not confirm that any listed individual participated in those activities.

Surveillance Tools Named in the Records

Palantir's Falcon platform, PenLink, and facial-recognition application Mobile Fortify all appear in the archive's reported tool references.

More than 700 accounts appear in a group referencing Signal, while more than 200 CBP accounts are linked to Mobile Fortify. Affected personnel reportedly span supervisors, tactical staff, intelligence agents, and special-response units, though group association does not establish active use or current access.

How the Data Was Obtained Remains Contested

The source group's account of the breach conflicts with Okta's public statement, leaving the acquisition method unresolved.

DDoSecrets attributed the archive to a DHS Okta login system, citing claims from the source group, which calls itself the Department of Peace. Okta stated publicly that it had no evidence its systems or data were compromised. DHS and the Justice Department did not respond to WIRED's requests for comment; the FBI referred questions back to DHS.

The Risks Security Experts Are Warning About

Cross-referenced with prior breaches and commercial data, even basic work records can enable phishing, impersonation, and operational mapping.

Security experts warn that names and work phone numbers gain significant value when combined with commercial data brokers and previously exposed records. The archive reportedly includes roughly 1,300 ICE enforcement accounts created after July 4, 2025, a period WIRED links to legislation funding 10,000 additional ICE officers; that connection is drawn from the reporting and has not been confirmed against enacted bill text or official agency records.

The Accountability Argument and Its Limits

Publication raises a transparency claim that does not automatically resolve the harm questions created by exposing undercover personnel and contractors.

SCOTT DETROW, HOST:

A new term at the Supreme Court is just getting started, but one theme is already clear. Immigration will dominate the justices' time. NPR's Carrie Johnson reports.

CARRIE JOHNSON, BYLINE: University of Virginia law professor Amanda Frost counts a half dozen immigration cases on the high court calendar, with more on the way.

JOHNSON: She says the Trump administration has been pushing the envelope to stretch old laws to do drastic new things.

FROST: This administration is trying to rewrite immigration law without actually getting Congress to do so.

JOHNSON: Congress has failed to act on immigration for decades. So presidents from both parties have used executive action to advance their agenda. Chad Maisel, a former official in the Trump Justice Department, says immigration has been top of mind for the president since his first political campaign.

CHAD MAISEL: Part of the reason why we're seeing so much of this is that that was Trump's promise to the American people that he was going to take border enforcement seriously.

JOHNSON: A Justice Department spokesman says the administration's approach is, quote, "grounded in common sense measures that uphold both the law and the integrity of our borders." Chad Maisel says if history is a guide, the president and his policies are in line for some significant victories.

MAISEL: The president has an unprecedented track record of success at the Supreme Court and nowhere is that more true than when we're talking about the immigration docket and the immigration cases.

JOHNSON: But civil liberties and immigrant rights groups say the human cost of Trump's tough enforcement could be devastating. Trina Realmuto is executive director at the National Immigration Litigation Alliance. She's been fighting for migrants at risk of being deported to third countries where they have no prior ties.

TRINA REALMUTO: They have families, they have jobs, and under this policy, they are being abruptly and suddenly ripped from their communities and their loved ones and being sent to third countries.

JOHNSON: A lower court judge has ruled the migrants need a chance to argue they could face torture or persecution before they're deported. But the Supreme Court has repeatedly bigfooted that judge in Massachusetts and allowed those deportations to proceed for now. The administration says it won assurances from third countries that the migrants will not be abused. But Trina Realmuto says her class members have routinely described being detained abroad by armed guards in what she calls horrendous living conditions.

REALMUTO: What we know is that those so-called assurances aren't worth the piece of paper that they're written on.

JOHNSON: The justices are set to hear the case about third country removals in December. Legal experts say a separate immigration case will be among the most important of the term. That case revolves around the president's effort to use mandatory detention for migrants without giving them access to a bond hearing. Michael Tan of the American Civil Liberties Union explains.

MICHAEL TAN: The policy at issue in these cases is truly a radical break with the law. For decades, it's been universally understood, including by the first Trump administration, that immigrants who are living in the country and detained for a deportation proceeding generally have the right to seek release at a bond hearing before an immigration judge.

JOHNSON: Last July, Tan says, the Trump administration declared those immigrants would be locked up even if they were in the process of seeking legal status.

TAN: If allowed, this rule would literally subject millions of immigrants to mandatory detention, amounting to the largest mandatory detention regime in U.S. history.

JOHNSON: Meanwhile the solicitor general has asked the justices to accept another set of immigration cases about an effort to revoke visas for scholars at Georgetown and Columbia University. text:
Tampa, FL — Five Cuban nationals and one U.S. citizen were sentenced today for their roles in a vast conspiracy involving alien smuggling, asylum fraud, and money laundering. As part of the conspiracy, aliens were charged between $1,500 and $40,000 for their smuggling services, and co-conspirators sometimes chartered private planes to move groups of aliens.

“The conspirators in this case used sophisticated methods to violate our nation’s immigration laws while personally seeking to enrich themselves,” said U.S. Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe for the Middle District of Florida. “We will continue to work with our task force partners to thwart these illegal activities and ensure that our borders are protected.”

“These defendants turned illegal immigration into a multimillion-dollar criminal enterprise, smuggling aliens into the United States to line their pockets and laundering millions in illicit proceeds to conceal their operations,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “Under President Trump, human smugglers and money launderers will never get a free pass. Operation Take Back America is empowering the Justice Department to put more criminals like these behind bars and enforce the rule of law.”

“This investigation exposed a transnational criminal organization that treated our immigration system as a profit center, exploiting vulnerable people, manufacturing fraudulent immigration claims, and laundering millions of dollars in ill-gotten gains,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Nicholas Ingegno of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Tampa. “These criminals undermined the integrity of lawful immigration processes and created significant public-safety and national-security concerns. HSI and our law-enforcement partners will continue to identify, investigate, and dismantle transnational criminal networks that exploit our borders and our communities for financial gain.”

“Today’s sentencing is a clear warning to anyone seeking to profit by exploiting, abusing, or undermining America’s legal immigration system,” said Director Joseph B. Edlow of U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS). “USCIS will bring to bear all law enforcement resources at its disposal to dismantle criminal operations threatening the American people.”

According to court documents, Liannys Yaiselys Vega-Perez, 27, Miguel Martinez Vasconcelos, 31, Layra Libertad Treto Santos, 30, Luis Emmanuel Escalona-Marrero, 32, Walbis Pozo-Dutel, 32, and Emanuel Martinez Gonzalez, 29, conspired with others to operate an alien smuggling organization (ASO), which encouraged or induced thousands of Cuban aliens to enter the U.S. The ASO smuggled the Cuban aliens illegally across the southern border and used fraudulent Electronic System for Travel Authorization (ESTA) visa waivers to help people enter through ports of entry. The defendants advertised their smuggling services and bogus immigration services across multiple social media platforms targeted toward Cuban nationals living in Cuba. The ASO advertised services included assisting Cubans with European citizenship to enter the U.S. on a European tourist visa waiver or ESTA and filed hundreds of fraudulent ESTA applications with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), using fake addresses and false information. Cuban residents are not eligible for the ESTA program, and to obtain ESTAs, the ASO made false representations that the applicants had not been present in Cuba since 2011. The defendants knew that Cubans are not eligible for the ESTA program, and that the applicants were residing in Cuba at the time the ESTA applications were submitted. The defendants also operated a fraudulent immigration benefits business. Once in the U.S., the ASO assisted many aliens with filing fraudulent asylum paperwork to remain in the country.

Passports and boarding passes obtained as part of the scheme

Social media account advertising ASO services

Social media account using photo from human smuggling event to advertise ASO services

Liannys Yaiselys Vega-Perez furthered the conspiracy by assisting in the logistics of moving aliens from their country of origin, including Cuba, into the United States, such as purchasing international and domestic flights for aliens to transport them towards, into, and throughout the United States. Vega-Perez was also the primary manager of the immigration benefits business and personally filed hundreds of fraudulent asylum applications. In addition, she and other defendants prepared, drafted, and submitted fraudulent asylum applications, immigrant visa applications, lawful permanent residence applications, and other applications for immigration benefits, in exchange for a fee.

Miguel Martinez Vasconcelos furthered the conspiracy by purchasing airline tickets to move individuals being smuggled from their country of origin towards the United States. He also provided funding to purchase charter flights to transport aliens to unlawfully enter the U.S., with the purpose of growing and advancing the ASO’s operations. Vasconcelos personally transmitted at least $150,000 to companies operating outside the U.S. in furtherance of these unlawful activities.

Layra Libertad Treto Santos furthered the conspiracy by personally filing fraudulent asylum claims on behalf of the immigration fraud benefits business while she was an employee and manager. Treto Santos used the ASO’s smuggling services for herself and her family members and referred multiple Cuban nationals to the ASO for smuggling services.

Luis Emmanuel Escalona-Marrero furthered the conspiracy by working with a co-conspirator in Mexico to ship Cuban passports to the United States. The purpose was to avoid the passports being confiscated by U.S. Border Patrol so that aliens could use the passports to apply for asylum once they entered the United States. He also formed a shell company that, along with other companies, was used to move illegal proceeds of smuggling through to conceal the funds’ source and nature before distributing the funds back to himself and his co-conspirators.

Walbis Pozo-Dutel furthered the conspiracy by assisting with the logistics of transporting foreign nationals from their countries of origin, including Cuba, into the United States. For example, Pozo-Dutel provided foreign hotel and flight information to facilitate the aliens’ travel along the route into the United States. Pozo-Dutel also instructed the individuals on what to say if questioned by CBP officers.

Emmanuel Martinez Gonzalez furthered the conspiracy by helping coordinate the logistics of transporting aliens. Martinez-Gonzalez worked with his paramour and codefendant, Marianny Lucia Lopez-Torres, to arrange the travel of aliens upon their arrival in the United States and accepted payments from those aliens as a part of the smuggling operation.

Vega-Perez, Martinez Vasconcelos, and others, conspired to regularly move funds to companies operating outside of the United States and to other places outside the United States, such as by purchasing international flights for aliens to travel into the U.S. Between July 2022 and November 2024, the ASO spent more than $600,000 with a single airline for commercial flights.

Vega-Perez, Escalona-Marrero, and Treto Santos and others conspired to conduct financial transactions that were designed in whole or in part to conceal and disguise the nature, location, source, ownership, and control of proceeds of alien smuggling. The defendants set up multiple shell companies, through which illegal proceeds were moved before distributing the proceeds to the defendants. Between 2021 and 2025, more than $22 million was laundered by the defendants.

Liannys Yaiselys Vega-Perez was sentenced to four years in prison. Vega-Perez previously pleaded guilty to conspiracy to smuggle aliens for financial gain, conspiracy to commit asylum fraud, conspiracy to commit international money laundering, and conspiracy to commit concealment money laundering. Miguel Martinez Vasconcelos was sentenced to two years in prison. Martinez Vasconcelos previously pleaded guilty to conspiracy to smuggle aliens for financial gain and conspiracy to commit international money laundering. Layra Libertad Treto Santos was sentenced to 30 months in prison. Treto Santos previously pleaded guilty to conspiracy to smuggle aliens for financial gain, conspiracy to commit asylum fraud, and conspiracy to commit concealment money laundering. Luis Emmanuel Escalona-Marrero was sentenced to two years in prison. Escalona-Marrero previously pleaded guilty to conspiracy to smuggle aliens for financial gain and conspiracy to commit concealment money laundering. Walbis Pozo-Dutel was sentenced to two years in prison. Pozo-Dutel previously pleaded guilty to conspiracy to smuggle aliens for financial gain. Emanuel Martinez Gonzalez was sentenced to two years in prison. Martinez Gonzalez previously pleaded guilty to conspiracy to smuggle aliens for financial gain. Escalona-Marrero was ordered to forfeit $2.9M, Vasconcelos was ordered to forfeit $150,000, and Treto Santos was ordered to forfeit $95,000.

Twelve individuals were charged in a superseding indictment for their roles in the conspiracy. Yuniel Lima-Santos, 32, and Gisleivy Peralta Consuegra, 41, pleaded guilty and are awaiting sentencing. Erik Ventura-Castro, 25, was sentenced on July 29 to 30 months in prison. Lazaro Alain Cabrera-Rodriguez, 29, was found guilty after trial in September and is awaiting sentencing. Marianny Lucia Lopez-Torres and Frandy Aragon-Diaz are at large.

This case was supported and prosecuted by Joint Task Force Alpha (JTFA), the U.S. Department of Justice’s lead effort in combating human smuggling and trafficking committed by cartels and Transnational Criminal Organizations throughout the Americas. In partnership with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS), JTFA investigates and prosecutes the most prolific and dangerous human smuggling and trafficking networks that impact public safety and border security. Led by the Criminal Division’s Human Rights and Special Prosecutions Section and supported by other Criminal Division components, JTFA has dedicated prosecutors from U.S. Attorneys’ Offices along the Southwest border, Southern Florida, Northern New York, and Vermont. JTFA partners with U.S. Attorneys’ Offices throughout the country and supports high-priority cases in any district. All JTFA cases rely on substantial law enforcement resources from DHS components, including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Homeland Security Investigations, and U.S. Customs and Border Protection, U.S. Border Patrol, and the Office of Field Operations. JTFA also partners with FBI and other law enforcement agencies. To date, JTFA’s work has resulted in more than 486 domestic and international arrests of leaders, organizers, and significant facilitators of alien smuggling and trafficking; more than 447 U.S. convictions; and more than 377 significant jail sentences imposed and forfeitures of substantial assets.

HSI Tampa, U.S. Border Patrol Miami Sector, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services’ Fraud Detection and National Security, and Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation led U.S. investigative efforts, with substantial assistance from HSI’s Human Smuggling Unit in Washington, D.C. and CBP’s National Targeting Center International Interdiction Task Force. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs and authorities in the Cayman Islands provided valuable assistance.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Courtney Derry for the Middle District of Florida and Trial Attorney Amanda Brown of the Criminal Division’s Human Rights and Special Prosecutions Section are prosecuting the case.

This case is part of Operation Take Back America, a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and other transnational criminal organizations, and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime. Operation Take Back America streamlines efforts and resources from the Department’s Project Safe Neighborhoods.

text:
By Andrew Goudsward

WASHINGTON, Oct 29 (Reuters) – President Donald Trump’s administration has demanded records from California as part of a criminal investigation into alleged voting by noncitizens – escalating its battle with the largest US state ahead of Tuesday’s midterm election.

The Los ​Angeles County Registrar-Recorder’s office received federal grand jury subpoenas last week seeking information about ‌the agency’s methods for detecting “unlawful voting by aliens” and preventing such ballots from being counted, according to copies of the subpoenas seen by Reuters on Thursday.

The Trump Justice Department has heaped pressure on California over alleged noncitizen voting, filing a civil lawsuit against the state and sending a series of letters this month warning election officials ‌that ​they risk criminal exposure if they do not verify voters’ ⁠citizenship status.

The subpoenas also seek records ⁠related to Los Angeles County’s response to those letters, according to the documents.

The demands are part of a nationwide effort by the Trump administration to identify cases of voter fraud, raising concerns among Democrats and other critics that Trump could use the issue to ​sow doubt about the results of the election, which will determine control of Congress.

“At every step, the US Department of Justice has taken a confrontational, adversarial approach,” Los Angeles County ⁠Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan said in a statement on Thursday. “Election ⁠officials are acting in accordance with state and federal law.”

It was not ​immediately clear if Logan’s office was the focus of the investigation.

LEGAL BATTLE

Though studies have repeatedly shown ​that voting by noncitizens is rare and has no impact on election results, the ‌Trump administration has intensely focused on the issue.

The Justice Department has charged 156 immigrants with voting or registering to vote unlawfully in a pre-midterm push, acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter told reporters on Thursday. The agency has used subpoenas to state and local election officials to build such ⁠cases.

A Justice Department spokesperson declined to comment on the latest subpoenas but said that California and the federal government “agree that noncitizen voting is properly addressed through criminal law.”

On Wednesday, a federal judge rejected ⁠a Justice Department request to temporarily ‌block California from counting mail-in ballots from a list of 20,000 ⁠voters the administration alleges are likely noncitizens. The DOJ has appealed the ​ruling.

Lawyers for ‌California have questioned the reliability of the Trump administration’s immigration data ​and argued ⁠that the federal government does not have the authority to intervene in its elections.

Under the US Constitution, states administer elections and not the federal government.

Before ruling against the DOJ, US District Judge David Carter told agency lawyers at a hearing on Tuesday that the “court believes that it would be wise that any threats to state and county election employees cease immediately.”

(Reporting by Andrew Goudsward; Editing by Jesse ​Mesner-Hage and Stephen Coates)
