text:
She called the policy to send pregnant children to South Texas “enraging.”

This spring, The California Newsroom and The Texas Newsroom published a joint investigation revealing the administration’s policy of detaining pregnant unaccompanied minors as young as 13 at a single shelter near the border with Mexico. The investigation detailed serious concerns that health experts inside and outside the government had raised about the policy, given that adolescent pregnancies are inherently high risk and there is a lack of specialized obstetric care in the region.

Since then, the administration has denied the policy exists and said it is ensuring that the girls have access to the care they need.

In an unsigned email in September, a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees ORR, wrote that "ORR's policies for placing children in its custody into care provider facilities are based on child welfare best practices in order to provide a safe environment and place the child in the least restrictive setting appropriate for the child’s needs. This is especially true for expectant minors in ORR care.”

Yet the administration’s own records, as well as interviews with multiple government officials, suggest otherwise.

The documents, which were obtained through a public records request, show that ORR explicitly directed its staff in July 2025 to send all pregnant youth to the shelter in San Benito, Tex., just outside Brownsville.

Several months later, internal agency data showed that pregnant girls started being funneled to a different shelter nearby instead, according to three ORR officials who asked not to be named because they feared retaliation.

Forty-eight Democratic members of Congress had also expressed concerns about the policy in a pointed letter to the Department of Health and Human Services back in April. They received a response in September from an assistant secretary at HHS, Alex J. Adams, who wrote that ORR “does not make placement decisions for pregnant youth based on a blanket rule or one-size-fits-all approach” and that it “takes seriously its responsibility to protect the health, safety, dignity, and well-being of every unaccompanied alien child in its custody.”

HHS did not respond to requests for comment about why, contrary to Adams' statement that there was no "one-size-fits-all approach," the government's own records indicate that all unaccompanied youth with known pregnancies have been sent to specific Texas shelters.

“They're definitely playing games,” said U.S. Rep. Gil Cisneros, (D-Calif.). “They're not looking out for the welfare of these young women.”

U.S. Rep. Joaquin Castro, D-TX, whose office authored the letter to HHS, called it “irresponsible that they would wait several months to respond to basic questions about the care of some of the most vulnerable people within the system,” adding that the administration failed to explain “what seems to be an informal but strict policy of sending these girls to deep South Texas, which lacks the medical care that the girls need.”

Unaccompanied migrant children have historically been placed in shelters across the United States, but this summer, the Trump administration began detaining far more of them — even those who are not pregnant — in Texas. According to internal reports provided independently by two officials at ORR, both of whom asked not to be named due to fear of reprisal by their supervisors, 95% of the roughly 300 children apprehended by immigration officials in September were placed in detention in Texas, up from 45% in June.

Advocates for unaccompanied migrant children, former government officials, and some Democratic members of Congress have criticized the move, arguing that the state is not prepared to handle an influx of vulnerable children who need special care.

The fact that ORR has had to transfer several pregnant unaccompanied minors from Texas to California, New York and Arizona to receive medical care, they say, proves their point.

“If the government had to fly or transport these pregnant children across the country to get them the medical care they need, why on earth did it deliberately send them to Texas in the first place?” said U.S. Rep. Judy Chu, D-Calif., who was unaware of the transfers until a journalist described the newsrooms’ findings. Chu’s district, California’s 28th, is home to several communities with high numbers of immigrants, such as Rosemead and Monterey Park.

Chu expressed concern that many of the pregnant children who enter federal immigration custody are victims of sexual assault.

“If there is a 13-year-old girl who has survived rape,” she said, “she should be met with compassion, safety and appropriate medical care. Instead, this administration is placing children like her in a state where they will be deprived of access to basic healthcare. It's dangerous, and it's cruel, and there's no excuse for treating children this way.”

Government records contradict Trump administration’s claims

Unlike Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), which detains migrant adults and families in large, prison-like facilities, ORR detains unaccompanied children in group or foster homes overseen by private contractors. Laws, agency regulations and court orders require that the children receive comprehensive healthcare and appropriate education while they’re detained.

In an unsigned email last month, a spokesperson for HHS said that placing children in Texas is “operationally efficient” and that ORR’s facilities in the state “provide all requirements and more.”

Records obtained through a public information request cast doubt on that assertion. The records show that between July of 2025, when ORR began placing pregnant girls in South Texas, and May of 2026, four of them had to be transferred to other states to receive medical care.

That’s roughly one in five of the more than 20 pregnant girls the agency placed in the region in that time frame, according to one ORR official.

In detailed notes for one of those cases, ORR staff wrote that a pregnant 12-year-old girl was transferred from South Texas to a shelter in New York on the recommendation of ORR’s division of health. The records note that the child needed access to specialists whose availability in South Texas is “extremely limited.”

In a note for another case, staff wrote that a pregnant girl was transferred to California due to an unspecified “high risk medical need.” In at least one case, a girl was transferred out of Texas because she had requested an abortion, the records show.

Marsha Griffin, a retired professor of pediatrics at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley School of Medicine, said such outcomes were inevitable. Griffin said the shelters have very few medical staff on hand and the region does not have enough specialized obstetricians.

“Young girls who are pregnant, especially those from 10 to 14 years of age, are automatically a high-risk population,” said Griffin, who oversaw medical students volunteering in ORR facilities in South Texas.

Internal communications, also obtained through a public records request, show that officials in ORR’s own division of health warned the agency’s leadership about the lack of pregnancy-related healthcare in the region of South Texas where the girls are held.

“Texas has one of the worst rates of maternal mortality in the U.S.,” wrote Joanna Gaines, who at the time was ORR’s acting health director, in a July 18, 2025, email to Melissa Johnston, the agency’s head of operations. Gaines added that the state “lack[s] access to quality perinatal healthcare” and that “Cameron County has one of the higher rates of infant mortality in Texas.”

Four days later, ORR issued a directive to begin placing “any pregnant children” at a shelter in Cameron County called Urban Strategies San Benito.

Tracey Wilkinson, a pediatrician in Indiana who specializes in reproductive healthcare access for minors, said that even if the government is transferring children to get medical care, waiting until they need it puts them in danger.

“When you're talking about labor or pregnancy complications, every minute counts,” Wilkinson said. “If it was a medical emergency that required this young person to be transported out of the state, the risk to her survival would be lower for no reason other than she was placed in the middle of nowhere, far away from medical care.”

‘They are trying to deliberately mislead Congress members’

Shortly after The California Newsroom and The Texas Newsroom revealed the Trump administration’s policy of detaining pregnant migrant youth in Texas, Castro launched an inquiry into the practice. He soon arranged a visit to the San Benito shelter.

By the time of his visit on April 7, internal agency data showed that ORR had stopped placing newly detained children with known pregnancies at the facility, three ORR officials said. Instead, the agency was sending them to a different shelter, in Los Fresnos, just 20 minutes away.

Castro said he was not told of the change at the time of his visit, nor was it mentioned in ORR’s formal response to the congressional inquiry last month.

In a recent interview, he described his visit to the San Benito shelter as “a very secretive process” and said he was not allowed to see or speak with any of the children there.

An HHS spokesperson did not respond to questions about the location change, writing only that “there have been no operational changes regarding the placement of pregnant unaccompanied children.”

Chu said she believed the Trump administration made the change in order to “deliberately mislead Congress members as well as the public from really knowing where these pregnant children have been.”

Compass Connections, the San Antonio-based nonprofit that operates the shelter in Los Fresnos where pregnant girls are now being held, is one of the largest ORR contractors; it has been awarded more than $1.9 billion in federal grants to house and care for unaccompanied minors over the past four years, according to USAspending.gov.

Asked for comment, the company referred the newsrooms to HHS.

In his letter to Castro, Assistant Secretary Adams wrote that “placement and transfer decisions are individualized and consider the child’s safety, medical and behavioral health needs, pregnancy-related needs, available services, legal access, family unity, least restrictive placement requirements, and the best interest of the child.”

‘In California, they would have more access to all reproductive healthcare’

Congress members and advocates in California said their state offers much more support for pregnant girls in federal custody than they can receive in Texas.

“One thing is very clear,” Chu said: “There are many of us that care about what's happening to our immigrants.”

As the Trump administration has withdrawn federal support for legal representation of unaccompanied children — and at the same time streamlined the process of deporting them — the state of California, as well as several of its cities and counties, have ramped up funding for their own legal services programs for undocumented kids.

“Pregnant unaccompanied children have rights to medical care, safety, family unity and due process, but those rights mean little without a lawyer to defend them,” said Marion "Mickey" Donovan-Kaloust, director of legal services at Immigrant Defenders in Los Angeles. “California's support systems can provide pregnant unaccompanied children with the stability, dignity and specialized care they need to be safe and thrive.”

In addition to concerns about their access to healthcare and legal services, advocates worry that the Trump administration is knowingly putting pregnant children at risk to advance an ideological goal: denying them access to abortions by placing them in Texas, where abortion is virtually banned.

Current federal regulations require the government to move detained minors who request abortions to states where it’s legal. In January, the Trump administration announced it plans to rescind that rule, though it hasn’t yet done so.

An HHS spokesperson said in February that claims the department is attempting to restrict unaccompanied children’s access to abortion are “completely inaccurate.”

Cisneros said that “In California, they would have more access to all reproductive healthcare, and then they could make decisions based on discussions with their healthcare professional and what's best for them.”

Chu noted that next month’s election will determine whether Democrats regain control of the House. If they do, she said, they will redouble their efforts to ensure pregnant children in federal immigration custody are given proper care.

“There will be greater oversight,” she said, “and we will hold the decision-makers responsible.”

Mark Betancourt is a freelance journalist based in Washington, D.C.

title: Birth rates and immigration policies are causing an enrollment crisis for schools - NPR
description:
Transcript A MARTÍNEZ, HOST: The number of children in U.S. public schools is falling.
MANN: And public school enrollment nationwide is expected to keep falling.
Officials in California say their state alone will lose another 700,000 public school students over the next decade.
Texas also lost roughly 76,000 public school kids statewide in 2025.
Because public school funding is typically tied to enrollment, these losses could cripple some public schools.
text:
Transcript

A MARTÍNEZ, HOST:

The number of children in U.S. public schools is falling. By the end of the decade, enrollment will be down by millions. Education experts say lower birth rates over the last two decades are the big factor. President Trump's immigration crackdown is also taking a toll. NPR's Brian Mann is covering this. Brian, so how many millions are we talking about?

BRIAN MANN, BYLINE: Well, it's a lot. Public schools now have been losing kids for years. Forty states have seen declines. And the U.S. Education Department projects that by 2030 - that's just a few years from now - the drop could reach 4 million children. And while this is happening in most of the U.S., some districts are being hit much harder. The Los Angeles Unified School District, A, has lost half its kids over the last 20 years. And superintendent Andres Chait announced this fall that he's launching a citywide program aimed at closing schools.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

ANDRES CHAIT: It is a simple if painful reality that we used to have 700,000 students, and now we have fewer than 400,000.

MANN: And public school enrollment nationwide is expected to keep falling. Officials in California say their state alone will lose another 700,000 public school students over the next decade.

MARTÍNEZ: Wow. Now, we mentioned some of the factors that go into this. Break that all down for us.

MANN: Yeah, so what most researchers say is that it's a one-two punch here caused first by low birth rates, and then now by Trump's immigration crackdown. There are roughly 700,000 fewer babies born every year in the U.S. That's compared with 20 years ago. So that's a lot fewer kids turning up for kindergarten. Until last year, in much of the country, that trend was offset at least partially by immigrants coming into the U.S. A lot of them put their kids in public schools. Now, at least in the short term, a lot of those students are suddenly vanishing.

MARTÍNEZ: Vanishing. What does that mean, vanishing?

MANN: Well, let's take LA again. After Trump's immigration crackdown began there last year, LA Unified School District officials say their enrollment decline got a lot worse. They lost twice as many kids as they expected. Texas also lost roughly 76,000 public school kids statewide in 2025. It's only the second drop in the state's modern school history. A study by state officials there found most of those losses came among Hispanic families and among the children of immigrants.

More big enrollment drops this year in some of Florida's school districts. The Trump administration there, of course, stripped a lot of Haitian immigrants of their temporary protected status. I spoke about all this with Thomas Dee. He's an economist who studies population and education trends at Stanford University. He thinks what Trump is doing will take a bigger and bigger toll on school districts.

THOMAS DEE: So it's really the effects of both an exodus of existing families and also stopping the inflow that would've normally occurred.

MANN: And here's an important thing. Because public school funding is typically tied to enrollment, these losses could cripple some public schools. Two education think tanks, Bellwether and WestEd, released a study this summer showing the budget impacts of all this could top $11 billion a year.

MARTÍNEZ: What has the Trump administration said about the impact of its immigration policy on schools?

MANN: Yeah, we asked the White House repeatedly for an interview. They haven't responded. In public statements, the Trump administration, A, has celebrated the fact that there are millions fewer foreign residents. That means legal and undocumented immigrants living in the U.S. Trump has described curbing immigration as one of the big policy wins of his second term. But with U.S. birth rates also falling - they hit a new record low last year - that means school districts around the country have to plan for a future with fewer children.

MARTÍNEZ: All right. That's NPR's Brian Mann. Brian, thanks.

MANN: Thank you.

text:
Governing Blind:

The Fiscal and Operational Impact of Immigration on Texas Public Systems

Written by Selene Rodriguez

Download the full paper here.

Key Points

Texas operates at the intersection of federal immigration policy and the day-to-day realities of sustaining its public systems, bearing substantial costs driven by national mandates. This is very evident in education and healthcare.

Unpaid healthcare costs are passed along to Texas taxpayers through higher insurance rates, public hospital funding, and other publicly funded health programs.

Due to the obligations established under Plyler v. Doe, the strain on public schools has accumulated over time as student populations have grown and diversified.

Because no state agency tracks student immigration status, no government entity currently measures the full scope of how many undocumented students are enrolled in Texas public schools, meaning policymakers cannot accurately assess the scale of the challenge they are managing, let alone design targeted solutions.

Texas cannot effectively manage the impacts on public education, healthcare, and emergency services without a clearer understanding of the populations interacting with those systems. Better data collection will not solve every challenge, but it will allow policymakers and local institutions to move from reactive decision-making to informed planning.

Executive Summary

Texas operates at the intersection of federal immigration policy and the day-to-day realities of sustaining its public systems, bearing substantial costs driven by national mandates. Nowhere is this more evident than within education and healthcare. This paper examines two critical areas where those pressures are most pronounced: the legal obligation to provide public education under Plyler v. Doe, and the growing burden of uncompensated care within the state’s healthcare system. This research shows that while Texas is required to deliver services driven by federal mandates, it lacks the standardized data necessary to fully quantify the associated fiscal and operational impacts.

Due to Plyler v. Doe, states are required to provide K-12 education regardless of immigration status, but there is no mechanism for states to track or isolate the costs tied to that mandate. As a result, Texas school systems face real and increasing demands—particularly in areas such as bilingual education, staffing, and infrastructure—without a precise accounting framework to measure those impacts.

A similar dynamic exists in healthcare. Texas hospitals, especially in high-growth and border regions, absorb significant levels of uncompensated care, driven in part by populations lacking access to traditional coverage. Federal restrictions on eligibility for public healthcare programs contribute to increased reliance on emergency services, shifting costs to providers, taxpayers, and insured patients. Yet here again, the absence of consistent, statewide data limits the states’ ability to distinguish between contributing factors, evaluate where system strain is encumbered, and plan accordingly.

Across both domains, the central challenge is not simply cost, but measurement. Current data collection practices are fragmented, inconsistent, and often reliant on indirect indicators. This limits policymakers’ ability to move beyond assumptions and toward evidence-based decision-making. To address this gap, this paper proposes the development of a standardized, statewide data-collection framework focused on the impacts of education and healthcare. Such a framework would enable Texas to produce defensible fiscal estimates, improve transparency, and better align policy responses with operational realities. By prioritizing accurate measurement, Texas can strengthen its ability to manage public resources, meet its legal obligations, and inform future policy debates with clarity and precision.

Introduction

Sharing 1,254 miles of international border with Mexico, Texas sits on the front lines of immigration policy. But the responsibility for managing its consequences does not end in Washington, D.C.; it is carried out daily in classrooms, hospitals, and local institutions across the state. While federal law establishes the framework, Texas is responsible for maintaining the systems that absorb the impact, without clear visibility into the full scope of the burden.

The true number of illegally present foreign nationals in the United States and specifically in Texas is unknown. There are many estimates, including the Migration Policy Institute’s estimate of 13.7 million nationwide as of 2023 (Migration Policy Institute, 2025), with particularly large populations concentrated in California and Texas. Similarly, Pew Research Center estimates 14 million illegally present foreign nationals as of 2023 (Pew Research Center, 2025).

As of January 2025, the Center for Immigration Studies released a report estimating that there are 15.4 million illegal aliens in the U.S., and that at least 15.8% of the total U.S. population is foreign-born (Camarota & Zeigler, 2025). While these estimates vary, many were produced prior to one of the largest sustained migration surges in modern U.S. history. As a result, even widely cited figures may struggle to fully capture the scale and speed of recent immigration flows into the United States.

From 2021-2024, during the Biden Administration, there were more than 10.1 million encounters by U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) nationwide (CBP, 2026). For many months during this timeframe, CBP recorded over 100,000 encounters per month. Yet the challenge facing Texas is not only the presence of this population, but the inability to measure its impact with precision. Without standardized, reliable data, policymakers are left to respond to visible strain without a complete understanding of the scope, cost, or long-term implications.

Healthcare

Under the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996 (PRWORA), illegal aliens are ineligible for federal health coverage programs like Medicaid and Medicare (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, 1996). PRWORA created the term “qualified alien” to describe certain status-holders who are eligible to receive public benefits. This list includes refugees, Cuban-Haitian entrants, Lawful Permanent Residents (LPR), battered aliens, etc. (8 U.S.C. §1641(b)). In recent years, the Trump Administration has pursued a series of executive actions aimed at restricting access to federal public benefits for illegal aliens and tightening eligibility standards more broadly. However, several of these actions have faced legal challenges in federal court, reflecting the continued instability and debate surrounding immigration-related healthcare policy.

This does not mean that illegal aliens cannot access healthcare services, as these may be provided under EMTALA, emergency Medicaid, or indigent care, or charity care. Federal law under EMTALA requires Medicare-participating hospitals to treat anyone with a medical emergency, regardless of immigration or insurance status (U.S. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, 2025). Nonprofit hospitals are required by federal and state law to provide uncompensated care to low-income populations as part of their charity care requirements. Each provider sets the standards for their charity care programs. This is different from indigent care administered by County Indigent Health Care Programs, which covers individuals who are ineligible for Medicaid and have incomes below 21% of the federal poverty level (FPL) (Texas Health and Human Services, n.d.). Indigent care may be eligible for reimbursement through the State Assistance Fund once a county’s qualifying expenditures exceed 8% of its General Revenue Tax Levy (GRTL). The state may then reimburse eligible costs above that threshold. (Gilberd, 2025). None of these programs verify immigration status before providing care. Ideally, if care under one of these welfare programs designed for Texans is provided to an illegal alien, the provider should be reimbursed to prevent strain on the program (House Research Organization, 2001). Unpaid costs are ultimately passed along to Texas taxpayers through higher insurance rates, public hospital funding, and other publicly funded health programs.

In August 2024, Gov. Greg Abbott issued an Executive Order directing the Texas Health and Human Services Commission (HHSC) to collect citizenship information at hospitals for inpatient and emergency care (Executive Order GA 46, 2024). HHSC is required to report that data annually to the Governor and the Texas Legislature so that the State of Texas may seek reimbursement from the federal government. According to HHSC’s fiscal year 2025 report, there were 313,742 visits by patients illegally present in the U.S., representing $1,050,642,864 in total healthcare costs, not solely uncompensated care (Texas Health and Human Services, 2025).

However, the current reporting framework has notable limitations. Hospitals are required to ask patients about their citizenship status during registration, but patients are not required to respond and may decline to answer. Additionally, there is no formal verification mechanism to confirm the accuracy of responses provided during intake. As a result, the available data likely captures only a partial picture of the true scope of uncompensated care associated with immigration-related healthcare utilization.

These challenges are not isolated to Texas. In 2023, “eight thousand migrants from Central America accounted for approximately 20,000 (hospital) visits” to the Denver hospital system (Lewis, 2024). Denver Health reported spending $10 million in 2023 on “migrant care.” (Summers, 2024).

Yuma, Arizona, sounded the alarm in 2023 when the Yuma Regional Medical Center announced spending more than $26 million treating illegal aliens. Like Texas, Arizona shares the U.S.-Mexico border and was overwhelmed by illegal crossings during the Biden Administration. A population of 100,000; 300,000 people entered from Mexico in one year, and they are the only hospital for 180 miles (Bennett, 2023). Robert Trenschel, a doctor at the Yuma Regional Medical Center, testified in Washington, D.C.:

Migrant patients are receiving free care that they have no ability to pay, we have no ability to bill anyone, we don’t know their final destination, we don’t know anything about them. We cannot provide completely free care to the residents of our community so the situation is simply not fair and concerning to them… Probably about 27 percent were maternity patients and many come in with no or little to no pre-natal care, so the babies when they are born are typically very sick, they typically wind up in our neonatal intensive care unit. Mom typically gets discharged earlier, but we want to keep mom and baby together obviously, so sometimes we put them up in a hotel. (Bennett, 2023)

These cases illustrate that uncompensated care pressures tied to immigration are not isolated incidents, but recurring operational challenges experienced across multiple states and healthcare systems.

Emergency Response Systems Under Pressure

The impact of immigration-related surges is particularly visible in emergency services, where demand is immediate. Texas urban and rural communities have experienced significant strain on public safety and healthcare infrastructure. For example, El Paso, Texas, a city with a population of over 600,000, spent $300,000 per day in 2022 in response to the increase in illegal aliens arriving in the city. El Paso’s Chief Financial Officer Robert Cortinas said in an interview that “It’s fire department, police department, public health—just about every department… is being impacted… this is not only unsustainable but simply unfair to our community” (Martinez, 2022). City Representative Claudia Rodriguez also noted that 50 firefighters were working at an immigrant welcome center instead of being available to respond to emergencies (Martinez, 2022).

Further south in Texas, the smaller border town of Eagle Pass also faced severe challenges. In 2023, 4,000 illegal aliens crossed into Eagle Pass in just one day, forcing the city to declare a state of emergency. A few days prior, the city saw 2,500 illegal aliens in a single day. Former Mayor Rolando Salinas said that the surge, close to 50% of the city’s population in one week, has “taken a toll on our local resources, especially our local police force and our fire department” (Martinez, 2023).

Notably, Eagle Pass took a hard hit to its emergency services department. Fire Chief Manuel Mello stated that his fire department was “doing up to 50 calls a day,” adding that “on a normal day, probably about 27, 30 calls a day. So an increase of about 20 calls and all (of them) migrant-related” (Ibarra, 2024). Like many border towns, Mello stated that their emergency room “is overwhelmed frequently” and that the department even had to add a fifth ambulance “strictly to treat migrants” (Ibarra, 2024).

Kinney County, an even smaller border county with roughly 3,000 people, has been pushed to its limits by the availability of emergency services. In 2022, the director of Emergency Medical Services for the county, Henry Garcia, stated that before the surge in illegal immigration, his department averaged about 235 calls a year, but from January to October 2022, they had 486 calls (Waldman, 2022). He further claimed that there were “over $40,000 in unbilled unpaid bills… nobody takes ownership. And they come back as unqualified patient, invalid report” (Waldman, 2022).

These cases highlight that when migration levels increase rapidly, emergency services become a frontline response system forced to absorb immediate demand without corresponding increases in funding or infrastructure.

Education

Plyler v. Doe

In 1975, the Texas Legislature authorized local school districts to deny enrollment to foreign-born children illegally present in the United States in public schools (HB 1126, 1975). Therefore, children who were illegally present were required to pay tuition to attend public schools within the state. In 1977, several families led a class-action lawsuit against a Texas school district, arguing that the legislation was unconstitutional. The United States Supreme Court granted certiorari in Plyler v. Doe (1982) to determine whether Texas laws denying undocumented immigrant children a free public education violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment (American Bar Association, 2018). By a 5-4 vote, the Court ruled that it was a violation and that all children, regardless of immigration status, have constitutionally protected access to a free public K-12 education. Further, it held that states cannot withhold funding for the education of illegally present students or deny enrollment of students based on their or their parents’/guardians’ immigration status.

English as a Second Language and Limited English Proficiency

English as a Second Language (ESL) refers to the instructional program designed to teach English to non-native English speakers, whereas Limited English Proficiency (LEP) is the federal designation for students who require these services. A 2022 study by the Federation for American Immigration Reform (FAIR) (2022) determined that more than 10 percent of all students in American public schools are designated as LEP, yet only 370,000 teachers hold the proper certifications to educate them. FAIR noted that “since the most recent cumulative data on this subject comes from 2020, it’s important to keep in mind that, unless otherwise noted, the figures detailed within this report do not take into account the massive surge of legal and illegal immigration into the United States” since this report (FAIR, 2022).

San Antonio is currently facing a shortage of fully certified bilingual and ESL teachers. The San Antonio Report reported over the past few years the district has received students that came from the Middle East, Nicaragua and Venezuela, noting that “During the 2022-23 school year, North East had an emergent bilingual population of 10,820. The next year, the district had 11,500. During the 2024-25 school year, the count went up to 11,700” (Garcia, 2025).

These pressures are neither unique to Texas nor recent in origin. The obligations established under Plyler v. Doe have been in place for decades, and the strain on public systems has accumulated over time as student populations have grown and diversified. Recent developments in cities like Chicago illustrate this broader pattern. Even prior to the massive influx of illegal aliens the United States took in under the Biden Administration, public schools across the nation struggled to meet state and federal requirements for bilingual education. The influx of new students has not created these challenges so much as exposed and intensified them, highlighting critical gaps that already existed within the system.

According to local reporting in Chicago, “the surge of new students… is exposing the cracks in a school system that has for years struggled to fully comply with state and federal laws around bilingual education” (Amin & Bloom, 2024), noting that students have fallen behind in their studies and the struggle of providing support to migrant students. In 2024, Chicago Public Schools estimated that its ESL student population increased by 12,000 students in one year, prompting state legislators to seek additional state and federal funding to support additional resources (Smylie, 2024).

FAIR estimates that LEP students cost taxpayers over $78 billion nationwide, a cost which is primarily borne at the state and local levels. In Texas specifically, their estimate is $11.4 billion (FAIR, 2022). In a 2023 Education Week survey, 61% of teachers reported that they did not feel adequately trained to teach English learners (Najarro, 2023). This disparity highlights a core challenge: as demand for specialized instruction grows, the system’s ability to meet that demand is not keeping pace.

Colony Ridge

Previous research by the Texas Public Policy Foundation (Oliver, 2020) examining the Colony Ridge development in Liberty County illustrates how rapid population growth—driven in part by immigration—can outpace local infrastructure and public systems. That analysis found that the area continues to experience significant strain on schools, public services, and local governance, as population growth has accelerated beyond the capacity of existing institutions.

Liberty County, Texas, is home to one of the fastest-growing Hispanic populations in the United States and to one of the fastest-growing school districts in Texas (Taylor, 2019; Fast Growth School Coalition, n.d.). Liberty County Sheriff Bobby Rader stated in an interview that the majority of the county’s immigrant population moved into Colony Ridge and does not respond to census takers (Doyle & Rezal, 2024). Though the exact population of Colony Ridge is unknown, Liberty County officials put the estimate between 75,000 and 100,000 mostly Latino residents (Doyle & Rezal, 2024).

As of September 2024, nearly 10,000 students had enrolled in Cleveland ISD over a decade, “an increase of 211% that makes CISD one of the fastest growing districts in the state,” and nearly 90% of the enrolled students live in the Colony Ridge community (Kelly, 2024). The rapid population expansion “has created exponential challenges for Texas’s fastest growing school district, including teacher retention, a school bus shortage, lack of facilities, substance abuse, and a financial deficit. [In 2023] the district spent $175 million, but Cleveland ISD only generated $165 million in revenue, leaving a $10 million deficit” (Doyle & Pérez, 2024; Cleveland ISD, 2024).

Further, roughly 60% of the student body are emerging bilingual students, and over 85% are Hispanic or Latino (Texas Education Agency, n.d.). Of the district’s 900 teachers, fewer than 30% are ESL-certified, and 15% are certified bilingual (Doyle & Pérez, 2024).

Colony Ridge serves as a localized example of a broader statewide challenge: when population increases occur quickly and outside of standardized measurement frameworks, the true scale of impact becomes difficult to quantify. This reinforces the central problem identified in this paper—not simply that systems are under pressure, but that Texas lacks the consistent data necessary to fully measure and respond to that pressure.

Texas Students Falling Behind

The strain on Texas public schools extends well beyond resource allocation—it is directly affecting student academic outcomes. The challenges facing districts like Cleveland ISD illustrate what happens when population growth outpaces a system’s capacity to respond. Cleveland ISD’s teacher turnover rate hovers around 40%, nearly double the state average, and the consequences are felt in the classroom (Doyle & Pérez, 2024). Only 57% of students are meeting grade-level expectations—roughly a 20% drop from the state average. Students themselves have borne the cost of these staffing failures. As Viví, a 17-year-old senior at Cleveland High School, described, “I didn’t have a math teacher for half the year… they would just send us to the gym and we didn’t learn for, like, half the year” (Doyle & Pérez, 2024).

These academic deficits do not exist in isolation. Approximately 60% of Cleveland ISD’s student body are emergent bilingual students, adding significant pressure to find teachers who are, or can be, certified as bilingual educators (Doyle & Pérez, 2024). Yet less than 30% of the district’s teachers are ESL-certified, and only 15% hold bilingual certification. A 2023 Education Week survey found that only 39% of teachers nationwide said they felt adequately trained to reach English-language learners, compared to 61% who said they did not (Doyle & Pérez, 2024). This gap compounds the problem at the classroom level.

Texas was already under pressure to improve its educational outcomes before these enrollment surges accelerated. The urgency of that reform mission makes the current data deficit all the more consequential. Because no state agency tracks student immigration status, no government entity currently measures the full scope of how many undocumented students are enrolled in Texas public schools, meaning policymakers cannot accurately assess the scale of the challenge they are managing, let alone design targeted solutions. This information gap affects not only fiscal planning but also the ability of counselors, administrators, and service providers to tailor support to students with unique needs, including limited prior schooling, language barriers, and traumatic backgrounds (Najarro & Harwin, 2026). Understanding who is in Texas classrooms is a prerequisite to meaningfully improving what happens inside them.

Unaccompanied Alien Children

Minors encountered at U.S. international borders without a parent or legal guardian are transferred into the care and custody of the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR). Federal law requires that ORR feed, shelter, and provide medical care for unaccompanied alien children until it is able to release them to safe settings with sponsors while they await immigration proceedings (Office of Refugee Resettlement, 2026).

According to ORR data, between 2015 and 2020, 31,635 unaccompanied aliens were released into Texas; between 2021 and 2025, 67,271; and so far in 2026, 81 (Office of Refugee Resettlement, 2026). Though one cannot determine that every single one of these minors entered into the Texas public school system, we do know that Texas spends around $12,000 per student (Texas Education Agency, 2022).

Setting aside the broader policy debate, the practical effect of sustained immigration flows is clear: increases in student population generate additional operational and fiscal demands for public school systems. In Texas, recent influxes have required school districts to expand capacity, adapt instruction for non-English speaking students, and absorb new costs in short timelines.

Additional Considerations

Any consideration of Plyler v. Doe today must also account for how significantly the immigration landscape has changed since the Court issued its decision in 1982. The constitutional holding remains binding, but the factual circumstances surrounding immigration, population flows, and demands on public systems have evolved considerably over the four decades since.

According to the Supreme Court’s opinion in Plyler v. Doe, “There is no evidence in the record suggesting that illegal entrants impose any significant burden on the State’s economy. To the contrary, the available evidence suggests that illegal aliens underutilize public services…” (Plyler v. Doe, 1982, p. 228).

It is fair to state that the immigration landscape facing the United States in 1982 is vastly different from what the country is experiencing today. A 1997 congressional report found that between 1966 and 1980, there were 6.4 million legal admissions into the U.S., and 12.6 million between 1981 and 1995 (Vialet, 1997). By comparison, between 2021 and 2024 alone, CBP recorded more than 10.1 million encounters nationwide (CBP, 2026). CBP Encounters represent law enforcement events rather than unique individuals and can include repeat encounters.

Importantly, border encounters alone do not capture the full scope of immigration flows. In recent years, federal immigration policy has increasingly relied on humanitarian parole programs and administrative entry pathways that allow foreign nationals to enter the country outside of traditional immigration processes. One example is the CHNV parole program, which permitted nationals from Cuba, Haiti, Nicaragua, and Venezuela to fly directly into the U.S. if approved. The Biden Administration later expanded this parole to Colombia, Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, and Ecuador (Bensman, 2024).

The broader point is that modern immigration flows are larger, more complex, and more administratively diverse than those contemplated at the time of Plyler v. Doe. As a result, the scale of potential impacts on public services today cannot be evaluated solely through the lens of historical immigration patterns.

In Plyler v. Doe, Justice Brennan acknowledged two realities that remain relevant today: that “the dominant incentive for illegal entry into the State of Texas is the availability of employment” and that “[a]ccess from Mexico into this country, across our 2,000-mile border, is readily available and virtually uncontrollable” (Plyler v. Doe, 1982, pp. 228-229). To a significant extent, Brennan was correct. Economic opportunity and access to public benefits continue to serve as powerful incentives for illegal immigration into the United States.

However, if one accepts the premise that these incentives drive migration flows, then it follows that policymakers must be willing to examine the policies and conditions that reinforce those incentives. Public services, employment opportunities, and inconsistent federal internal enforcement all contribute to the broader calculus that encourages unlawful entry and continued unlawful presence.

At the same time, the notion that the border is “virtually uncontrollable” should not be accepted as an immutable fact. While securing a lengthy international border presents undeniable challenges, both border security and interior enforcement are achievable when pursued with sustained political will, operational coordination, and consistent policy enforcement. The issue is not whether enforcement is possible, but whether governments are willing to prioritize and maintain it over time.

Recommendations

Establish a Statewide Public Education Impact Reporting Framework

What Plyler v. Doe does not prohibit is requiring the tracking, identifying, and calculating of the impact of illegal immigration on our public school system, which today is substantial. To improve statewide planning, Texas should establish a standardized statewide reporting framework through the Texas Education Agency to better measure the impact of immigration on public systems. School districts should be required to collect and report relevant demographic and instructional data during enrollment, including citizenship or immigration status, English language learner designation, country of origin, interrupted formal education history, and other indicators directly tied to instructional and infrastructure planning.

The Texas Education Agency should further publish annual statewide and regional impact assessments identifying high-growth districts, emerging bilingual population trends, ESL staffing needs, and other operational pressures tied to rapid demographic change. This information would provide the state with a more accurate understanding of enrollment trends, instructional needs, and the fiscal impact on public education systems. Standardized statewide tracking and reporting would allow Texas to better plan for long-term resource demands while maintaining compliance with federal law.

Codify Hospital Citizenship Data Collection

To ensure continuity and reliability in data collection, the Texas Legislature must codify Executive Order GA-46 into statute, establishing a permanent, statewide requirement for the collection and reporting of patient citizenship information. To produce meaningful and complete data, the policy should also require responses to this question as part of the intake process, while maintaining full compliance with federal law requiring the provision of emergency medical care regardless of a patient’s ability to pay or immigration status.

The reporting system should include standardized statewide methodology, annual public reporting, and centralized data aggregation through the Texas Health and Human Services Commission. Hospitals should be required to collect citizenship information during patient intake while maintaining full compliance with federal law requiring the provision of emergency medical care. Additionally, policymakers should evaluate mechanisms to improve data reliability, as the current framework relies largely on self-reported responses without independent verification. A comprehensive statewide reporting framework would allow Texas to better quantify uncompensated care costs, identify regional system strain, improve fiscal planning, and strengthen the state’s ability to pursue federal reimbursement where applicable. More importantly, it would shift the conversation about immigration-related healthcare impacts from assumptions to measurable evidence.

Additional Consideration: Emergency Services Capacity Reporting

Texas should build upon its existing statewide EMS reporting framework to better measure the fiscal and operational impacts associated with immigration. Texas already requires licensed EMS providers to report emergency runs to the Department of State Health Services. The Legislature should expand those requirements to capture additional information necessary to understand immigration-related demands on local emergency response systems. Where legally permissible and operationally feasible, reporting should include relevant patient demographic information as well as uncompensated response costs, changes in call volume, ambulance utilization, staffing demands, resource diversion, and other measurable pressures associated with periods of elevated migration. Standardized data across providers, aggregated at the state level, can allow policymakers to identify regional trends without relying primarily on isolated reports from individual jurisdictions. A more complete understanding can also help policymakers identify communities experiencing disproportionate strain, evaluate whether existing EMS capacity is sufficient, determine where additional infrastructure or resources may be necessary, and, importantly, better account for the cost borne by Texas communities and taxpayers.

While Texas aims to account for immigration impacts, other states have similar data-recording and reporting frameworks. One example is Kansas, which has a law (2019) directing the Kansas Board of Emergency Medical Services to maintain a statewide system that collects and analyzes EMS information. There are privacy protections around the system, and the state produces a monthly report with the data it receives (Kansas Board of Emergency Medical Services, 2026).

Conclusion

Ultimately, this issue is not simply about immigration; it is about governance. Texas cannot effectively manage the impacts on public education, healthcare, and emergency services without a clearer understanding of the populations interacting with those systems. Better data collection will not solve every challenge, but it will allow policymakers and local institutions to move from reactive decision-making to informed planning. In public education specifically, understanding the composition and needs of student populations allows school systems to establish clearer protocols, allocate resources more effectively, and better support both educators and students. Whether through bilingual instruction, staffing, transportation, or classroom capacity, sustainable solutions depend on accurate information. While a more accurate measurement will not eliminate strain, it will allow the state to respond with greater precision, accountability, and sustainability.

No state will ever possess a perfectly precise accounting of every foreign national present within its territory. However, uncertainty cannot justify the absence of measurement altogether. If Texas is expected to maintain public systems that absorb these impacts, then the state must be willing to pursue the clearest possible understanding of how immigration affects education, healthcare, emergency services, and local infrastructure.

text:
Why It Matters

The defensive asylum grant rate in U.S. immigration courts fell from 25% in fiscal 2017 to 3% in the third quarter of fiscal 2026, a 22-percentage-point decline, according to a new Congressional Research Service (CRS) report examining credible fear screening and defensive asylum processes. ​

Abandonment was the most common outcome in the third quarter, accounting for 92,081 cases, nearly 37% of dispositions. Immigration judges also issued 90,288 in absentia removal orders involving asylum applicants during the first three quarters of fiscal 2026, the highest number reported since at least fiscal 2008.

Section 90003 of H.R. 1, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, enacted as Public Law 119-21 on July 4, 2025, appropriated $45 billion to Immigration and Customs Enforcement for detention capacity and related activities. CRS reports that congressional appropriations have substantially expanded immigration detention capacity since 2025.

The Big Picture

Under the second Trump administration, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) expanded expedited removal to the fullest extent authorized by 8 U.S.C. § 1225(b)(1), as outlined in a January 2025 Federal Register notice. The positive credible fear determination rate stood at 80% in fiscal 2016, fell to 38% in fiscal 2020, and reached 43% in fiscal 2025.

Multiple enforcement policies face ongoing legal challenges. The Circumvention of Lawful Pathways rule was vacated following a May 7 district court order, with the government's appeal, No. 26-4982, pending in the Ninth Circuit. The Securing the Border rule is also subject to litigation after a district court found its asylum restrictions unlawful, with the government's appeal, No. 25-5313, pending in the D.C. Circuit.

Proclamation 10888, which sought to suspend access to asylum at the southern border, was found unlawful by the D.C. Circuit insofar as it circumvented statutory removal procedures and restricted access to humanitarian protections. The court stayed its mandate on July 27, leaving asylum restrictions temporarily operative while preserving access to withholding of removal and Convention Against Torture protections. The Supreme Court still has the administration's petition in Mullin v. RAICES, No. 26-239, pending.

Advertisement

A February Executive Office for Immigration Review interim final rule would have allowed the Board of Immigration Appeals to summarily dismiss most appeals unless it affirmatively accepted them for review and shortened the appeal deadline from 30 to 10 days for many cases. A federal district court vacated those provisions on March 8 for failure to comply with notice-and-comment requirements. The 30-day deadline remains in effect, and the court also upheld other procedural changes.

The Bottom Line

A proposed DHS rule would increase the waiting period to apply for asylum-based employment authorization from 150 to 365 days, potentially delaying when applicants receive work authorization. The proposal's comment period closed April 24, and as of Oct. 29, no final rule has been issued. The Supreme Court's handling of the proclamation challenge and any final action on the employment authorization proposal remain two consequential pending decisions affecting asylum applicants' access to protections and employment.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico have amended their lawsuit against President Donald Trump’s White House press ban, citing “continued retaliatory and viewpoint-discriminatory deprivation” by the Trump administration.
In recent weeks, the Trump administration has repeatedly excluded CNN and Politico from Trump’s Air Force One trips, even after a federal judge issued an order halting Trump’s broader original ban.

text:
CNN, MS NOW and Politico have amended their lawsuit against President Donald Trump’s White House press ban, citing “continued retaliatory and viewpoint-discriminatory deprivation” by the Trump administration.

The three news outlets are once again accusing the administration of violating the First and Fifth Amendments.

The updates to the lawsuit concern the White House’s interference with the press pool, a decades-old tradition that has news outlets take turns covering the president in close quarters, including Air Force One and the Oval Office.

In recent weeks, the Trump administration has repeatedly excluded CNN and Politico from Trump’s Air Force One trips, even after a federal judge issued an order halting Trump’s broader original ban.

“To be clear,” the expanded lawsuit states, the news outlets “do not claim an unrestricted right to enter the Oval Office or travel aboard Air Force One. But once the White House opens those spaces to selected journalists for newsgathering and reporting, the White House may not exclude plaintiffs because it dislikes their coverage.”

Last week, the outside counsel for the three news outlets, Ted Boutrous, threatened further legal action if the White House continued to bar reporters from specific areas, such as Air Force One.

Boutrous asked for confirmation that the administration would “abandon any policy of excluding CNN from the Oval Office and Air Force One” and stop preventing assigned pool reporters from doing their duties. The administration did not respond.

So Wednesday afternoon’s court filing is the next step.

The amended complaint asks the court for another ruling in favor of the news outlets: “The court should declare unlawful the President’s ban of plaintiffs and the White House’s further unconstitutional actions, including its continued exclusions of plaintiffs from specific White House press areas for retaliatory and viewpoint-discriminatory reasons, and enter permanent injunctive relief in favor of CNN, MS NOW, and Politico.”

The amended complaint comes two weeks after US District Judge Timothy P. Kelly granted a preliminary injunction restoring the outlets’ White House access, finding that Trump’s ban likely violated the First Amendment by discriminating against journalists based on their coverage of his administration.

Kelly had previously issued a temporary restraining order on Fifth Amendment grounds. The administration is appealing Kelly’s ruling.

When a CNN reporter asked the White House for comment about the amended lawsuit on Wednesday, a White House official said, “the Fake News has no place demanding a spot in the President’s Oval Office.”

The White House complied with Kelly’s court’s order and reinstated journalists’ press credentials late last month, but CNN, MS NOW and Politico say the administration has continued to retaliate against them by disrupting the press pool.

CNN has been barred from traveling aboard Air Force One on all six occasions when it was scheduled to serve as the designated TV network pooler since Trump announced the ban on September 18.

The TV pool role is one that “CNN has fulfilled for more than four decades,” the revised lawsuit points out. The five major US TV networks have a well-established pool rotation, and the other networks have shown support for CNN amid the dispute.

Politico has also been barred twice from its scheduled out-of-town pool assignments in recent weeks.

And MS NOW “has not participated in the secondary television pool since September 18,” the day Trump announced the ban, the revised lawsuit states. The secondary pool spot is selected by the White House.

When blocking the news outlets from fulfilling pool duties, the administration appears to be relying on an ongoing court case involving The Associated Press, which filed suit last year when Trump blocked AP reporters from areas with limited space for the press pool.

Trump took action against The AP because the news wire didn’t immediately start using his new name for the Gulf of Mexico like he wanted.

In June 2025, an appeals court panel partially lifted the stay obtained by The AP and stated that the news wire was not likely to succeed on the merits “because these restricted presidential spaces” like Air Force One and the Oval Office “are not First Amendment fora opened for private speech and discussion.”

But the ruling was “non-binding and non-precedential,” as Boutrous pointed out in his letter last week, so it is not binding on other cases.

The revised lawsuit asserts that the Oval Office and Air Force One have been “two of the primary spaces for journalists to interact with, gather news about, and publish reporting on President Trump and other officials.”

“While the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room remains a critical forum for reporters to gather and report the news, of the nearly 5,000 questions the President has entertained from reporters in these traditional areas, 97% were either in the Oval Office or in connection with his travel aboard Air Force One,” the lawsuit states.

Boutrous said in a statement on Wednesday that by excluding the banned news outlets from spaces like Air Force One, the administration is continuing “to violate the First Amendment and due process.”

“These exclusions, intended to punish and chill coverage of the administration that the President doesn’t like, make it harder for the press to cover some of the most important events in the world for the benefit of the American people,” Boutrous said. “CNN, MS NOW and Politico will continue to fight to vindicate their rights to report the news.”

title: Immigration shapes 2nd Congressional District race between Mitchell and James | Iowa Public Radio
description:
In the race for Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District seat, Republican Joe Mitchell and Democrat Lindsay James have both pledged to maintain secure American borders.
Two years later, some voters in the district are weary of immigration crackdowns, and the issue could shape the outcome one of the nation’s most competitive midterm congressional races.
Alongside the major party candidates, Libertarian Rick Stewart and independent Dave Bushaw are running to represent the district.
“Working-class solidarity isn’t defined by a border,” Bushaw said at an Oct. 21 campaign stop in Waterloo.
As voters critique both Biden and Trump-era immigration policies, those political memories could shape which candidate they choose this election – and what party secures control of Congress.
text:
In the race for Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District seat, Republican Joe Mitchell and Democrat Lindsay James have both pledged to maintain secure American borders.

That promise helped Republicans secure control in Washington, D.C., in 2024 after the country saw high levels of attempted border crossings under President Joe Biden. Two years later, some voters in the district are weary of immigration crackdowns, and the issue could shape the outcome one of the nation’s most competitive midterm congressional races.

Alongside the major party candidates, Libertarian Rick Stewart and independent Dave Bushaw are running to represent the district.

Biden-administration policies linger in midterm race debates

Mitchell, a housing developer from Clear Lake, uses the immigration issue to cast his opponent James, a state lawmaker from Dubuque, as a “radical left liberal.”

“She's somebody that missed over half her votes in the Legislature, and when she was there, she was voting to give illegal immigrants housing benefits, state Medicaid and food stamps,” he said at a Sept. 12 Republican fundraiser in Iowa City.

Mitchell appears to reference a law signed by Gov. Kim Reynolds in June (SF 2422) that revokes food assistance eligibility from some immigrant groups. James was absent from both House votes on the legislation. Fox News reported she missed 177 of 342, or 51.7%, of votes in the 2026 legislative session.

In her campaign, James has distanced herself from her party’s approach to immigration.

“The Biden administration didn't have strong enough policies when it came to securing the border,” she said at an Oct. 1 debate on Iowa’s News Now. “I am someone who has departed from my political party on several different occasions because I have courage of conviction.”

Nevertheless, Mitchell has attempted to tie his opponent to Biden-era immigration policy.

“You had tens of millions of illegal immigrants pouring over the border,” he said at the debate. “Joe Biden did nothing about, and he had the ability to do something about it. He could have closed the border; he did not.”

Strong feelings across the political spectrum

Tough talk on immigration helped Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson secure her third term representing the region in 2024. Hinson now leaves the seat open as she runs for the Senate, and some voters say GOP immigration crackdowns are motivating their choices this November.

Elizabeth Duff-Popplewell, a presbyterian minister in Waterloo, said she works frequently with the city’s immigrant communities and has seen the destabilizing effect of Trump administration policies. The outcome has disturbed her. Polling from earlier this year indicated many Americans feel similarly.

“These are people that have left home, and they want to make a life for their families, and they've done what our government asked them to do, and now the government has changed the rules,” Duff-Popplewell said.

It’s a motivating issue for young voters as well. University of Northern Iowa senior Abigail Lindgren said her peers follow talk about politics often.

“My friends who are immigrants from outside of the country — they're terrified that their student visas are going to get taken away someday,” Lindgren said. “I cannot afford to just turn my eyes away from what's going on in this world, and neither can my friends.”

Lindgred, a political communication major, works with the nonpartisan group PanthersVote to register students, hoping to turn those concerns into ballot box participation.

But two years later, the memory of Biden-era immigration policy remains a motivating issue for President Donald Trump’s base. Vice Chair of the Tama County GOP Central Committee Moe McWhirter said Biden’s immigration policies “essentially destroyed this nation.”

McWhirter said it was clear for decades the nation needed a border wall.

“It wasn't until Trump came along that we finally got somebody off the dime to do it, and it works,” he said.

Meeting the region's workforce needs

A New York Times/Siena poll released in October found Iowans are more likely to name affordability or the general economy as a top issue, over immigration. But they are intertwined.

Many cities in the district — like Dubuque, Waterloo and Cedar Rapids — have meatpacking, manufacturing or construction industries. Changes to immigration policy could have an economic impact because those industries recruit immigrant workers.

Professor emeritus of economics at UNI Bryce Kanago said increasing the pipeline of foreign workers could help reduce “labor costs” and slow inflation.

“We might revise immigration laws in a way that makes them more beneficial to the United States and to potential immigrants, and that somehow allows for a better path for businesses that want to hire workers on a temporary basis,” he said.

James has voiced support for such reforms. In a debate on Oct. 1 she called on both parties to “create a meaningful pathway to citizenship.”

“We can address the worker crisis and the needs that we have right now,” she said.

Mitchell, who has called for a ban on H1-B visas, said the state can meet its own workforce needs.

“American jobs for should be for Americans,” he said, “Iowan jobs should be for Iowans.”

According to Mitchell, the proposed Mesabi Metallics steel plant in southeast Iowa is the type of project which will spur economic development, including in the 2nd District.

“John Deere, they're going to save costs because of that steel mill. Kinze Manufacturing, they came out with a big letter last week saying their business will be better because of that steel mill, and so jobs for Iowans is a good thing,” he said on IPR’s River to River.

Independent Dave Bushaw of Hawkeye rejected the idea that immigrant workers and Iowans are in competition.

“Working-class solidarity isn’t defined by a border,” Bushaw said at an Oct. 21 campaign stop in Waterloo.

A squash farmer and musician, Bushaw said he previously worked at Postville’s Agri-Star Meat and Poultry plant, often alongside immigrants and first-generation Americans. Bushaw called for reforms to protect all workers in the United States, regardless of origin.

“We need to look at fixing our immigration system here because a lot of these workers coming in on H1-B or H2-A visas are being exploited,” he said.

Excluding them from labor protections “drives down competitive wages and benefits for working-class Americans,” he added.

As voters critique both Biden and Trump-era immigration policies, those political memories could shape which candidate they choose this election – and what party secures control of Congress.

text:
Immigrants’ Rights Organizations File Lawsuit to Stop ICE from Hiding Locations of Detained People

New Trump administration policy subjects thousands to intentional disappearance, keeping attorneys and families in the dark

A group of legal services organizations today filed a lawsuit challenging the federal government’s new policy of hiding the locations of thousands of people detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The policy unlawfully interferes with communication between detainees, their families, and their lawyers.

Jackie Kelley, director of immigration legal services at the Rian Immigrant Center: “We cannot allow the United States government to indefinitely disappear human beings. If we cannot locate our clients, we cannot pursue the relief for which they are legally eligible. The law gives our clients the right to seek protection. This policy obstructs that right when our clients need it most.”

The lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts on behalf of Greater Boston Legal Services, Rian Immigrant Center, Florence Immigrant and Refugee Rights Project, and Amica Center for Immigrant Rights. The groups argue the new policy unlawfully blocks them from locating, communicating with, and providing legal services to their clients and potential clients.

For over 16 years, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security has made the location of detained noncitizens available via its Online Detainee Locator System. In September, DHS abruptly changed course and stopped sharing the location of detained people with final orders of removal, either via the locator service or in direct response to queries from family members or attorneys. This policy of mass disappearance has thrown thousands into an administrative black box without any justification.

The new policy facilitates the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign by making it more difficult to provide detainees with access to attorneys and the judicial system — and thus more difficult to challenge unlawful detention and pursue lawful pathways to remain in the United States. Noncitizens with final orders of removal may still pursue a number of legal remedies to challenge their detention and deportation — but if they cannot access legal counsel or the courts, they may never have a chance to seek these remedies before they are deported.

The lawsuit alleges that ICE’s implementation of this new policy is arbitrary and capricious, and thus a violation of the Administrative Procedure Act. The complaint also alleges that ICE’s policy violates the plaintiffs’ First Amendment rights. Finally, the complaint alleges violations of the Freedom of Information Act because the government failed to publish details of their new policy. The plaintiffs are asking the court to vacate the new policy, and will shortly file a motion to stay the new policy while their case proceeds.

The plaintiffs are represented by the National Immigration Law Center, National Immigration Project, the American Civil Liberties Union, the ACLU of Massachusetts, and Annelise Araujo Law.

The following are statements from the other plaintiffs and their legal counsel:

Attorneys representing the plaintiffs: “The Trump administration’s new policy of mass disappearance should send a chill through everybody’s spine. By choosing to hide even the most basic information about thousands of people in its custody, the government is unlawfully blocking their access to legal counsel and the courts, and keeping desperate loved ones in the dark. This shockingly malicious policy was implemented suddenly, without any legal basis or justification, and with immediate, devastating impacts for our clients and the people they serve. The government must reverse course immediately, restore the Online Detainee Locator System, and stop hiding people in its vast network of detention facilities.”

Jacquelynne J. Bowman, executive director of Greater Boston Legal Services: “No one should be denied a meaningful opportunity to defend their rights because the government has made it impossible for their lawyer to find them. Even with representation, navigating the legal system is complex for immigrants facing deportation. This arbitrary new administrative change leaves hundreds of thousands of people at risk of potentially life-altering consequences without essential legal help.”

Laura St. John, legal director at the Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project: “The Trump administration is disappearing people within the immigration detention system. This should terrify every single one of us. Thousands of people are no longer being shown on the online detainee locator system, making it impossible for attorneys to locate their clients or identify people who might need emergency legal assistance. How can people in detention possibly have access to due process and safety if there is no way for their families or advocates to know where they are being held?”
