title: No bond, no judge: The case that could redefine immigrant rights in the United States
authors: María Constanza Costa, christian perry, Sahra Ali, Flozell Daniels, Justin Hansford, Esther Maddox, Ashanti Williams, Kyle Paoletta
description:
At issue is whether the federal government can hold immigrants in deportation proceedings without granting them a bond hearing before an immigration judge.
In the case of Barbosa da Cunha, his application for legal status has been pending since 2016, when he was granted a valid work permit.
According to the ACLU, nine out of 10 judges ruled that the Trump administration’s misinterpretation of immigration law is illegal.
An immigration judge later determined that Barbosa da Cunha did not pose a danger to the public or a significant flight risk and ordered his release.
Far more than one man’s case Although the case bears Barbosa da Cunha’s name, its consequences could extend far beyond his particular circumstances.
text:
As immigration returns to the center of the US political debate, the Supreme Court is preparing to decide a case that could fundamentally reshape the nation’s immigration detention system. At issue is whether the federal government can hold immigrants in deportation proceedings without granting them a bond hearing before an immigration judge.

Immigrant rights advocates argue that what is at stake extends far beyond an administrative procedure. The decision could determine how far executive authority reaches when depriving noncitizens of their liberty, and what constitutional protections remain available to them while their immigration cases are pending.

At the center of this legal battle is the case of Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha, a Brazilian national whose circumstances have become a critical test of the federal government’s detention powers. After entering the United States around 2004 or 2005 without formal inspection, Barbosa da Cunha spent the next two decades building a life in the country, raising a family, running a small construction business, applying for asylum, and obtaining authorization to work. He had no criminal record.

In September 2025, Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arrested him in Massachusetts on his way to work. Shortly afterward, the Department of Homeland Security initiated deportation proceedings against him.

Until recently, someone in Barbosa da Cunha’s position would typically have been able to request a bond hearing and argue before an immigration judge that he did not pose a danger to the community or a flight risk. But the Donald Trump administration adopted a new interpretation of immigration law under which individuals who entered the country without inspection may be subject to mandatory detention without access to a bond hearing, even if they have lived in the United States for decades.

A new interpretation of an old law

At the heart of the dispute is the Trump administration’s 2025 reinterpretation of an immigration statute enacted in 1996. This reinterpretation has led to the detention of thousands of immigrants eligible for legal status who have been waiting years for the US government to review their applications. In the case of Barbosa da Cunha, his application for legal status has been pending since 2016, when he was granted a valid work permit.

For decades, both Republican and Democratic administrations operated under the understanding that immigrants arrested within the United States could seek release on bond while contesting their deportation cases. The current administration has decided against this longstanding interpretation, arguing that the law requires mandatory detention for immigrants who entered the country without formal admission.

Under the Trump administration new reading of the statute, immigrants with no criminal history can remain detained throughout their removal proceedings—a process that often takes months and sometimes years.

“What the administration has done with this new interpretation of the law is massively expand their authority to detain people who have been here years, decades.”

After his arrest, Barbosa da Cunha filed a lawsuit brought by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) arguing that his detention without a bond hearing violated both federal immigration law and constitutional due process protections. According to the ACLU, nine out of 10 judges ruled that the Trump administration’s misinterpretation of immigration law is illegal. Nine federal appeals courts agreed.

A federal district court and the Second Circuit Court of Appeals both concluded that the relevant statute entitled Barbosa da Cunha to seek a bond hearing. An immigration judge later determined that Barbosa da Cunha did not pose a danger to the public or a significant flight risk and ordered his release. The government appealed, and the case ultimately reached the Supreme Court.

For Michelle Lapointe, legal director of the American Immigration Council, the case represents an extraordinary expansion of federal detention authority over immigrants who have lived in the country for years. Lapointe warned that the administration’s new interpretation is not aimed only at recent border crossers but also at long-term refugees waiting for their requests for asylum.

“What the administration has done with this new interpretation of the law is massively expand their authority to detain people who have been here years, decades. We’re talking long-term residents in the interior of the country and saying that they have no right to challenge their detention,” she said.

Lapointe added that, according to some estimates, “about six million people could be vulnerable to arrest and detention without bond under this new interpretation.”

A deep divide in the federal courts

The controversy has exposed a significant split among federal courts. While nine out of 11 federal appellate courts, have rejected the administration’s interpretation, the Fifth and Eighth Circuits sided with the government, creating the conflict that prompted Supreme Court review.

Lapointe confirmed that the Trump administration’s position has been consistently rejected across much of the federal judiciary. Judges appointed by both Democratic and Republican presidents have concluded that immigrants must be given an opportunity to seek release. According to Lapointe, “The vast majority of judges said that’s not permitted under the law. You have to give somebody the chance to argue for release on bond.”

The Supreme Court is currently being asked to resolve a question of statutory interpretation rather than constitutional law. The broader due process debate is already moving through the courts.

The policy shift has already triggered a wave of litigation.

The American Immigration Council served as lead counsel in a separate challenge before the Fifth Circuit, where detained immigrants argued that prolonged detention without an opportunity to seek release violates constitutional due process protections, even if the government’s interpretation of the statute is ultimately upheld.

“Three judges said, yes, due process under the Constitution requires that individuals be able to challenge their detention,” Lapointe said.

Far more than one man’s case

Although the case bears Barbosa da Cunha’s name, its consequences could extend far beyond his particular circumstances.

The Trump administration argues that it may detain without bond any immigrant who entered the country without formal admission, even if that person has spent years building a life in the United States. Legal experts say the outcome could affect tens of thousands of people currently in removal proceedings and shape the legal rights of millions of undocumented immigrants living in the country.

The policy shift has already triggered a wave of litigation. Thousands of detained immigrants have filed habeas corpus petitions challenging detention without access to a bond hearing.

Following the Second Circuit’s ruling in Barbosa da Cunha’s favor, Michael Tan, deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project and one of the attorneys involved in the case, argued that the Trump administration cannot simply reenvision the law to eliminate longstanding procedural protections. According to Tan, immigration law clearly requires that people like Barbosa da Cunha receive at least an opportunity to seek release before being held in prison for extended periods.

“The court was right to conclude the Trump administration can’t just reinterpret the law at its own whim. The law is clear: The government can’t lock up immigrants like Mr. Barbosa da Cunha without giving them the basic due process of a bond hearing. This ruling is an important victory, and we are thrilled for our client and his family,” Tan stated in a press release issued by the ACLU.

A question about liberty

The government’s argument is largely administrative. Officials contend that detention helps ensure that immigrants appear for court proceedings and do not abscond before a final removal order can be carried out.

The White House maintains that Congress granted the executive broad authority to manage immigration enforcement, and that detention is a legitimate tool for carrying out that responsibility. But for civil rights organizations this case touches on fundamental constitutional principles, not just immigration policy. In their view, permitting prolonged detention without meaningful judicial review would substantially expand the government’s power to deprive individuals of their liberty with limited oversight.

Deborah Fleischaker, vice president of immigration policy and strategy at UnidosUS, told NPQ that the current administration’s position cannot be understood in isolation from its broader deportation agenda.

“The Trump administration changed the interpretation of something that had been understood for many, many years, was never in question previously,” Fleischaker said. She argued that the shift seeks to maximize the government’s ability to hold immigrants in custody throughout removal proceedings.

A decision with lasting consequences

If the Supreme Court justices side with the government, mandatory detention without bond hearings could become a central feature of US immigration enforcement. If they rule in favor of Barbosa da Cunha, the decision will impose significant constraints on executive power and preserve the right of thousands of immigrants to seek release before an immigration judge.

For Fleischaker, a Supreme Court ruling in the government’s favor would not create a new reality so much as reinforce and accelerate existing enforcement practices. “We’re watching the impact of that play already, and if the Supreme Court agrees with the Trump administration, it just means that we’re going to see more of what we’re already seeing,” Fleischaker said.

In her view, that means a continued expansion of detention and deportation efforts, with more immigrants held for longer periods and a growing number of people swept into the enforcement system.

The case, therefore, is not simply about how a particular statute should be interpreted. It is also a test of how far the federal government can go in pursuing its mass deportation agenda, and how much judicial oversight will remain over one of its most powerful enforcement tools. Whatever the outcome, the court’s ruling is likely to become one of the most consequential immigration decisions of the Trump era, shaping the balance between executive authority and individual liberty for years to come.

text:
Why It Matters

The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights is lobbying to support S. 3779, the ICE Out of Our Faces Act, which would ban U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) from using facial recognition and other biometric surveillance technologies and require deletion of all previously collected biometric data within 30 days of enactment. The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights is the only organization listed in the Legis1 bill record for S. 3779, the ICE Out of Our Faces Act. ​

By the Numbers

The third-quarter 2026 report from the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights lists a filing amount of $270,000. That is up $50,000 from the in-house second-quarter 2026 report of $220,000. Year over year, in-house spending is down $260,000 from the $530,000 reported in the third-quarter 2025 report. Outside firm NVG LLC filed a separate third-quarter 2026 report for the same client, listing $60,000, bringing the combined client total to $330,000 this quarter.

Four lobbyists are named on the in-house filing:

Rahul S. Randhava, who served as a legislative assistant to Rep. Barney Frank (D-MA-4) in 2000

Jonathan Walter, senior policy counsel, who has prior government experience

Meeta Anand, senior director, Census and Data Equity

Maya Wiley, president and CEO

Broader Context

Frank Torres III, who appeared on the second-quarter 2026 in-house filing, is not listed on this quarter's report. S. 3779 was introduced Feb. 4, by Sen. Edward J. Markey (D-MA) and referred to the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs; the House companion, H.R. 7363, sponsored by Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-WA-7), remains in committee. The Electronic Frontier Foundation publicly supports S. 3779, and cosponsors include Sens. Ron Wyden (D-OR), Jeff Merkley (D-OR), Angela Alsobrooks (D-MD), and Bernie Sanders (I-VT).

The filing also lists support for the Facial Recognition and Biometric Technology Moratorium Act by title, without a bill number. On Sept. 25, Sens. Markey (D-MA) and Merkley (D-OR) and Reps. Jayapal (D-WA-7), Rashida Tlaib (D-MI-12), and Ayanna Pressley (D-MA-7) announced the bill's reintroduction, with cosponsors including Sens. Wyden (D-OR) and Warren (D-MA) and several House members. Sponsors argue the technology disproportionately exposes Black and Brown communities to misidentification, citing research that Black, Brown, and Asian people are up to 100 times more likely than white men to be misidentified, and that nearly half of U.S. adults' faces are already in facial-recognition databases. A broad coalition backs the moratorium bill, including the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), Fight for the Future, Color of Change, Access Now, and UnidosUS.

In May 2026, Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman (D-NJ-12) opposed H.R. 2853, a bill that she said would give the Department of Homeland Security sweeping new power to collect, analyze, and share Americans' personal data; her press release listed the Leadership Conference among the organizations opposing it.

Advertisement

H.R. 9125, the Sectoral AI Governance Act of 2026, was introduced June 3, 2026, by Rep. Sara Jacobs (D-CA-51), and its most recent action is its referral to the Committee on the Judiciary and, in addition, the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform. S. 4143 would extend federal minimum wage and labor protections under the Fair Labor Standards Act to incarcerated workers in government-run and privately operated facilities.

The Bottom Line

Both the Senate and House versions of the ICE Out of Our Faces Act have been referred to committee, with the House bill listed as "In Committee," and the in-house filing names one fewer lobbyist than the second-quarter report because Frank Torres III no longer appears.

text:
ICE agents tailed, boxed in, and then slashed the tire of observers’ vehicle before driving away

October 29, 2026 9:22 am

Media Contact

125 Broad Street

18th Floor

New York, NY 10004

United States

PORTLAND – Two Portland-area residents filed an administrative complaint with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (“DHS”) today describing how ICE agents tailed and boxed them in with vehicles and slashed their car’s tire after they observed and filmed agents in a parking lot in Hillsboro, a suburb of Portland, Oregon. The video of the agents slashing the tire can be viewed here.

The incident took place on October 7, 2026, amid a surge of ICE activity across the state of Oregon. The increase in ICE activity also coincided with a DHS social media post promising to target so-called “sanctuary” jurisdictions like Oregon. It is also the latest example of a pervasive pattern of retaliation against observers occurring all over the country; nationwide, federal agents have intimidated and harassed people observing and filming them in public, including by threatening them, tailing them, pulling them over without reasonable suspicion, surveilling their homes, and even assaulting and arresting them.

“What happened to us is not unique, and that is what is so terrifying,” said A.P and M.P., ACLU clients. “We observe and record public ICE activity in order to shine a light on their abusive behavior and to create a record of what our government is up to. Because of that, they are terrorizing us and anyone else who dares to exercise their First Amendment right to hold our government accountable. We hope that sharing our story will bring attention to their reckless and unconstitutional attacks on our communities.”

Over the past 18 months, the ACLU and its affiliates have brought several cases, including in Los Angeles, Chicago, and Minneapolis, representing observers who have been surveilled, intimidated, and harassed, for filming federal agents performing their duties in public. Most recently, the ACLU filed a case in Memphis, TN, where a federal task force has been terrorizing local communities for over a year and where observers describe a relentless retaliation campaign against them for filming task force agents.

“The right to record publicly visible law enforcement activity is fundamental to our democracy,” said Scarlet Kim, senior staff attorney with the ACLU’s Speech, Privacy, and Technology Project. “Like many people across the country, our clients have been observing and recording ICE activity in their community. These videos have proven critical to exposing ICE’s abuses. If we cannot see and document what our own government is doing on our streets, we cannot hold it accountable for running roughshod over our rights.”

“Masked federal officers have no business coming to Oregon to injure or intimidate people,” said Kelly Simon, legal director of the ACLU of Oregon. “Oregonians have the right to support their neighbors and communities by filming and documenting government abuses, and Oregonians should not have to fear retaliation when they exercise their right to record law enforcement.”

The complaint demands that DHS investigate the incident, preserve all relevant evidence, and discipline the responsible agents. It further demands that DHS undertake a comprehensive investigation of the nationwide pattern of ICE agents retaliating against individuals observing and recording their activities.

text:
The Trump administration is still detaining pregnant migrant youth in a region of Texas where a lack of specialized obstetric care can be life threatening for them, an investigation by The Texas Newsroom and The California Newsroom has found. The practice continues despite vocal concern from its own current and former officials, and from members of Congress.

Government records also show that at least four pregnant girls in detention have had to be transferred out of state since last July to receive specialized medical care, including at least one abortion, that is unavailable in Texas.

“The first time that happened should have been a wake-up call for the administration, and they should have stopped placing kids in any remote area where they can't get care,” said Jen Smyers, who during the Biden administration helped oversee the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR), which is responsible for migrant youth who are apprehended without a parent or guardian.

She called the policy to send pregnant children to South Texas “enraging.”

This spring, The Texas Newsroom and The California Newsroom published a joint investigation revealing the administration’s policy of detaining pregnant unaccompanied minors as young as 13 at a single shelter in the Rio Grande Valley. The investigation detailed serious concerns that health experts inside and outside the government had raised about the policy, given that adolescent pregnancies are inherently high risk and there is a lack of specialized obstetric care in the region.

Since then, the administration has denied the policy exists and said it is ensuring that the girls have access to the care they need.

In an unsigned email in September, a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees ORR, wrote that "ORR's policies for placing children in its custody into care provider facilities are based on child welfare best practices in order to provide a safe environment and place the child in the least restrictive setting appropriate for the child’s needs. This is especially true for expectant minors in ORR care.”

Yet the administration’s own records, as well as interviews with multiple government officials, suggest otherwise.

The documents, which were obtained through a public records request, show that ORR explicitly directed its staff in July 2025 to send all pregnant youth to the shelter in San Benito, just outside Brownsville.

Several months later, internal agency data showed that pregnant girls started being funneled to a different shelter nearby instead, according to three ORR officials who asked not to be named because they feared retaliation.

Forty-eight Democratic members of Congress expressed concerns about the policy in a pointed letter to the Department of Health and Human Services back in April.

They received a response in September from an assistant secretary at HHS, Alex J. Adams, who wrote that ORR “does not make placement decisions for pregnant youth based on a blanket rule or one-size-fits-all approach” and that it “takes seriously its responsibility to protect the health, safety, dignity, and well-being of every unaccompanied alien child in its custody.”

HHS did not respond to requests for comment about the discrepancy between the statements in Adams’ letter and the government’s own records.

“Obviously, they’re not being honest about their policy,” said U.S. Rep. Joaquin Castro, a Democrat from San Antonio, whose office authored the letter to HHS.

“It's irresponsible that they would wait several months to respond to basic questions about the care of some of the most vulnerable people within the system,” Castro said, adding that the administration failed to explain “what seems to be an informal but strict policy of sending these girls to deep South Texas, which lacks the medical care that the girls need.”

U.S. Rep. Dan Crenshaw, a Republican from Texas who has been vocal about the welfare of unaccompanied children and serves on a congressional committee that oversees HHS, did not respond to requests for comment.

Unaccompanied migrant children have historically been placed in shelters across the United States, but this summer, the Trump administration began detaining far more of them in Texas.

According to internal reports provided independently by two officials at ORR, both of whom asked not to be named due to fear of reprisal by their supervisors, 95% of the roughly 300 children apprehended by immigration officials in September were placed in detention in Texas, up from 45% in June.

Advocates for unaccompanied migrant children, former government officials, and some members of Congress have criticized the move, arguing that the state is not prepared to handle an influx of vulnerable children who need special care.

The fact that ORR has had to transfer several pregnant unaccompanied minors out of Texas to receive medical care, they say, is proving their point.

“If the government had to fly or transport these pregnant children across the country to get them the medical care they need, why on earth did it deliberately send them to Texas in the first place?” said U.S. Rep. Judy Chu, a Democrat from Southern California, who was unaware of the transfers until a journalist described the newsrooms’ findings.

Chu pointed to the fact that many of the pregnant children who enter federal immigration custody are the victims of sexual assault.

“If there is a 13-year-old girl who has survived rape,” she said, “she should be met with compassion, safety and appropriate medical care. Instead, this administration is placing children like her in a state where they will be deprived of access to basic healthcare. It's dangerous, and it's cruel, and there's no excuse for treating children this way.”

Government records contradict Trump administration’s claims

Unlike Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), which detains migrant adults and families in large, prison-like facilities, ORR detains unaccompanied children in group or foster homes overseen by private contractors. Laws, agency regulations and court orders require that the children receive comprehensive healthcare and appropriate education while they’re detained.

In an unsigned email last month, a spokesperson for HHS said that placing children in Texas is “operationally efficient” and that ORR’s facilities in the state “provide all requirements and more.” But records obtained through a public information request cast doubt on that assertion.

The records show between July of 2025, when ORR began placing pregnant girls in South Texas, and May of 2026, four of them had to be transferred to other states to receive medical treatment.

That’s roughly one in five of the more than 20 pregnant girls the agency placed in the region in that time frame, according to one ORR official.

In detailed notes for one of those cases, ORR staff wrote that a pregnant 12-year-old girl was transferred from the Rio Grande Valley to a shelter in New York on the recommendation of ORR’s division of health. The records note that the child needed access to specialists whose availability in South Texas is “extremely limited.”

In a note for another case, staff wrote that a pregnant girl was transferred to California due to an unspecified “high risk medical need.” In at least one case, a girl was transferred out of Texas because she had requested an abortion, the records show.

Marsha Griffin, a retired professor of pediatrics at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley School of Medicine, said such outcomes were inevitable. Griffin said the shelters have very few medical staff on hand and the region does not have enough specialized obstetricians.

“Young girls who are pregnant, especially those from 10 to 14 years of age, are automatically a high-risk population,” said Griffin, who oversaw medical students volunteering in ORR facilities in South Texas.

Internal communications, also obtained through a public records request, show that officials in ORR’s own division of health warned the agency’s leadership about the lack of pregnancy-related healthcare in the Rio Grande Valley.

“Texas has one of the worst rates of maternal mortality in the U.S.,” wrote Joanna Gaines, who at the time was ORR’s acting health director, in a July 18, 2025, email to Melissa Johnston, the agency’s head of operations. She added that the state “lack[s] access to quality perinatal healthcare” and that “Cameron County has one of the higher rates of infant mortality in Texas.”

Four days later, ORR issued a directive to begin placing “any pregnant children” at a shelter in Cameron County called Urban Strategies San Benito.

Tracey Wilkinson, a pediatrician in Indiana who specializes in reproductive healthcare access for minors, said that even if the government is transferring children to get medical care, waiting until they need it puts them in danger.

“When you're talking about labor or pregnancy complications, every minute counts,” Wilkinson said. “If it was a medical emergency that required this young person to be transported out of the state, the risk to her survival would be lower for no reason other than she was placed in the middle of nowhere, far away from medical care.”

'They are trying to deliberately mislead Congress members'

Shortly after The Texas Newsroom and The California Newsroom revealed the Trump administration’s policy of detaining pregnant migrant youth in Texas, Castro launched an inquiry into the practice. He soon arranged a visit to the San Benito shelter.

But by the time of his visit on April 7, internal agency data showed that ORR had stopped placing newly detained children with known pregnancies at the facility, three officials said. Instead, the agency was sending them to a different shelter, in Los Fresnos, just 20 minutes away.

Castro said he was not told of the change at the time of his visit, nor was it mentioned in ORR’s formal response to the congressional inquiry last month.

In a recent interview, he described his visit to the San Benito shelter as “a very secretive process” and said he was not allowed to see or speak with any of the children there.

An HHS spokesperson did not respond to questions about the location change, writing only that “there have been no operational changes regarding the placement of pregnant unaccompanied children.”

Chu, the Congresswoman from California, said she believed the Trump administration made the change in order to “deliberately mislead Congress members as well as the public from really knowing where these pregnant children have been.”

Compass Connections, the San Antonio-based nonprofit that operates the shelter in Los Fresnos where pregnant girls are now being held, is one of the largest ORR contractors; it has been awarded over $1.9 billion in federal grants to house and care for unaccompanied minors over the past four years, according to USAspending.gov. Asked for comment, the company referred the newsrooms to HHS.

In his letter to Castro, Assistant Secretary Adams wrote that “placement and transfer decisions are individualized and consider the child’s safety, medical and behavioral health needs, pregnancy-related needs, available services, legal access, family unity, least restrictive placement requirements, and the best interest of the child.”

'In California, they would have more access to all reproductive healthcare'

Congress members and advocates in California said the state offers much more support for pregnant girls in federal custody than they can receive in Texas.

As the Trump administration has withdrawn federal support for legal representation of unaccompanied children — and at the same time streamlined the process of deporting them — the state of California, as well as several of its cities and counties, have ramped up funding for their own legal services programs for undocumented kids.

“Pregnant unaccompanied children have rights to medical care, safety, family unity and due process, but those rights mean little without a lawyer to defend them,” said Marion "Mickey" Donovan-Kaloust, director of legal services at Immigrant Defenders in Los Angeles. “California's support systems can provide pregnant unaccompanied children with the stability, dignity and specialized care they need to be safe and thrive.”

In addition to concerns about their access to healthcare and legal services, advocates worry that the Trump administration is knowingly putting pregnant children at risk to advance an ideological goal: denying them access to abortions by placing them in Texas, where abortion is virtually banned.

Current federal regulations require the government to move detained minors who request abortions to states where it’s legal. In January, the Trump administration announced it plans to rescind that rule, though it hasn’t yet done so.

An HHS spokesperson said in February that claims the department is attempting to restrict unaccompanied children’s access to abortion are “completely inaccurate.”

Congressman Gil Cisneros, a Democrat from Southern California, said, “In California, they would have more access to all reproductive healthcare, and then they could make decisions based on discussions with their healthcare professional and what's best for them.”

Chu noted that the midterm elections will determine whether Democrats regain control of the U.S. House of Representatives. If they do, she said, they will redouble their efforts to ensure pregnant children in federal immigration custody are given proper care.

(Wilkinson), from Board of Immigration Appeals.
text:
Where an immigration judge concluded a woman seeking asylum failed to show that a Honduran gang was responsible for the disappearance of her husband and her brother’s death, and the Board of Immigration Appeals, or BIA, affirmed this decision, but the woman then received death threats from her husband’s suspected killers, the BIA erred when it failed to consider whether, with the benefit of the new evidence, a reasonable inference may now be formed that the gang did commit those crimes.

Background

An immigration judge, or IJ, and the BIA denied the asylum applications of Jenyfer Fajardo-Rivas and her young daughter, who came to the United States to evade a gang in Honduras. But after receiving death threats from her husband’s suspected killers, Fajardo-Rivas asked the BIA to take a second look. It declined, reasoning that the threats were not enough to warrant reopening the proceedings.

Analysis

Under the Immigration and Nationality Act, applicants must show “persecution or a well-founded fear of persecution on account of” a protected ground such as “race, religion, nationality,” or “membership in a particular social group.” An applicant’s immediate family can be a “particular social group.” Persecution occurs “on account of” such a group when membership in the group is “‘at least one central reason for’ the feared persecution.”

The BIA’s most recent opinion denied Fajardo-Rivas’s motion to reopen on the grounds that her claim of persecution lacked the requisite nexus to a protected group. A credible threat of death categorically qualifies as persecution, but the agency found that Fajardo-Rivas could not establish she was persecuted “on account of” her membership in the particular social group of her husband’s family.

The government defends the BIA’s decision by framing this case as a personal, private dispute dressed up as family-based persecution. The threatening notes call Fajardo-Rivas a “snitch,” suggesting that the gang is retaliating against her for accusing them of abducting Jorge. According to the government, this indicates “personal animus”—anger because she reported the crime—rather than an attempt to target her because of her membership in Jorge’s family.

Yet this case is notable for all the government does not contest. Most importantly, the government accepts petitioners’ evidence that members of the 18th Street Gang likely delivered the threatening notes. As discussed, the individuals who delivered the notes had tattoos indicating membership in the 18th Street Gang. When asked about the tattoos at oral argument, the government acknowledged that this evidence “does suggest that a gang member actually left the notes.”

The government nonetheless emphasizes it is unclear whether the 18th Street Gang is responsible for Jorge’s abduction or Geovanny’s murder. Fajardo-Rivas has submitted no proof that Honduran authorities identified the culprits of either crime. Without such evidence, the government says, the BIA did not abuse its discretion in determining that Fajardo-Rivas’s persecution lacks a nexus to her membership in Jorge’s family group. After all, the “gang may well have threatened a non-family member for reporting the kidnapping as well.”

The government’s argument is hard to square with this court’s prior decisions. With these precedents in mind, Fajardo-Rivas’s new evidence compels the conclusion that she has satisfied the nexus requirement. Her relationship to Jorge “was a central reason why she, and not another person,” reported his abduction to the police, triggering retaliation.

Fajardo-Rivas did not “happened upon” the crime. The assailants abducted her husband from the family’s home. And they did so, she contends, because of the family’s connection to a different opponent of the gang, her husband’s brother. Then, years later, the gang sent death threats directed not only at Fajardo-Rivas, but at her daughter and other members of the family. To deny the connection between Fajardo-Rivas’s persecution and her family group obscures why she got caught up in this morass.

The government would like this court to defer to the IJ’s finding in 2018 that Fajardo-Rivas failed to show that the 18th Street Gang was responsible for harming Jorge and Geovanny. But the IJ’s finding preceded the death threats. The BIA’s 2025 decision does not seriously consider whether, with the benefit of the new evidence, a reasonable inference may now be formed that the gang did commit those crimes.

The BIA placed too much weight on the IJ’s pre-death-threat findings and too little weight on petitioners’ new evidence. The BIA’s focus on the IJ’s uncertainty about who committed the underlying crimes—Jorge’s abduction and Geovanny’s murder—led the BIA to neglect uncontradicted evidence that (1) Fajardo-Rivas gave the police information about those crimes, exposing the gang to scrutiny, and (2) members of the gang, identified by their gang tattoos, threatened to kill her and other members of her family.

Petition for review granted. Vacated and remanded.

Fajardo-Rivas v. Blanche, Case No. 25-1280, Oct. 13, 2026. 4th Cir. (Wilkinson), from Board of Immigration Appeals. Margot Pyne Kniffin for Petitioners. Sharon Michele Clay for Respondent. VLW 026-2-361. 12 pp.

title: Trump's Proposed Census Rule Changes Are a Threat to Democracy | Common Dreams
description:
For the first time in history, Trump’s Census Bureau has proposed removing questions on race and ethnicity from the census and excluding noncitizens without a green card from the census count.
The proposed rule changes are part of this administration’s racist and anti-immigrant agenda to unravel civil rights protections and erase immigrants from our nation.
The open comment period on the proposed census rule changes ends on November 2.
The proposed rule changes are part of this administration’s racist and anti-immigrant agenda to unravel civil rights protections and erase immigrants from our nation.
The open comment period on the proposed census rule changes ends on November 2.
text:
With the nation’s focus on the upcoming midterm elections, the Trump administration is quietly proposing changes to rules for the 2030 census that would threaten American democracy for decades to come. If we don’t act now, the next census could erase millions of people from the count.

The last Census in 2020 undercounted Latinos by almost 5%, three times the undercount of the 2010 Census, making this racial-ethnic group second only to American Indians and Alaska Natives in undercount. Latinos are now at even more risk of being undercounted by the next Census. The Trump administration has created fear and mistrust of the government by unleashing Immigration and Custom Enforcement (ICE) terror on our communities and is now scheming to strip us of political power and economic resources.

For the first time in history, Trump’s Census Bureau has proposed removing questions on race and ethnicity from the census and excluding noncitizens without a green card from the census count. The proposed rule changes are part of this administration’s racist and anti-immigrant agenda to unravel civil rights protections and erase immigrants from our nation.

Excluding immigrant residents would harm every person in the communities where they reside, including US citizens. States with substantial immigrant populations could receive fewer congressional seats.

Our organization, LatinoJustice PRLDEF, is sounding the alarm on how these changes would harm Latino and immigrant communities. Census undercounts have real world consequences, not only in the loss of congressional representatives, but also in the reduction of lifesaving resources like funding for Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutritional Assistance Program (SNAP) as well as funding for public education and school lunches. More than 300 federal programs allocate resources based on Census data.

The constitution mandates a numerical count of every person living in the United States every 10 years, regardless of immigration status, and requires that congressional seats and federal tax money be apportioned based on the number of people living in each state. The census has included questions on race since it was first initiated in 1790.

Removing questions on race and ethnicity would make it harder to track whether Black and brown communities have equal access to education, housing, and healthcare, and make it more difficult to monitor and address racist exclusion from resources and opportunities.

The proposed rule to exclude noncitizens without a green card would not only exclude undocumented immigrants but also exclude refugees, asylees, and residents with pending immigration applications. LatinoJustice objects to treating such residents as absent from our communities for purposes of representation.

Excluding immigrant residents would harm every person in the communities where they reside, including US citizens. States with substantial immigrant populations could receive fewer congressional seats.

Adding a question on immigration status to the census would further discourage Latinos—regardless of their immigration status—from participating in the count at a time when trust in the government is at an all time low in our communities. ICE terror has made many immigrants afraid to interact with the government in any way—whether to report being the victim of a crime, access medical care, or accept disaster assistance. A census designed to heighten those fears could erase millions from the count.

The Trump administration is proposing another rule change that would cause even more confusion and lead to an undercount of students, snowbirds, and those in non-traditional housing by using tax records to establish residence. All of these proposed changes seem aimed at reducing census participation and undercounting vulnerable communities.

LatinoJustice PRLDEF has worked to promote participation in the census—as imperfect as it is—because we know what a huge impact the count has on our communities. We submitted commentary opposing the dangerous rule changes proposed by the Trump administration. It’s not too late for you to submit your objections, too. But you need to act now.

The open comment period on the proposed census rule changes ends on November 2. We’re calling for the comment period to be extended at least another 90 days so that advocates and experts have the opportunity to weigh in, but we don’t know if the extension will be granted.

Latinos’ enormous contributions to our economy and society make America what it is. Each and every one of us deserves to be counted.

text:
A transgender woman claims she was unlawfully arrested by ICE agents this week after her flight home landed at the Rochester airport.

The agents shouted her name – Clara Tan – to confirm her identity before taking her into custody, she said. She then was taken to the detention facility in Batavia that only houses men but released hours later after a physical examination confirmed she did not have male genitalia.

"I’ve just had one of the worst 18- hour periods of my life," Tan wrote of the incident on Facebook. "I think it’s an important story to share."

Tan, 33, says four men who identified themselves as Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents approached her around 12:30 a.m. Tuesday as she left the Frederick Douglass Greater Rochester International Airport. She asked if they had a warrant, she said, then attempted to use her phone. That is when she alleges the men tackled and handcuffed her, injuring her left foot.

"I felt pain like you never felt before," she said, "and the next thing I knew, I was on the ground. And I'm thinking, all right, here we go."

ICE did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment.

Tan is originally from Singapore, and came to the United States in 2019 to attend the American Musical and Dramatic Academy in New York. She filed a petition for asylum in 2019, and had a work permit.

She was returning from California, having traveled there for a concert that got cancelled because the Japanese performers could not obtain visas.

“There's a sort of poetry symmetry about it," she said. "I only went to L.A. for a show that got canceled because of immigration shit, and then I spent the end of my trip in immigration detention."

Tan says she spent her time in California attending Cosplay Trackside instead, an anime gathering in Arcadia. She included pictures from her trip in her account of the arrest and detention on Facebook.

"I wouldn’t have chosen any other way to spend a week," she wrote, "even if the flight there and back was what put me on ICE’s radar."

While in Batavia, Tan alleges, she was told she would be kept at the all-men's facility, despite identifying as a woman.

In January of 2025, President Donald Trump issued an executive order requiring all federal offices only recognize two genders, and defining biological sex as assigned at birth. Later that year, ICE released updated National Detention Standards to align with the order, essentially abolishing any guidance on the healthcare and housing of transgender individuals in detention.

Tan started hormone therapy in 2016, and underwent gender-affirming surgery in 2024.

After voicing her concerns at Batavia, she said, a guard summoned two female medical staff.

"They were like, we need to check to make sure that you don't have a penis," Tan said.

After the examination, Tan says she was released, and that a guard dropped her off at the gate of the facility, where she was picked up by a friend and taken to Strong Memorial Hospital.

Tan has an order to appear in immigration court Dec. 8, and for now is on supervised release, fitted with an ankle monitor.

text:
FRUITRIDGE POCKET, Calif. —

Sacramento City Manager Maraskeshia Smith has issued a directive to the Sacramento Police Department, instructing officers not to assist U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents unless a credible public safety threat is established.

The directive follows an incident on Tuesday morning near 16th Avenue and 47th Street in South Sacramento, where police responded to reports of a car driving recklessly and detained the individuals inside while officers conducted an investigation. Police said a report will be completed documenting the incident.

According to NorCal Resist, a local immigration watchdog group, the three people detained were observers documenting ICE activity.

NorCal Resist shared video footage after the incident, which they said shows Sacramento police officers interacting with federal agents.

"We'll be seeking accountability and transparency on exactly what happened. But we have no doubt that ICE called this in, and Sac PD responded in the way they did," Giselle Garcia, programs director with NorCal Resist, said.

In response to the incident, Smith sent a letter to Interim Sacramento Police Chief Zachary Bales stating that Sacramento police officers "are not, and shall not act as, a security detail for ICE or its immigration enforcement operations."

She emphasized that officers should not be dispatched solely because individuals are following, observing, or recording ICE agents, as such actions do not constitute a public safety emergency.

The letter outlined that dispatchers must establish clear and articulable facts of a credible threat before sending officers to assist ICE. Smith provided examples of situations that may justify a response, such as specific threats of violence, assaults, or other criminal conduct posing an imminent risk to safety.

KCRA 3 reached out to the police department for a response to the letter. A spokesperson for the department directed us back to the City Manager’s Office.

The letter provides clear direction regarding requests for assistance from ICE, however, it is not clear who reported the car to police. NorCal Resist believes ICE agents made the call to police, but the department stated it does not release the identities of callers.

The Department of Homeland Security also declined to confirm who made the call, stating, "For operational security and the safety of our officers, ICE will not disclose or discuss law enforcement operations."

name: Litigation
title: Bonus 259: City of Baltimore v. Texas - by Steve Vladeck
description:
On Tuesday morning, the Supreme Court handed down a one-sentence order denying an emergency application, with no noted dissents, in a case with a strange caption, City of Baltimore v. Texas.
Within hours, the two nominal adversaries filed a joint motion asking Judge O’Connor to rule for Texas.
And now the Supreme Court has done the same.
Federal courts aren’t supposed to be notaries for agreements between parties who want the same thing, and the Supreme Court has said as much for more than 130 years.
For those who aren’t paid subscribers, we’ll be back (no later than) Monday with our regular coverage of the Supreme Court.
text:
On Tuesday morning, the Supreme Court handed down a one-sentence order denying an emergency application, with no noted dissents, in a case with a strange caption, City of Baltimore v. Texas. The ruling didn’t get a lot of attention, perhaps because the case comes wrapped in some fairly dense immigration court (and appellate) procedure, and perhaps because, for some reason, it took the Court almost a full day to post the order to its website.

But I think the entire dispute deserves a lot more attention than it has thus far received. On June 22 of this year, Texas sued the U.S. Department of Justice in the Wichita Falls Division of the Northern District of Texas (where there was a 100% chance that the suit would be assigned to Chief Judge Reed O’Connor), challenging a 2024 Biden-era rule that allows immigration judges to “administratively close” (that is, temporarily shelve) certain removal cases. Within hours, the two nominal adversaries filed a joint motion asking Judge O’Connor to rule for Texas. He did so that same day, vacating the entire rule nationwide and permanently enjoining the Justice Department from adopting anything like it in the future (yes, this last part is especially wild).

Both sides waived their right to appeal. When three cities and an immigration legal services provider (Centro Legal) tried to step in and defend the rule that no one else would, Judge O’Connor held that they lacked standing. The Fifth Circuit, without a written opinion, declined to disturb any of this. And now the Supreme Court has done the same.

Reasonable people can (and do) disagree about the validity of the Biden-era administrative closure rule. But the way it was eliminated ought to bother just about everyone. The way to get rid of a rule is to rescind it, not to enter into a collusive settlement with a state that challenged it. Federal courts aren’t supposed to be notaries for agreements between parties who want the same thing, and the Supreme Court has said as much for more than 130 years. Four of the current justices have even complained about a milder version of this very maneuver—albeit back in 2022, when the ideological shoe was on the other foot.

And if the whole thing sounds even more familiar, it should: This is the second time in barely a year that the Justice Department, the Texas Attorney General’s Office, and Judge O’Connor have combined to make an arguably valid rule disappear in a single day.

Today’s bonus post explains how we got here, it summarizes why this is both a sequel to last year’s in-state tuition case and something quite different from the “sue and settle” practices Republicans spent the Obama and Biden presidencies decrying, it describes how the lower courts let it happen (and why each step was a problem on its own), and it takes up what, to me, is the hardest question: Why didn’t any of the Democratic appointees publicly dissent from, or at least write with respect to, the Supreme Court’s denial of a stay?

For those who aren’t paid subscribers, we’ll be back (no later than) Monday with our regular coverage of the Supreme Court. For those who are, please read on.

title: Social media surveillance case faces uncertainty after judge's death - CSMonitor.com
authors: Varsha Bansal, The Christian Science Monitor
description:
“Plaintiffs’ allegations are of an ongoing surveillance program that is actively chilling the speech of their members and otherwise causing harm.
In its filing, the government acknowledged the practice of reading some immigrants’ social media posts, but described it as a targeted effort.
“We are still far away even from an injunction being granted to shut down the challenged surveillance program,” she says.
The current lawsuit also cites such similar examples, and explains the role of social media surveillance.
In some cases, members have deleted online posts or disabled their social media accounts.
text:
The future of a lawsuit challenging the Trump administration’s right to surveil immigrants’ social media posts using artificial intelligence was thrown into doubt Wednesday following the sudden death of a federal judge who only weeks ago ruled the case could move forward.

“Plaintiffs’ allegations are of an ongoing surveillance program that is actively chilling the speech of their members and otherwise causing harm. ... I agree,” U.S. District Court Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein wrote on Oct. 1.

In the wake of Judge Hellerstein’s death, a new judge will be “randomly” assigned to his cases, according to the district executive for the Southern District of New York.

The surveillance suit, brought by three of the nation’s major labor unions, argues that the government’s monitoring of millions of visa and green card holders’ online activity is a form of “viewpoint discrimination” that violates the First Amendment. The unions say that’s already resulted in “adverse immigration action” based on the beliefs those immigrants profess.

The groups, which include the United Auto Workers, Communications Workers of America and American Federation of Teachers, also allege the State Department and Department of Homeland Security failed to follow federal rules when they implemented the program, violating the Administrative Procedure Act.

The government had sought to quash the suit, arguing the unions lacked standing. In its filing, the government acknowledged the practice of reading some immigrants’ social media posts, but described it as a targeted effort. “There is no monolithic government surveillance program,” Assistant U.S. Attorney Jennifer Jude wrote in a motion to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that the plaintiffs collected unrelated instances to craft their complaint.

No injunction to block social media review

Judge Hellerstein’s death would appear to be a setback to plaintiffs, which might now have to proceed before a less favorable jurist or face delays as the judge’s cases are reassigned.

Judge Hellerstein, who was in his 90s, was a senior federal judge in the U.S. District Court in Manhattan. Appointed by President Bill Clinton in 1998, he handled litigation that stemmed from the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, and was presiding over the prosecution of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Last year, he blocked the Trump administration from using the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 for deportation from his district.

For now, the Trump administration’s surveillance programs will be allowed to continue.

That’s because, while Judge Hellerstein allowed the case to proceed, he did not impose an injunction that immediately ordered the Trump administration to stop reviewing immigrants’ social media posts.

Margaret Hu, a law professor at William & Mary Law School, says the case is in early stages and is moving slowly. “We are still far away even from an injunction being granted to shut down the challenged surveillance program,” she says.

A case management conference, where the judge is expected to set rules for discovery, is scheduled for Nov. 12.

A State Department spokesperson said the agency doesn’t comment on ongoing litigation. A DHS spokesperson declined to comment on investigative methods or ongoing investigations, but in an email offered this on the department’s general use of technology: “Like other law enforcement agencies, ICE employs various forms of technology while respecting civil liberties and privacy interests.”

The plaintiffs argue the government could not surveil at scale by manually scouring the internet, since there are about 55 million visa holders in the country. But, by using “automated and Al systems,” it alleges that the government “can review and process large volumes of social media and online activity at a scale previously difficult or impossible to analyze with human review alone.”

Citing federal contracts, the complaint shows that the State Department and the DHS have bought access to a range of AI-powered online activity monitoring tools: including Fivecast ONYX, which its maker says can “track shifts in sentiment and emotion” in a person’s posted data; and Penlink’s Tangles, which the complaint says is a “social media monitoring product” that can perform facial recognition on images, sentiment analysis on posts, and add specific social media accounts to a “watch list.”

The complaint also refers to a 2025 report about the State Department’s “Catch and Revoke” program that surveils student visa holders, saying that when they “find those who have supported terrorists or otherwise abused our hospitality, their visas are instantly revoked.”

Saira Hussain, a senior staff attorney at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, and one of the lawyers representing the plaintiffs said the surveillance represented a form of retaliation, “designed to stop people from speaking in ways that the government doesn’t want them to be speaking.”

What makes this lawsuit unique, legal experts say, is that it’s targeting the system of surveillance.

It’s “an interesting attempt to attack the government repression of immigrants’ free speech rights at a systemic level by addressing the surveillance policies rather than the individual deportation cases,” says Michael Kagan, a law professor at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas.

Case hinges on issue of free speech for noncitizens

Two main questions tug at the core of this lawsuit, Mr. Kagan adds: “Do noncitizens have the right to free speech? And if yes, what is the remedy when the government represses that speech?”

This isn’t the first time courts are debating these questions. Last year, U.S. District Judge William Young, an appointee of Republican President Ronald Reagan, ruled that lawful noncitizens have the same free speech rights as citizens. That case was filed by a group of university associations that cited early arrests like that of green-card holder and Columbia University graduate Mahmoud Khalil, a leader in campus protests against Israel’s military campaign in Gaza.

But earlier this year, Judge Young limited the protection his ruling provided to the members of the group that brought on this case.

The current lawsuit also cites such similar examples, and explains the role of social media surveillance. The lawsuit alleges that Homeland Security Investigations analysts compiled online information and social media posts by Mr. Khalil – an Algerian citizen – where he expressed support for Palestinians, following which he was arrested in March 2025. During the same month, the complaint says the administration “made a very public example” by arresting Rümeysa Öztürk, a Tufts University graduate student and F-1 visa holder. They alleged that Ms. Öztürk was surveilled online and her online op-ed in the Tufts student newspaper was obtained by HSI analysts as evidence that eventually contributed to her visa to be revoked.

A month later, the complaint alleges, Mohsen Mahdawi, at the time a student at Columbia University, was arrested right after his naturalization interview, in part because screenshots of his social media posts showed support of Palestinians.

The surveillance program, the complaint says, has made several noncitizens reluctant to share union posts online or join union-related group chats. In some cases, members have deleted online posts or disabled their social media accounts.

“They’re seeing their members disengaging both online, but also in person in real life,” says Ms. Hussain. “Because of concerns that if they’re associated with the union, if they speak too loudly on behalf of the union, or if they speak at all, that could be something that the government uses against them and terminates their student visa or whatever other status they have.”

Rachel Levinson-Waldman, director of the Brennan Center’s Liberty and National Security Program, says this case is “a really strong endorsement of First Amendment protections for speech of non-citizens in the U.S.” while also showing the significant impact of the administration’s threats to punish dissenting viewpoints.

While the plaintiff’s claims are compelling, according to Ms. Levinson-Waldman, the more important detail in the case moving ahead is that the court iterated how the government does not have total discretion as soon as anything immigration-related comes into the picture. “Instead, where a case does not specifically involve an individual’s removal proceeding, courts can consider the issues and ensure that constitutional protections, democratic rights, and the rule of law are upheld,” she says.

title: Trump's mandatory immigration detention policy fails the textualist test - Reason Magazine
authors: Jeremy Etelson, Chelsea Follett, Eric Boehm, Damon Root, Veronique de Rugy, C.J. Ciaramella
description:
Should federal immigration law treat that person the same way it treats someone who was just apprehended at the border?
The legal dispute turns on two phrases in one section of this federal immigration law.
But if nearly everyone who ever illegally entered the country is already subject to mandatory detention, as the administration asserts, then all of those carefully drawn separate categories for mandatory detention suddenly become superfluous and pointless for noncitizens who illegally entered the country, an objection that Douglas raised in dissent⁠.
The administration may believe mandatory detention makes immigration enforcement faster or more effective.
Whether mandatory detention would accelerate Trump's deportation program is a question of policy.
text:
Assume the following: A person unlawfully entered the United States 20 years ago and has since started a business and raised U.S.-citizen children, has no criminal record, and has never been found to be dangerous. Should federal immigration law treat that person the same way it treats someone who was just apprehended at the border? Should the law treat that person as if Congress had specifically made them subject to mandatory detention for criminal or terrorism-related conduct?

Under the Trump administration, the answer is yes. President Donald Trump's current policy treats noncitizens who entered without lawful admission as subject to mandatory detention without bond throughout removal proceedings, even if they have lived in the United States for decades and have no criminal record⁠. The executive branch adopted that position in new Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) guidance issued in July 2025⁠, reversing its prior interpretation of the same detention law.

The U.S. Supreme Court will now decide whether Congress actually required the result Trump is seeking. On October 1, the justices agreed to hear the case of Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha⁠. Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha, a Brazilian national, entered the United States without inspection around 2005. He later applied for asylum, received work authorization, and eventually bought a home. He operates a small construction business and lives with his wife and two U.S.-citizen children. He has no criminal record. But immigration officers still arrested him while he was driving to work in Massachusetts in September 2025.

After Cunha challenged his detention, a federal court ordered a bond hearing and an immigration judge found that he posed neither a danger nor a flight risk and therefore released him on bond while his case proceeded. The Trump administration then appealed to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit and lost. Now the Supreme Court will have the final word⁠.

The Supreme Court is not deciding whether Cunha may ultimately remain in the country. Instead, it is deciding the narrower question of whether the Immigration and Nationality Act mandates detention pending removal proceedings for someone like Cunha who is present in the United States without having been lawfully admitted⁠.

The legal dispute turns on two phrases in one section of this federal immigration law. According to Section 1225, a noncitizen present in the United States who has not been legally admitted is considered an "applicant for admission." But when Congress imposed mandatory detention later in that same section, it used additional language, applying it to an applicant for admission who is "seeking admission."

That distinction may sound technical and trivial, but its consequences are enormous. If every statutory "applicant for admission" is automatically still "seeking admission," then the government can treat someone who crossed the border 20 years ago the same as someone arriving today and keep them in jail without the possibility of bond. If the two phrases mean two different things, however, then Cunha and others like him are generally eligible for a bond hearing under Section 1226, which permits both detention and release on bond or conditional parole⁠.

The Trump administration argues that if Congress has deemed someone an applicant for admission, that person must necessarily still be seeking the admission for which they are considered an applicant. But the administration's argument asks the Court to stretch federal law beyond its reasonable limits. Congress expressly deemed certain people "applicants for admission." It did not separately deem them to be "seeking admission."

This case, in short, is about textualism. And as the late Justice Antonin Scalia and his co-author Bryan Garner argue in their book, Reading Law: The Interpretation of Legal Texts, one of the key principles of textualism is that "a material variation in terms suggests a variation in meaning." When Congress uses different words in closely related provisions, in other words, courts should hesitate before assuming that the different words mean the exact same thing.

In ordinary English, it is certainly difficult to describe a man driving from home to work after living in the United States for over two decades as presently "seeking admission." He is not seeking to enter the U.S.; he already entered decades earlier. The 2nd Circuit's unanimous opinion—written by Judge Joseph Bianco, a Trump appointee—reached this conclusion, holding that "seeking admission" describes ongoing activity rather than merely a retained statutory status⁠.

Meanwhile, when the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit upheld the administration's position in a similar case, Judge Dana Douglas, an appointee of former President Joe Biden, invoked the same Scalia-Garner textualist principles in dissent.

The legal dispute, therefore, does not follow neat partisan lines. Judges from different ideological backgrounds have both concluded that the administration's reading goes beyond the words that Congress wrote.

The broader statutory structure also supports that conclusion. Congress has long required mandatory detention in Section 1226 for specified criminal and terrorism-related grounds⁠. And the Laken Riley Act of 2025 expanded those mandatory-detention categories⁠. But if nearly everyone who ever illegally entered the country is already subject to mandatory detention, as the administration asserts, then all of those carefully drawn separate categories for mandatory detention suddenly become superfluous and pointless for noncitizens who illegally entered the country, an objection that Douglas raised in dissent⁠.

History also clarifies the point. For nearly 30 years, across five presidential administrations (including Trump's first), the government generally treated people like Cunha as potentially eligible for bond. Trump only reversed course in July 2025. The 2nd Circuit thus accurately described the earlier interpretation as a well-established executive branch practice⁠.

Of course, past executive practice cannot override clear statutory language. But if Congress really did mandate a sweeping detention regime in 1996⁠, it is striking that every presidential administration since then has operated under a totally different understanding⁠.

None of this gives Cunha lawful immigration status. Nor does it guarantee his release or prevent the government from deporting him. Rather, it allows an immigration judge to ask a basic question: Is keeping this particular person in jail actually necessary while his case proceeds?

The administration may believe mandatory detention makes immigration enforcement faster or more effective. And Congress is free to adopt that policy if it chooses to do so. But Congress does have to choose it first.

Protecting the constitutional separation of powers is one of textualism's most important functions. Textualism is often described as a conservative method of statutory interpretation. But its deeper value is constitutional. It forces both courts and presidents to follow the law Congress actually passed. Sometimes that produces harsher results. Sometimes it produces more humane ones. But either way, it restrains the executive and judicial branches from exceeding their proper spheres.

Whether mandatory detention would accelerate Trump's deportation program is a question of policy. Whether it is just is a question of ethics. Whether Congress authorized it is a question of law.

text:
Four legal services organizations have filed a federal lawsuit in Boston to halt a Trump administration policy that strips thousands of detained immigrants from the government's official tracking database — a change advocacy groups call unlawful and cruel, and one that severs vulnerable people from the legal help they need before a deportation flight ever leaves the ground.

How the Policy Took Effect Without Warning

The case centers on an unannounced change implemented by Immigration and Customs Enforcement on September 15: the removal of detainees who carry final deportation orders from the agency's Online Detainee Locator System, a publicly searchable database that families, attorneys, and advocacy organizations have depended on since its launch in June 2010. Neither ICE nor its parent agency, the Department of Homeland Security, issued any formal announcement of the shift, and both have since declined to publicly confirm it.

The policy affects more than 16,000 of the nearly 69,000 people currently held in ICE custody. All of them received final removal orders from an immigration court, yet all still retain legal standing to contest those orders — including the right to seek to reopen their cases and the right to file habeas petitions challenging the constitutionality of their detention in federal court.

When Attorneys Can No Longer Find Their Clients

For immigration lawyers, the fallout has been immediate and disorienting. Atenas Burrola Estrada, a deputy program director with the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, confirmed that every single one of her clients with a final removal order had vanished from the locator — 17 individuals in total as of her last check. Among those who disappeared from the system are eight Somali men being held at the U.S. military installation at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba.

Greg Chen, senior director of government relations at the American Immigration Lawyers Association, described the turmoil cascading through both families and legal teams. Relatives feared that loved ones had already been deported without any notice, while attorneys abruptly lost the ability to reach clients whose detention locations no longer appeared in the only government system built to make that information public. Knowing a detainee's facility is not merely a matter of convenience — it is a legal necessity, because a habeas petition challenging the legality of someone's detention must be filed in the federal court that holds jurisdiction over the specific facility where that person is confined.

The four organizations behind the Boston filing — Greater Boston Legal Services, the Rian Immigrant Center, the Florence Immigrant and Refugee Rights Project, and the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights — frame the situation not as a procedural inconvenience but as a deliberate attack on constitutional due process. Attorneys who cannot locate their clients are unable to file emergency motions, unable to request stays of removal, and unable to intervene before someone is placed on a deportation plane.

A Tool Created Precisely for This Purpose

The Online Detainee Locator System was established in 2010 in direct response to a longstanding problem: immigration detainees were routinely transferred between facilities without any notification to outside parties, making them nearly impossible for families and lawyers to track. The United Nations Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances — the body established in 1980 to assist families searching for people taken by government agents — had advocated for the locator's creation and later supported its 2024 expansion to cover people detained by U.S. Customs and Border Protection as well.

The International Dimension: A UN Body Steps In

That same UN body is now being called upon to act again. A coalition of more than 30 human rights organizations, including Amnesty International, Human Rights First, and the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, submitted an emergency petition asking the working group to declare the ICE policy a form of enforced disappearance under international law. The petition calls on the U.S. government to publicly list all detainees' locations within one hour of their arrest and to give detainees' legal representatives 24 hours' notice before any transfer takes place.

The Government's Defense Falls Short, Advocates Say

DHS responded to the controversy by casting it as a routine enforcement issue, stating that "the appropriate process due to an illegal alien with final deportation orders is removal, plain and simple." The agency also rejected the characterization that detainees were being made to disappear, pointing to the fact that people in custody retain the ability to place phone calls to relatives and legal counsel.

The Boston plaintiffs argue that defense is divorced from reality. ICE's telephone system, they allege in court filings, is riddled with long hold times, unexplained disconnections, and staff who either do not know or will not provide location information — conditions that render the phone-call option largely meaningless in practice. The consequences have been concrete: legal filings missed, court deadlines lapsed, and representation collapsed in cases involving individuals facing removal to countries where they have no ties and, in some instances, a documented risk of persecution or serious harm.

Why the Stakes Extend Far Beyond the People Already Detained

Approximately 1.4 million people living in the United States carry final orders of removal, placing the broader implications of this case well beyond the immediate population whose names have been erased. The Boston filing demands the reinstatement of all affected detainees in the locator, arguing that the system is not optional infrastructure but a constitutional safeguard — one the executive branch has no unilateral authority to dismantle.
