description:
The lawsuit, filed in Tennessee, seeks details of ICE’s instructions to state and local law enforcement agencies about whether to release records requested under state laws.
The requested records would shed light on what ICE tells state police and other local law enforcement to do when they receive public record requests regarding their collaboration with ICE.
In August, the plaintiffs in this lawsuit filed a FOIA request with ICE seeking records of the instructions ICE gave to state and local law enforcement.
ICE has rapidly expanded its partnerships with local law enforcement across the state, with 163 agreements in place as of September 2026.
Tennesseans deserve to know what their local law enforcement agencies are doing and who is being affected.
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C., October 28, 2026 — The American Immigration Council, the Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition (TIRRC), and researcher Meghan Conley filed a lawsuit today seeking information about what ICE is telling local police and sheriffs about sharing immigration enforcement records with the public.

The lawsuit, filed in Tennessee, seeks details of ICE’s instructions to state and local law enforcement agencies about whether to release records requested under state laws. The requested records would shed light on what ICE tells state police and other local law enforcement to do when they receive public record requests regarding their collaboration with ICE.

According to the lawsuit, ICE has told local police and sheriffs they need to check with federal officials before sharing certain records with the public, even when state transparency laws say otherwise. This raises concerns that ICE may be making it harder for journalists, advocates , and the general public to find out how local police and sheriffs are working with federal immigration authorities.

In August, the plaintiffs in this lawsuit filed a FOIA request with ICE seeking records of the instructions ICE gave to state and local law enforcement. ICE did not produce the records sought.

The lawsuit comes as ICE is working with a growing number of police and sheriff departments across the country to carry out the Trump administration’s mass deportation agenda, an effort that is increasingly unpopular with Americans and is inflicting enormous harm on families and communities across the country.

“As ICE works with more local police and sheriffs across the country, more people are going to have questions about what these partnerships mean for their communities. How is taxpayer money being spent? What role are local police officers playing in immigration arrests? How are people being treated in detention? The public deserves answers to these questions, and ICE shouldn’t be making it harder to get them,” said Raul Pinto, deputy legal director for transparency at the American Immigration Council.

In Tennessee, the push for answers is particularly urgent. ICE has rapidly expanded its partnerships with local law enforcement across the state, with 163 agreements in place as of September 2026. This has led to a four-fold increase in immigration arrests and detentions, the majority involving people with no criminal record.

“Families across Tennessee are living with the consequences of this horrific immigration crackdown. Longtime U.S. residents are being arrested in their neighborhoods, families are being separated, mothers pulled away from their children, and local police and sheriffs are playing a growing role in making it all happen. Tennesseans deserve to know what their local law enforcement agencies are doing and who is being affected. We can’t hold our government accountable if we can’t even get basic information about what’s happening in our communities,” said Spring Miller, Senior Legal Strategy Director at TIRCC.

description: This happened two weeks ago, on October 14, after they received a letter for their immigration check-in at the Woodlawn ICE offices.
text:
WICHITA, Kan. (KAKE) - Immigration Enforcement agents detained another Wichita business owner, along with her family.
This happened two weeks ago, on October 14, after they received a letter for their immigration check-in at the Woodlawn ICE offices.
Pablo Hernandez, the boyfriend of Yessica Olivas, dropped her and three other family members, Mario, Maribel, and Marisela, off at the ICE office that day.
Hernandez was told he would be allowed to pick them up for lunch at noon.
“I got there at exactly 12 o’clock on October 14,” Hernandez said. “I dropped food off and everything. I was waiting for them to come out, and nothing. It was like one, two passed, nothing.”
Hernandez said that after three hours, an ICE agent came out asking for the Olivas’ family friend, Raquel Reyes.
“An agent came out of the office and asked me to come pick up their paperwork while I was on the phone with Pablo,” Reyes said. “I went in, and we didn’t get to see them that day at all. So from there they went to Chase County.”
Reyes says Yessica, the eldest daughter and founder of Lady Burritos, a food delivery service in Wichita, built strong connections in town.
“She is a giving person,” Reyes said. “She’s a caring person. She thinks of others before herself. She has given when she has nothing, and selflessly and without question. If somebody needs help, she’s willing to do what she can do within her limits.”
A family friend of 10 years, Gisela Pena, adds that the family has been giving to people in Wichita, such as Yessica, and they didn’t deserve to be in the situation they’re in.
“Whenever they can, they help the community,” Pena said. “I can only say that this family is like so many others here. We’ve all come here chasing a dream, you know, the dream of improving our lives.”
Reyes says the Olivas family doesn’t have a criminal record.
For now, Reyes and many others have started a
GoFundMe
to help the Olivas family with legal fees and transition costs.
Reyes also says scheduled orders with Lady Burritos will most likely be completed, but the business will then be on hold until they know what happens next.
A spokesperson from the Department of Homeland Security says that in 2013, the Olivas family entered the U.S. through Columbus, New Mexico, and were released into the country by the Obama Administration.

text:
The US Supreme Court declined on Tuesday to reinstate the authority of immigration judges to temporarily postpone deportation cases, keeping in place an agreement between President Donald Trump’s administration and Republican-governed Texas that bars the once common practice.

The justices denied an emergency request by three US cities, including Baltimore, and an immigrant legal advocacy group to halt for now the deal ending the practice, known as “administrative closure”, while litigation continues in the dispute.

The supreme court’s decision, issued as a brief, one-sentence order, did not offer any explanation, as is common when it handles emergency requests. None of the justices publicly dissented from the decision.

This dangerous abuse of the judicial process threatens the rule of law and sets a troubling precedent for dismantling federal policies without meaningful public participation or judicial scrutiny

— Baltimore and the other litigants

The administration and Texas filed the agreement in a federal court in Texas on June 22, the same day that the state sued to challenge the immigration court procedure. A federal judge swiftly approved the agreement on the same day.

Baltimore and the other litigants said the federal government improperly colluded with Texas to secure the rule’s invalidation. The litigants and the lawyers representing them from the liberal legal group Democracy Forward expressed disappointment in Tuesday’s decision.

“Eliminating these protections puts vulnerable people at greater risk of deportation and undermines public safety in communities across the country,” they said.

“This dangerous abuse of the judicial process threatens the rule of law and sets a troubling precedent for dismantling federal policies without meaningful public participation or judicial scrutiny,” they added.

Representatives from the justice department and the Texas attorney-general’s office did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Immigration judges relied on administrative closure for decades to clear certain deportation cases off their busy dockets, including when separate proceedings involving the same person are pending that could prevent removal, such as on a visa petition or an appeal of a criminal conviction.

Critics, including Texas and the Trump administration, have said administrative closure has allowed immigrants who lack legal status to remain indefinitely in the US, acting in effect like an amnesty.

Hundreds of thousands of cases

Administrative closure has been applied over the years in hundreds of thousands of deportation cases. Ending the practice is part of Trump’s hardline approach towards immigrants.

In 2024 Joe Biden’s administration adopted a regulation that formally codified administrative closure procedures, concluding that it lets judges efficiently manage their caseloads and promote the fair treatment of immigrants. That regulation replaced a previous rule adopted in 2020 during Trump’s first term in office that had been judicially blocked.

After Trump returned to office in 2025, the justice department office that oversees immigration courts, the executive office for immigration review, announced it would not defend the Biden rule against a legal challenge.

The need for interim relief is underscored by the collusion that infected this suit from its inception

— The cities and Centro Legal de la Raza

In a lawsuit, Texas argued that the rule lets immigration judges “effectively grant indefinite amnesty to aliens illegally present in this country”.

Trump’s administration and the state then jointly asked US district judge Reed O’Connor in Wichita Falls, Texas, to approve an agreement declaring the Biden rule unlawful. O’Connor did so, blocking it permanently, nationwide.

Three municipalities — Baltimore; New Haven, Connecticut; and Columbus, Ohio — and the legal services provider, Centro Legal de la Raza, sought to intervene in the case to defend the rule, but O’Connor rejected their bid. The cities say they all have substantial immigrant populations.

The New Orleans-based 5th US Circuit Court of Appeals declined to put the agreement on hold pending an appeal of O’Connor’s decision.

The cities and Centro Legal de la Raza told the supreme court in a filing that Trump’s administration circumvented a federal law governing agency procedures by using “manufactured litigation” with “ideologically aligned” Texas to eliminate a regulation it disliked.

“The need for interim relief is underscored by the collusion that infected this suit from its inception,” they wrote.

title: Chelsea mother claims in lawsuit that ICE officers 'violently attacked' her in front of her child
description:
A Chelsea mother and green card holder says in a new lawsuit against the Trump administration that she was “violently attacked” by masked federal immigration officers last year.
The federal lawsuit alleges the ICE officers’ conduct violated the Fourth and Fifth amendments, federal statute and ICE’s own standards of conduct.
When she cried out to the ICE officers that her brother had autism, one told her to “shut up,”’ reads the complaint.
The son, who Ramirez Sanan said has trouble communicating verbally, witnessed the entire arrest.
“Local police intervened and requested that the ICE officers check Ms. Ramirez Sanan’s identification.
text:
A Chelsea mother and green card holder says in a new lawsuit against the Trump administration that she was “violently attacked” by masked federal immigration officers last year.

Hilda Ramirez Sanan sued the federal government in the U.S. District Court of Massachusetts on Tuesday after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers arrested her during a September 2025 encounter near Chelsea District Court. Other plaintiffs in the federal lawsuit are her U.S. citizen children— her daughter, Michelle Ramirez Sanan, 18, and her now 14-year-old son, identified in the suit as J.R.S.

Ramirez Sanan, who has lived lawfully in the country for more than 20 years, says the officers didn’t check her identification nor look at her green card.

In an interview with GBH News on Tuesday, Ramirez Sanan tearfully recounted how the incident caused long-lasting harm that upended the lives of her family members. “I want justice. It’s not just us— we’re humans, we’re not animals. We have rights. We’re human beings,” said Ramirez Sanan.

“I didn’t have any immigration issues or open case. I don’t know why they did this,“ she said. “No one listened to me. No one asked for my identification. I begged them to listen because my son was witnessing this and was being held by four ICE agents who were armed, and this has caused us such profound trauma.”

Ramirez Sanan has been unable to work due to injuries from the arrest, going to occupational therapy for her injuries to her hand, legs and feet every eight days.

The family is suing for the physical and emotional trauma experienced during the arrest, which their attorneys at Lawyers for Civil Rights and Zimmer, Citron & Clarke LLP say was illegal.

“The family is courageously bringing this suit to seek justice for themselves, and to stand up to government abuses towards immigrant communities more broadly. ICE’s attack of the family was illegal, unconstitutional, and unconscionable, and we intend to seek justice,” said Jillian Lenson, senior attorney at Lawyers for Civil Rights in an interview.

In late 2025, the family submitted an administrative claim to the Department of Homeland Security and ICE a required precursor for a federal lawsuit. In the claim, they sought a million dollars in damages.

Under the Federal Tort Claims Act, once six months have elapsed, a lawsuit may be filed in federal court. Lenson said the federal government never “resolved” the complaint from last December.

The federal lawsuit alleges the ICE officers’ conduct violated the Fourth and Fifth amendments, federal statute and ICE’s own standards of conduct.

“We are seeking damages on behalf of the family for the enduring emotional trauma and pain and suffering they’ve continued to feel since the violent attack,” said Lenson.

LCR posted a video of the interaction on its website.

Case history

On Sept. 26, 2025 Ramirez Sanan, 51, was accompanying a family member to a court hearing in Chelsea with her son in the backseat, according to the lawsuit. A group of unmarked vehicles surrounded and blocked her car two blocks from the courthouse, and eight armed and masked officers surrounded the car, the lawsuit says.

In a video of the incident, masked agents tell Ramirez Sanan, a green card holder, to get out of the car and she refuses. The agents eventually smash the car glass, pull Ramirez Sanan out and forcibly restrain her.

They also unbuckled the seat belt and pulled her then 13-year-old, who has autism, out of the car while he cried. He was asked his legal status. The vehicle, according to the complaint, had a prominently displayed disability placard hanging in the front.

When Ramirez Sanan’s eldest daughter arrived at the scene, she was physically blocked from talking to her mother and brother. She’s shown in another video being kept away.

“‘[An ICE officer] forcibly holding her hands and wrists, and physically preventing her from approaching her mother and brother. When she cried out to the ICE officers that her brother had autism, one told her to “shut up,”’ reads the complaint.

The son, who Ramirez Sanan said has trouble communicating verbally, witnessed the entire arrest. Agents grabbed him by the shoulder and kept him against the fence. They threatened to arrest him if he did not answer their questions or show them his papers.

According to the complaint, one of the agents kicked Ramirez Sanan, twisted her arms behind her back, and pushing her to the ground face-first. Ramirez Sanan said she “lost consciousness” during that time.

Ramirez Sanan said in the complaint that as she was being dragged to an unmarked vehicle, local police showed up.

“Local police intervened and requested that the ICE officers check Ms. Ramirez Sanan’s identification. Now under the watch of local law enforcement, the ICE officers reviewed Ms. Ramirez Sanan’s identification, released her from their custody, and left the scene,” said the complaint.

An ambulance then took her and her children to a hospital emergency room for medical evaluation. She has been in occupational therapy weekly for her leg and her hands for the past year, and is in the process of getting behavioral health support for her child, who she described to GBH News as “immensely impacted.”

Doctors gave Ramirez Sanan a blood test, several X-rays, and a CT scan for her head and spine to determine her injuries, the lawsuit said. The doctors assessed that she likely had a radial nerve injury and referred her to a consult with a hand surgeon, according to the complaint, and that she was potentially concussed.

JRS is now taking medication for anxiety and depression, and has had trouble walking since the incident. He’s seeing a neurologist and physical therapist.

The complaint describes changes in his mental health. “Since the attack, he has suffered migraines, frequent crying fits, and nightmares. He has woken up from his nightmares screaming, “don’t kill my mom.”

text:
The Briefing

The U.S. Supreme Court issued an unsigned order on October 27 rejecting an emergency request to restore immigration judges' authority to temporarily close deportation cases, leaving in place a June 2026 Texas federal court judgment that eliminated the Biden administration's formal administrative closure rule.

More than 361,000 immigration cases — the vast majority involving Latino immigrants — currently sit off active court dockets, and attorneys warn those cases now face an accelerated path toward hearings and potential removal orders.

Crime victims holding U visa applications, immigrants with pending family petitions, and people appealing criminal convictions face the sharpest exposure, as the ruling removes the only procedural mechanism available to pause their deportation cases while separate legal proceedings play out.

What the Supreme Court Ruled — and What It Deliberately Left Open

Without a single dissent or a word of written reasoning, the U.S. Supreme Court on October 27 refused to block a lower court judgment that stripped immigration judges of their power to temporarily suspend deportation proceedings. The court's unsigned order rejected an emergency application filed by three cities and a legal services group asking the justices to pause that judgment while they fought to intervene in the underlying case.

Crucially, the court did not declare administrative closure unconstitutional, nor did it settle whether immigration judges retain some residual authority to close cases outside a formal regulation. The order simply left the existing Texas federal court judgment in place — a meaningful distinction for practitioners, even if the practical effect for immigrants in the system is immediate and severe.

Decades of Practice, Eliminated in a Single Day

Administrative closure developed over decades inside the immigration court system as a practical caseload tool. When a person facing deportation had a separate proceeding in progress — a pending visa petition with a U.S. citizen spouse, a U visa application filed after cooperating with police, or a criminal conviction under appeal that could affect their removability — a judge could temporarily remove that case from the active calendar. The deportation case did not close; it paused.

The Biden administration formally codified the practice in 2024 under the regulation known as the "Efficient Case and Docket Management in Immigration Proceedings" rule, giving it a regulatory foundation it had previously lacked. That foundation was eliminated on June 22, 2026, and the Supreme Court's October 27 order confirms that elimination will stand.

The Texas-DOJ Agreement That Set This in Motion

On the morning of June 22, 2026, Texas filed a lawsuit in the Northern District of Texas challenging the 2024 administrative closure rule. Within hours of that complaint being docketed, Texas and the Trump administration's Justice Department jointly moved for entry of a consent judgment — in effect settling a case that had been filed that same morning. Chief U.S. District Judge Reed O'Connor signed the final order the same day, vacating the rule in its entirety, permanently barring DOJ from enforcing it, and prohibiting any future administration from issuing similar regulations without express Congressional authorization. Both sides waived the right to appeal.

The challengers told the Supreme Court the arrangement amounted to "egregious collusion" — a coordinated maneuver to kill a federal regulation through manufactured litigation, bypassing the notice-and-comment process that the Administrative Procedure Act requires for standard rulemaking. Texas and the administration argued the opposite: that the practice had operated as an unauthorized indefinite stay for people with no legal path to remain in the country.

Who Filed the Emergency Appeal — and Why They Failed

After the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals declined to grant emergency relief and allow the coalition to formally intervene in the case, three cities — Baltimore, Columbus, Ohio, and New Haven, Connecticut — together with Centro Legal de la Raza, an immigrant legal services organization, brought an emergency application to the Supreme Court on October 9. The application was first directed to Justice Samuel Alito and subsequently referred to the full court.

In their filings, the cities argued that eliminating administrative closure would generate measurable harm at the local level: fewer undocumented crime victims willing to report offenses to police, accelerated removal of longtime residents who contribute to local tax bases, and an erosion of the due process protections the courts had recognized for decades. The Supreme Court's silent denial on October 27 ended that argument without response.

What the 361,000 Paused Cases Face Now

According to EOIR adjudication statistics generated on July 31, 2025, there were 361,614 cases classified as inactive pending — held off active immigration court dockets by administrative closure orders. The average case in that pool had been closed for approximately 16½ years; the median was roughly 11½ years. Those figures span both immigration court and Board of Immigration Appeals cases.

The DOJ maintained during litigation that the June 2026 judgment does not require immigration courts to immediately reopen every closed case. But immigration practitioners warn the distinction is narrowing quickly: cases are already being recalendared, and without any regulatory authority to request closure, there is no procedural mechanism left to resist that process.

The geographic concentration of the impact falls hardest on communities with the heaviest immigration court backlogs. TRAC data from February 2026 shows Miami-Dade County leading the country with 143,817 pending deportation cases, followed by Cook County, Illinois at 112,686, Queens County, New York at 103,791, and Los Angeles County at 98,792. A substantial portion of those cases previously had the protection of administrative closure.

Crime Victims and U Visa Applicants Face the Sharpest Risk

Congress created the U visa specifically to encourage undocumented crime victims to cooperate with law enforcement, offering a path toward legal status in exchange for assistance with investigations and prosecutions. The program's annual approval cap sits at 10,000 principal visas per fiscal year — far below the volume of applicants, producing a multi-year waiting list for people who have already been vetted by law enforcement.

Since 2021, USCIS had been issuing what are called "good faith determinations" — official acknowledgments that a U visa petition meets the baseline criteria for review — and those documents offered a measure of protection from removal while applicants waited. According to NBC News reporting, immigration attorneys and legal experts now say the Trump administration has taken the position that good faith determinations no longer shield applicants from deportation or detention. That means a person who reported a crime, received law enforcement certification, and holds a USCIS good faith determination can still be arrested and removed while their visa application remains unresolved.

The Track Record of Closed Cases — and What It Reveals

Prior research tracking outcomes for immigrants whose administratively closed cases were later returned to active dockets has found that the majority of those individuals ultimately receive authorization to remain in the United States. Advocates have long cited this data to argue that administrative closure has functioned not merely as a scheduling tool but as a reliable signal that a credible legal claim exists. The Supreme Court's refusal to intervene leaves that protection unavailable to the more than 361,000 people whose cases had depended on it.

What Families and Attorneys Should Do Immediately

For anyone whose immigration case is currently in administrative closure, the most urgent priority is confirming whether that case has been or is likely to be recalendared. Those with a pending I-130 family petition, an active U visa application, or a criminal conviction still under appeal retain potential routes forward — but only if they act before a hearing is set and a removal order is issued.

The EOIR automated case inquiry system allows individuals to check the current status of an immigration court case using their A-number at no cost. The same information is available by calling 1-800-898-7180. Consulting a qualified immigration attorney before any hearing date is scheduled remains the most effective protective step available.

Hedley, who told U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia M. Faruqui earlier that day that he was acting senior litigation counsel at the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division, had warned in court that the jury could not agree on an indictment. Hedley didn’t mention a name, but the Post’s sources said it was Hutchinson.

President Donald Trump and his Republican allies have been seeking charges against Hutchinson for months, accusing her of lying to the investigative committee. In March, Representative Barry Loudermilk referred her to the Department of Justice, and House Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan signed off on it.

Hutchinson was one of the star witnesses in the committee’s hearings, claiming that Trump was very agitated on January 6, 2021, and fully aware of the potential for violence. She testified that he wanted to march with his supporters on the Capitol, and was furious when his aides and Secret Service detail said that it wouldn’t be safe.

Trump even tried to grab the steering wheel of the presidential limousine known as The Beast, and when a Secret Service agent took his arm, Trump grabbed the agent’s neck, Hutchinson said. Along with then–White House chief of staff Mark Meadows, she said that Trump wanted his armed supporters to march that day, and overheard a conversation where Trump said that Mike Pence “deserves it,” regarding chants of “hang Mike Pence” heard during the riot.

For now, though, Hutchinson won’t face criminal charges, although MAGA Republicans may try to indict her again. Trump keeps trying to settle old scores in his second term as president. For instance, his Department of Justice just charged former FBI Director James Comey for a third time.

A federal judge tore into Department of Justice prosecutors Tuesday for attempting to file a new criminal complaint alleging that two ex-FBI agents had lied to Congress during the investigation into Hunter Biden’s laptop.

At a hearing, Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui refused to rubber-stamp a superseding complaint, which would have added an obstruction charge against former intelligence analyst Nikki Floris, who ran the intelligence division at the Washington field office, and Bradley Benavides, a former deputy assistant director for counterintelligence.

Faruqui told the prosecutors that if they wanted to file a superseding complaint, then a judge would first have to find probable cause that a crime had actually been committed. Instead, the government had transmitted the complaint in the middle of the night and expected the judge to sign it.

Faruqui said that he believed the government had broken precedent by seeking a superseding complaint without first receiving a judge’s signature.

“I’m concerned with your view as to what the law is,” he said. “Why today, on this one case, have you changed the entire history of how you charge cases?”

After Floris and Benavides surrendered on arrest warrants last week, Faruqui had ordered a hearing on Tuesday in order to establish probable cause for the initial complaint. Notably, the DOJ did not obtain a grand jury indictment against the ex-officials.

On Monday night, the government submitted an unsworn affidavit it claimed would support an additional obstruction charge. Faruqui refused to sign the complaint without reviewing it or finding probable cause, and proceeded to hold the hearing on just the first complaint.

At one point in the interview, Blanche vaguely mentioned testimony that alleged Epstein and Trump were involved with a 14-year-old, asking if Maxwell recalled “any obviously under-18 women coming to give him a massage?”

Maxwell volunteered that she believed Blanche was “talking about Jane.” But Blanche didn’t bite, instead responding simply, “yeah”—evidence that he was aware of the victim’s accusations.

As soon as Maxwell began to address Jane’s claims, Blanche “cut her off and instructed her not to share specifics,” according to the report. At other points, Blanche interrupted Maxwell to redirect her attention away from Jane’s allegations, arguing that he didn’t want to “get into … he said, she said.”

“Absolutely, not. I’m not—I don’t want to go there either,” Maxwell responded, adding, “I’m not going to do that.”

Maxwell tried to independently mention Jane later in the interview but was again shut down by Blanche, who abruptly cut her off to say he didn’t want to “talk about individuals.”

“The whole point of the conversation was not to uncover information but to create a conspiracy of silence and strategically deter Ghislaine Maxwell from sharing information that was not public at the time regarding the relationship between Trump and Epstein,” the report alleges.

Flávio Bolsonaro has fled to the United States after losing Brazil’s presidential election to incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Brazil on Sunday, according to multiple outlets.

Bolsonaro’s allies reported his escape to CNN Brasil, and Reuters also confirmed he is headed to the United States, citing two sources.

Brazilian outlet O Globo reported that the far-right senator “was convinced he could be arrested.” While both Bolsonaro’s departure point and destination are uncertain, another Brazilian outlet, Metropoles, reported that he was on his way to Florida to seek asylum. Bolsonaro’s father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, is currently serving out house arrest in Brazil for attempting his own version of January 6. He also fled to Florida in late 2022 briefly before his arrest.

Bolsonaro, who has still not conceded the election to Lula, had his passport canceled by the Brazilian Supreme Court due to an active money-laundering case against him. He had until 11 a.m. Tuesday to turn his passport in, but of course didn’t show—fueling questions about his whereabouts.

The Trump administration has been quite friendly to Bolsonaro’s family and antagonistic toward Lula’s left-leaning government.

The Supreme Court ruled Tuesday that immigration judges can’t postpone deportation cases, giving President Trump another tool in his mass deportation agenda.

The court denied an emergency request to reinstate administrative closure, the practice that allows judges to temporarily delay deportation cases, after the Trump administration made an agreement with the state of Texas to end it in June. The request came from three cities—Baltimore; New Haven, Connecticut; and Columbus, Ohio—and from nonprofit legal aid organization Centro ⁠Legal de la Raza.

The court’s denial was one sentence long without any explanation, a standard practice for emergency requests, and there were no reported dissents.

The agreement to end administrative closure was made in federal court in Texas on the same day the state sued to challenge the practice. A judge also approved the agreement the same day, which the plaintiffs cited in their lawsuit as proof the White House colluded with Texas to get rid of the rule.

“The need for interim relief is ​underscored by the collusion that infected this suit from its inception,” the cities and organization wrote.

Administrative closure used to be common, with immigration judges using the tool to clear packed dockets, especially when a person had proceedings that could prevent their deportation such as a visa petition or appeal of a criminal conviction. Conservative politicians in places like Texas argue that the practice allows immigrants without legal status to stay in the country indefinitely.

The Biden administration tried to make the practice permanent in 2024, but after Trump returned to the White House, the Department of Justice announced it would no longer defend administrative closure. Tuesday’s ruling follows Friday’s federal appeals court decision that immigrants aren’t entitled to bond hearings. In less than a week, the Trump administration has successfully eroded immigration law in order to deport more people.

text:
Congressional Democrats have again demanded urgent reforms to the country’s immigration court system after The Washington Post revealed a veteran judge’s allegations that she was ordered to reverse rulings and urged to conduct sham bond hearings.

Democratic Sens. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland and Dick Durbin of Illinois, both longtime critics of President Donald Trump’s immigration policies, renewed calls this week to pass a bill that would remove immigration judges from the authority of the executive branch.

They spoke out in response to the story of Karen Donoso Stevens, a former Homeland Security prosecutor who joined the bench in 2016. After persistent interference by Justice Department officials, Donoso Stevens alleged, she was pulled from court mid-hearing, demoted and eventually fired.

Her accusations contradict repeated assertions by the Trump administration that – as required by law – immigration judges serve as independent arbiters of justice.

“Unfortunately, this Administration has shown time and time again that they have no regard for our Constitution or the rule of law – as we’ve seen in the case of Karen Donoso Stevens,” Van Hollen said in a statement. “This abuse of power must be stopped.”

Unlike federal judges who are protected from political retaliation by lifetime tenures and the constitutional separation of powers, immigration judges work for the executive branch. Since Trump retook office, his administration has dismissed more than 100 of the nation’s approximately 700 immigration judges and replaced many with what officials call “deportation judges.”

“Judges who decline to follow precedent undermine the integrity of the system and potentially engage in professional misconduct,” Kathryn Mattingly, a spokesperson for the Justice Department’s Executive Office for Immigration Review, said in a statement. “EOIR cannot tolerate judges who decline to follow the law in lieu of their own personal preferences.”

Mattingly – who provided no evidence that Donoso Stevens or any other judge fired without cause had declined to follow the law – also alleged that The Post’s investigation “contains several misleading statements or misrepresentations,” but she did not name any.

Every year, Donoso Stevens, 53, had denied asylum in more than half the applications that came before her, a record consistently in line with national averages.

“I stand with Judge Donoso Stevens and the many others like her … who have been fired for simply doing their jobs,” said Durbin, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee. “We urgently need an independent immigration court to prevent these abuses from ever happening again.”

Durbin and Van Hollen have joined other Democrats, including Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, to push a bill that would afford the court true independence. Without Republican support, though, the legislation has little chance of passage.

On Tuesday, the Supreme Court strengthened the president’s control over immigration courts, clearing the way for his administration to restrict a policy that had allowed judges to close thousands of deportation cases each year.

Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), who respectively chair the Senate and House judiciary committees, did not respond to requests for comment about whether they found Donoso Stevens’s allegations troubling or would call for an investigation.

“All illegal aliens receive full due process and have their claims heard,” Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement. “No lawbreakers in the history of human civilization have been treated better than illegal aliens. Once again, Democrats are running to the defense of illegal aliens and continue to ignore the victims of illegal alien crime.”

The Trump administration, Donoso Stevens told The Post, first violated her judicial independence in September 2025.

For decades, undocumented immigrants who weren’t apprehended until after they entered the country were allowed to request bond, leaving judges to decide whether it was safe to release them as their cases proceeded. But the Board of Immigration Appeals, stocked with members appointed under Trump, suddenly decided that anyone who came unlawfully should remain jailed, even those with clean records and family ties.

The opinion, Donoso Stevens and other judges discovered, failed to account for children who came to the United States without a parent or guardian and had since reached adulthood, a group that, in their view, fell under distinct legal guidelines. She granted bond in four such cases.

On Sept. 17, Eric Dillow, her supervisor at the Annandale Immigration Court, called. He wanted to discuss bond, “a hot topic,” according to her notes.

Dillow, who did not reply to a request for comment, emailed her a separate ruling that, he believed, meant she could have denied bond. Donoso Stevens told him she could see the merits of the argument, but she said Homeland Security should either file a motion asking her to reconsider or request that the appellate board intervene. He agreed, according to her notes, but called back a few minutes later.

“He said higher-ups said I had to vacate my decs sua sponte,” Donoso Stevens wrote in a note that abbreviated “decisions” and used a Latin phrase that refers to judges reversing their own rulings unprompted.

Dillow did not name the “higher-ups,” so Donoso Stevens pressed for an explanation: “Why can’t DHS file a motion to reconsider?”

“Oh no,” he replied. “They’re not going to do that.”

To Donoso Stevens, Dillow had not only told her how to rule, directly violating the executive office’s vow of judicial independence, he’d implied that Homeland Security had ordered the court system to acquiesce.

“Immigration judges – like almost all judges in the American judicial system – are required to follow precedent,” Mattingly wrote in her statement. “As the quotes from only Democratic lawmakers demonstrate, only the most tendentious and partisan advocates would view that requirement as ‘being told how to rule,’ and no serious lawyer views it as infringing a judge’s decisional independence.”

The Post described the allegation to three legal experts, and all of them condemned it as an unacceptable infringement of a judge’s decisional independence.

John Woodrow Cox reports for The Washington Post.

text:
OSHKOSH, Wis. (WBAY) - An Oshkosh teacher who was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement is in detention awaiting deportation.

According to ICE, agents arrested Wendy Mendez in Milwaukee on Oct. 14. ICE said she was allowed to come to the U.S. from Costa Rica on a temporary basis in August 2020 and was supposed to leave the country in February 2021.

In a statement to WBAY, the Department of Homeland Security said:

“On August 10, 2020, Mendez legally entered the United States on a temporary basis, but in violation of our laws, failed to depart by February 9, 2021. On February 18, 2026, she was placed into removal proceedings, and on September 9, was ordered removed by an immigration judge for failing to show up for her removal proceedings. She received due process and will remain in custody pending her removal from the United States.”

Friend disputes hearing notice

A friend of Mendez disputes the DHS account, saying on Facebook that the hearing notice was sent to a previous address from more than three years ago. She said U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services had the family’s new address within days of moving.

School district response

The Oshkosh Area School District website says Mendez is employed as a teaching assistant in the English Speakers of Other Languages program at Vel Phillips Middle School.

In 2025, Mendez was named an Oshkosh School District Employee of the Year.

The district called Mendez “an employee in good standing” and said she was placed on unpaid leave “due to unforeseen circumstances.”

“At no point was this a school safety or performance-related issue,” the district said. “Our primary focus remains on supporting our students and staff and keeping learning moving forward in our classrooms.”

Students at Vel Phillips Middle School were told Tuesday that she will not be returning to school for the foreseeable future, according to the district.

The district told Vel Phillips families that counselors and support staff are available for students.

ICE statement

In a statement to Action 2 News, ICE said “being in detention is a choice” and indicated Mendez won’t be allowed to return after she’s deported.

“The United States is offering illegal aliens $3,000 and a free flight to self-deport now. We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the U.S.”

Community reaction

Mushe Subulwa, a Vel Phillips parent, said his son thought Mendez was out sick before the district released official information Tuesday.

“I could see how students, how young people are also affected when they think about their teacher who they love is sick. When their teacher who they love is not in class, they are concerned. So my son was already concerned the last nine days or so. I can’t just imagine how they feel today if the school district has broken that news to them,” Subulwa said.

Community members said concerns are growing.

Molly Smiltneek, a local immigration attorney and advocate, said Mendez is “a very respected role model, who’s worked her way up in the school district, and is beloved amongst her coworkers and her students.”

Vigil planned

Advocates said a vigil, billed as “A Vigil for the Missing,” is planned for Oct. 30 from 6 to 7 p.m. at Oshkosh Opera House Square. Organizers described it as a peaceful place to process together.

“This vigil is not just for Wendy. This vigil is for me. This vigil is for my friends. This vigil is for all our students that have that humanity. We’re going to come together and cry together,” Subulwa said.

title: Racism needs to be understood as a global phenomenon – our humanity depends on it
description:
This global racism, which I name and define in my new book Global Racism: A Challenge for the World, is dangerous – it underpins wars and threatens our very humanity.
Global racism is an old story and an evergreen one.
Understanding global racism reveals why this gap matters.
Today, because of social media and new technology, global racism moves throughout our human ecosystem with rapid speed, making it possible anywhere and everywhere people are.
Launching an effective campaign to combat global racism starts with dismantling the ideological architecture that allows racism to thrive.
text:
Around the world, racism is fueling a new wave of global unrest. In recent weeks, demonstrations in France turned violent amid mounting frustrations over socioeconomic and racial inequities, led by a younger generation that has had enough. Earlier this month, the Green party of England and Wales’s decision to define Zionism as a form of racism sparked controversy and renewed public debate about what racism is and who gets to decide it. In September, electoral gains by Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party raised alarms in a nation with a dangerous history of racist, antisemitic fascism. And for the past year, the Trump administration has pushed ahead white supremacist agendas throughout the United States, highlighted by violent Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids targeting people by race, regardless of citizenship status.

To understand each of these examples of racism in isolation would be a mistake. They are connected. Racism is not merely a series of random occurrences affecting certain people in certain places. It is more than institutional discrimination in schools or workplaces or even systemic inequalities in healthcare and policing. Racism is an interconnected, global phenomenon, spreading throughout our human ecosystem and embedded in world order. This global racism, which I name and define in my new book Global Racism: A Challenge for the World, is dangerous – it underpins wars and threatens our very humanity.

Global racism is an old story and an evergreen one. It is often powered by leaders who seek to divide humans through dehumanizing “us v them” narratives. In 1095, for example, Pope Urban II called upon Frankish nobles and common folk alike to take up arms against the Seljuk Turks, urging them in one account of his speech “to destroy that vile race from the lands of our friends”. Nearly nine centuries later and a continent away, the Hutu Ten Commandments, published in 1990 in a Rwandan newspaper, invoked ideologies of racial superiority that created the conditions in which the Rwandan genocide unfolded four years later. The worst things we humans have ever done to one another – slavery, genocide, segregation, apartheid – have been justified and sustained by ideologies underlying global racism. When this racist fervor subsides, we realize that such acts have not only killed countless people but diminished our humanity.

Today, evidence of racism’s global disruption is clear. According to the United Nations, racial discrimination is among the most common forms of discrimination worldwide, often intersecting with gender discrimination against women and girls. A Pew survey found that across 36 countries a median of 68% of adults consider racial or ethnic discrimination as a significant worldwide problem. The international community recognized the need to confront such challenges back in 1965 when nations created the first treaty banning racial discrimination, defined as certain acts of discrimination on the basis of race, color, descent, national or ethnic origin (but not nationality). A laudable first step, the treaty failed to define and ban racism, alongside racial discrimination.

Understanding global racism reveals why this gap matters. Racism can’t be eliminated by banning acts of racial discrimination, nation by nation, alone. Racism’s deeper roots are embedded not only in how humans and the institutions we create behave, but in what we believe. White supremacist movements, for example, teach followers to believe that being white makes someone inherently superior to everyone else. This ranking of humans by group based on a construct that has no basis in biology isn’t accidental. It is by design and always has been. Today, because of social media and new technology, global racism moves throughout our human ecosystem with rapid speed, making it possible anywhere and everywhere people are.

Consider the racist, anti-immigrant riots that erupted last June across Northern Ireland after a knife attack in Belfast, where people violently targeted minority communities, setting fire to homes and vehicles. It exposed how far-right ideologies amplified online could help drive people to commit racist crimes. Like a spark that turns into a raging wildfire, racism doesn’t go viral without hot, dry, windy conditions in the air that allow it.

Launching an effective campaign to combat global racism starts with dismantling the ideological architecture that allows racism to thrive. Many governments, however, have been reluctant to do this, privileging free speech and ideas even when the unfettered exercise of those freedoms enables the spread of racial hatred. But protecting the right to express an idea, however objectionable, should not mean allowing racist beliefs to become systems of power. An idea, after all, is not the same as an ideology. The difference, according to Merriam-Webster, is between an idea as a “formulated thought or opinion” and an ideology as a “systematic body of concepts”. The goal isn’t to police an individual’s ideas; it is to stop national leaders who command military power and vast resources from spreading ideologies of racial superiority that threaten peace and security.

WEB Du Bois warned of precisely this danger in 1935 in an unpublished essay, A Pragmatic Program for a Dark Minority. He described a world in crisis, where leaders of nations amassed power built on platforms of racist ideologies that promised a bleak future for everyone. “All this,” he wrote, “must inevitably move toward an increase of race hate and war.” History proved him right. The Holocaust, the Rape of Nanjing, and US internment of Japanese Americans, among other horrors, were all built on ideologies of racial superiority. Du Bois understood something we still miss today: racism is not a national peculiarity but a global force, one that degrades those who wield it as surely as those who suffer under it – and that, left unchecked, threatens to plunge the world into chaos and war.

Racism is, indeed, a global force, but so is our ability to overcome it. Recognizing global racism is the first step. For nations, this requires banning racism, alongside racial discrimination, under international law. For the rest of us, this means giving up the allure of ideologies of racial superiority. Like all global challenges, real solutions will require collective action. We can start by demanding dignity from our leaders and from ourselves. Why should we try? Because the future of our human species depends upon us acting as one.

text:
Houston police officers contacted federal immigration agents 88 times from July through the end of September, according to data issued by the department on Thursday.

The calls happened when officers found people with immigration warrants. On average, officers detained people for approximately 45 minutes while waiting for agents with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to respond.

According to the figures from the Houston Police Department (HPD), 58 people were released after the calls, 13 were taken to jail for new charges, and 17 were taken into ICE custody.

Sign up for the Hello, Houston! daily newsletter to get local reports like this delivered directly to your inbox.

In 33 cases, officers were responding to a call for emergency services when they encountered someone with an immigration warrant. The data report doesn’t make clear whether the person placing the call for help was the subject of the warrant.

"Out of 300,000 contacts [between HPD and citizens] that have 17 end with ICE involvement speaks for itself," Houston Mayor John Whitmire told reporters on Wednesday. "Very small, very small number. And for anyone to say different about our involvement is just wrong."

Related: Houston police responded to a man in a mental health crisis. ICE arrested him

Authorities did not provide full details on each interaction, but records obtained by Houston Public Media for incidents from April through June showed contacts between HPD and ICE during responses to a mental health crisis, a suicide attempt and domestic disturbances.

Asked by a Houston Public Media reporter about community trust, particularly when contacts involve victims of crimes, HPD Chief Noe Diaz said, "I won't diminish that because that's real. People feel that. But for us, statistically speaking, the calls for service haven't changed in the last quarter."

"No survivor or Houstonian seeking help from the police should have to fear that calling 911 could lead to them or a loved one being detained by ICE." council member Alejandra Salinas said in a written statement. "I once again call on HPD to explain how calling ICE on crime victims keeps our community safer."

Interactions between HPD and ICE have been the subject of deep controversy in Houston over the past year. In April, the city council passed an ordinance intended to curtail coordination and require regular reporting about those interactions. After Texas Gov. Greg Abbott intervened, threatening to revoke more than $110 million in public safety funding, city officials rolled back rules prohibiting officers from detaining people due to civil immigration warrants — but they kept the reporting requirements in place.

Still, HPD leadership has been reluctant to provide additional details about the interactions beyond the required data. Diaz skipped a public safety committee meeting in August, citing ongoing litigation filed by a man who was deported after a nearly two-hour traffic stop. At the time, city attorneys cited ongoing litigation as justification for his absence.

Related: HPD Chief Noe Diaz skips meeting on HPD-ICE coordination, city attorney curtails transparency

"It was my decision, based on the city attorney's advice," Whitmire told reporters, Diaz sitting next to him. "I made the decision today to invite the chief to have this roundtable discussion to get the facts out and answer any questions."

Salinas spearheaded the changes in April using relatively new powers granted by Proposition A. Approved by Houston voters in 2023, it allows three or more city council members to place items on the city council's agenda — a power previously held only by the mayor.

Before releasing the data, Salinas told Houston Public Media she wants to see HPD's policy change.

"HPD is detaining crime victims and calling ICE on crime victims, which is just a terrible policy that we will continue to urge (Mayor John Whitmire's) administration to change, but to date they have refused to do so," Salinas said. "I am continuing to have conversations with my colleagues and the administration, and if I ever believe there is a path forward for Prop A, I will certainly bring it."

description:
The first European third-country “return hub” for failed asylum seekers will be established in Rwanda, sources told RTL Nieuws.
Rwanda is reportedly ready to host asylum seekers.
There is also an empty residential area intended to house asylum seekers who can’t return to their home countries.
They also did not say what Rwanda would get in return for taking Europe’s asylum seekers.
Refugee advocacy groups and human rights organizations are against the practice of sending failed asylum seekers to third countries - non-European countries that they have no connection to.
text:
The first European third-country “return hub” for failed asylum seekers will be established in Rwanda, sources told RTL Nieuws. In recent months, the Netherlands, Germany, Austria, Denmark, and Greece have been jointly exploring the possibilities for such a facility in a non-European country where asylum seekers whose applications have been rejected will await deportation to their countries of origin.

According to RTL’s sources, a proposal has now been put forward for Rwanda. The plan will be officially announced at a special meeting in Vienna on November 16.

Rwanda is reportedly ready to host asylum seekers. In a deal with the United Kingdom that fell through in 2024, the country already established the Hope Hostel intended to house individuals deported from the UK. The hostel is currently vacant.

“There is space for 100 migrants. They share double bedrooms and communal washrooms, a dining hall, a garden with palm trees, and sports fields. It fits the ideal picture for the Netherlands and other European countries that are promising a ‘safe return hub,’” RTL’s Africa correspondent said after visiting the site. There is also an empty residential area intended to house asylum seekers who can’t return to their home countries.

RTL’s sources did not say whether the Hope Hostel was part of the European deal with Rwanda, but it seems the logical choice. They also did not say what Rwanda would get in return for taking Europe’s asylum seekers.

Refugee advocacy groups and human rights organizations are against the practice of sending failed asylum seekers to third countries - non-European countries that they have no connection to. Vluchtelingenwerk previously also raised concerns about the human rights situation in Rwanda.

"Independent monitoring of human rights is virtually impossible in Rwanda. Furthermore, the [immigration service] IND itself has concluded that Rwanda cannot be classified as a safe third country,” Vluchtelingenwerk director Sjoerd Warmerdam told RTL Nieuws. “The United Kingdom previously attempted to strike a 'deal' with Rwanda, but that fell through—rightly so—precisely because of the human rights situation.”

Minister Bart van den Brink of Asylum and Migration declined to comment to the broadcaster.

text:
Voting rights groups sued the Trump administration Wednesday seeking to halt its program allegedly targeting thousands of non-native US citizens in election-related probes.

A problem, among several, is that the investigations rely on outdated or incorrect data and the methods used are “untested, unverifiable, and suspect,” the lawsuit said. However, the effects on the targets are real and can lead to further scrutiny by the federal government, according to the civil rights lawsuit filed in the US District Court for the Northern District of California.

“Through the Unlawful Voter Initiative, Defendants have created a rushed, flawed process that brands naturalized and derivative citizens as potential criminals in the federal government’s eyes and then tries to disenfranchise them,” the lawsuit said.

The suit was filed six days before Election Day in this year’s midterm cycle, which will decide control of Congress. President Donald Trump and many of his allies, like they have in previous elections, have made unfounded statements regarding voter fraud, even though multiple studies show it’s exceedingly rare.

But multiple wings of the current administration have made combating voter fraud a priority, including the Department of Homeland Security and its US Citizenship and Immigration Services, according to the lawsuit.

It also comes after the administration sued California earlier this month to try to block officials there from counting 20,000 mail-in ballots from people the federal government claims are likely non-citizens registered to vote.

That lawsuit was referenced in the new case, which was brought by the American Civil Liberties Union and two of its California affiliates, OCA-Asian Pacific American Advocates and two of its California affiliates, Common Cause, Asian Americans Advancing Justice, and Asian Americans Advancing Justice Southern California.

The groups also seek an order barring the federal government from demanding that state and local elections officials refuse to provide a ballot to or count a ballot by any person based on their being on a list of suspected noncitizen voters.

USCIS reassigned hundreds of agents to investigate people flagged as having voted while not being a citizen, the lawsuit said. Agents use people’s personal information to search state voter records to compile a voting history, according to the lawsuit. They also used the information compiled in the investigations to demand states not send ballots to voters identified as potential noncitizens, segregate ballots received from them, and not count their ballots until their citizenship is confirmed, the lawsuit said.

“The administration can’t keep creating political stunts to sow distrust in our elections and lay the groundwork to question results they don’t like,” Theresa J. Lee, a senior staff attorney with the ACLU’s Voting Rights Project, said in a news release.

DHS didn’t immediately respond to an email seeking comment.

The case is one of several filed to challenge the Trump administration’s efforts in this arena. A federal judge in California last week barred DHS from conducting voting-related field operations through Election Day that involve known US citizens in nine states.

The plaintiffs are represented by the ACLU, ACLU of Northern California, ACLU of Southern California, Asian Americans Advancing Justice, and Asian Americans Advancing Justice Southern California.

description:

text:
In Israel, there’s no clear winner so far in Tuesday’s national election. The final tally could take days. It was Israel’s first election since the October 7, 2023, attack and the ensuing wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. With over 70% of the vote counted, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party leads with 27 seats, ahead of former military chief Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party at 22. Neither candidate is on track to form a governing majority of 61 seats in the Knesset. According to Haaretz, a possible pro-Netanyahu coalition currently has 54 seats, while a possible pro-Eisenkot bloc has 49 seats. Palestinian parties — the Joint List and Ra’am — have won 17 seats, their strongest showing ever. But both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have ruled out governing with Palestinian-led parties. Meanwhile, millions of Palestinians living under Israeli occupation in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza were ineligible to vote. This is Netanyahu speaking on Tuesday.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu: “We must form a right-wing, national, strong government. That is what must be done. We must not — must not — endanger Israel and establish a government that is backed by anti-Zionist Arab parties.”

In the occupied West Bank, Israeli troops violently dispersed a protest in Hebron against Israel’s military operation to displace thousands of Palestinians in the region. This comes after the deaths of two Israeli soldiers shot by Palestinian gunmen last week. This is a displaced Palestinian who attended Tuesday’s protest.

Noura Nassar: “I don’t know how to get to my home. I had to take alternative routes to get to my doctor, because I had an appointment and I had to go. I am shocked that these are people who call for democracy. Where is the democracy in all of this? Their elections are today, but what about us? Aren’t we human beings? We want to go out. We want to visit the doctor. It’s shameful.”

Topics:

West Bank

In Iran, the Oscar-nominated director Jafar Panahi has been sentenced in absentia by a Tehran court to five years and one month in prison. He was already facing a one-year sentence. The court also issued an order to confiscate Panahi’s assets, and put in place a two-year ban on using social media and a two-year travel ban. The charges are unclear. Panahi’s lawyer said that he learned of this latest sentence when he went to the prosecutor’s office after Panahi’s bank accounts were frozen. The prosecutor’s case file stated incorrectly that Panahi was living outside Iran, when in fact he returned in March. Panahi was on Democracy Now!, here in our studio in New York, back in January when we asked him about returning to Iran.

Jafar Panahi: “I will return to Iran in any possible way, under any circumstances, because it is there that I know I have to exist. It is there where I know I can make films and do what I like to do. Yes, I will return. I will definitely return.”

Topics:

Iran

In Egypt, the editor of the independent outlet Mada Masr, Lina Attalah, was released from police detention Tuesday after several hours in custody. Attalah was also reportedly informed of a one-year prison sentence issued against her in absentia back in 2024, on charges of publishing false news and managing an unlicensed website — charges she previously did not know about. She faces a retrial in the 2024 case in two weeks. This comes after an Egyptian court ordered the closure of Mada Masr, one of Egypt’s last independent news outlets, and fined Attalah over $50,000 after a sham hearing where her lawyers could not present evidence.

In Saudi Arabia, Ansar Allah, known as the Houthis, say they have hit the kingdom’s largest oil refinery with a ballistic missile. It comes as fighting has escalated in Yemen between the Saudi-backed government and the Iran-aligned Houthis since the outbreak of the U.S. war on Iran. Meanwhile, Drop Site News is reporting that the United Arab Emirates is now backing Ansar Allah in its conflict against Saudi-backed forces inside Yemen. This follows recent news that Egypt’s Parliament authorized Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi to help Saudi Arabia in its fight against Ansar Allah.

The Trump administration is reportedly considering lifting U.S. sanctions on Russia’s government investment fund headed by Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev. That’s according to The New York Times, which spoke to an unnamed U.S. official who said the Treasury Department is looking to remove restrictions on the fund as part of Trump’s major energy deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import millions of tons of Russian diesel. The Biden administration first imposed sanctions on the fund in 2022, just days after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

This comes as the U.N. special rapporteur on human rights in Russia warns the Kremlin is persecuting critics both at home and abroad. This is U.N. Special Rapporteur Mariana Katzarova.

Mariana Katzarova: “Russia is one of — Russia is in third place out of 10 states that are responsible for 70% of the physical attacks on critics abroad in the past decade. That’s quite a serious place that Russia is holding in the world as a perpetrator of transnational repression. And the machine that produces these enemies of the state is a strategy by the Russian government. And this is what I devoted my report on at the General Assembly.”

Topics:

Russia

Flávio Bolsonaro has fled to the United States following his defeat in Brazil’s presidential election against Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Bolsonaro reportedly left Brazil after Brazilian police this week asked him to turn over his passport as he’s being investigated in a money laundering case. Flávio Bolsonaro is the son of former far-right Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for orchestrating a failed coup attempt after he lost the 2022 election to Lula. The State Department has confirmed it will issue Flávio Bolsonaro and his family U.S. visas. President Lula responded to the news.

President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva: “This act of leaving Brazil is shameful. When I was asked to surrender my passport, I did so. He should have done the same. If the Federal Police suspected he was going to leave Brazil, he ought to have surrendered his. Regrettably, that is the Bolsonaro family for you. Brazil is their second homeland. Their first homeland is the United States.”

Topics:

Brazil

The Pentagon struck another boat in the eastern Pacific, killing at least five people on Tuesday. The U.S. military again claimed, without providing any evidence, that the vessel was transporting drugs. Since President Trump returned to office, there have been more than 70 boat strikes in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, killing more than 240 people. Human rights advocates have condemned the attacks as illegal extrajudicial killings at sea.

Alex Pretti’s parents have accused the federal government of protecting the Customs and Border Protection agents who fatally shot their son in January in Minneapolis, and said the Trump administration has stonewalled them from the investigation in the nine months since Pretti was killed. This is Alex Pretti’s father, Michael, who spoke alongside his wife, Susan, from Minneapolis on Tuesday.

Michael Pretti: “We believe in the rule of law and that people should be held accountable through that law. However, our experience with the Department of Justice has left us wondering how Alex will ever get justice. We hear the federal government is not sharing information. Then we hear that they are sharing information. Then, last week, we learned again that they said in court documents they are not sharing evidence. This is not normal. This is not justice. It is morally wrong.”

Pretti was a 37-year-old intensive care nurse who worked at the Minneapolis Veterans Affairs Health Care System. Click here to see our coverage of this case.

In California, another immigrant has been confirmed dead in ICE custody. Roberto Jimenez Gutierrez was found unresponsive while jailed at the for-profit Otay Mesa Detention Center in San Diego. The 43-year-old immigrant from Guatemala was being held in solitary confinement, awaiting deportation to Mexico despite not being a citizen of that country. This marks at least 61 deaths in ICE custody during Trump’s second term and comes just days after an immigrant from El Salvador died at an ICE processing center in Folkston, Georgia, last week.

In more related news, the Associated Press reports ICE has detained a mentally ill U.S. citizen for nearly one year. The Trump administration is seeking to deport Phillip James to Jamaica, even though public records show he was born in Florida. The 39-year-old is being detained at an ICE jail in Indiana dubbed “Speedway Slammer.” James suffers from paranoid schizophrenia and reportedly mistakenly told federal immigration officers he’d been born in Jamaica and was the illegitimate son of a former Jamaican prime minister. His mother and legal team are urging for his release.

The U.S. Supreme Court has declined to restore a Biden-era rule that allowed immigration judges to temporarily suspend some deportation cases, a practice known as “administrative closure.” In an unsigned order, the Supreme Court rejected a request from three U.S. cities that have large immigrant populations: Baltimore; Columbus, Ohio; and New Haven, Connecticut. Back in June, Texas filed a lawsuit petitioning the Trump administration to block the policy. Judges used the discretion to temporarily prevent the deportation of asylum seekers and others in need of relief and protection.

Malik Williams, a Democratic candidate for a seat in Texas' state legislature, called for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and for legalizing marijuana during a Tuesday rally for U.S. Senate nominee James Talarico in Lubbock, Texas.

"We can legalize and tax THC and cannabis. We're gonna abolish ICE, we're gonna tax the rich and we're going to get my friend, the next United States senator from the state of Texas, James Talarico, elected!" Williams exclaimed to raucous applause.

Talarico, a Democrat running in a historically Republican state, has shied away from making such direct calls to abolish ICE while on the campaign trail.

During a joint CNN and Jubilee town hall, Talarico directly denied wanting to abolish ICE when asked if he supported the idea.

JAMES TALARICO TORCHES BIDEN BORDER POLICIES IN STUNNING ATTACK AD AS PROGRESSIVE TRIES TO FLIP TEXAS BLUE

"No, and I never have," Talarico responded, adding, "We need Immigration and Customs Enforcement in this country, but that's not what we're seeing. What we've seen over the last year is a secret police force, and that's what we don't want in this country."

EXCLUSIVE: RESURFACED VIDEO SHOWS JAMES TALARICO DISCUSSING ‘EXCITING’ OPPORTUNITY TO END ‘OVER-POLICING’

Talarico's recent remarks, however, depart from past comments. In January, during a primary debate with Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas, Talarico said it was time to "tear down" ICE.

"ICE shot a mother in the face. ICE kidnapped a 5-year-old boy. ICE executed a man in broad daylight on our streets just this morning. It's time to tear down this secret police force and replace it with an agency that actually is going to focus on public safety," he said.

FOX NEWS POLL: MAJORITY SAYS IMMIGRATION ENFORCEMENT HAS CROSSED THE LINE

text:
October 28, 2026 12:07 pm

CALIFORNIA — A coalition of civil rights groups today filed a federal lawsuit to stop an unlawful and discriminatory program by United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) that systematically targets, investigates, and intimidates naturalized U.S. citizens.

The lawsuit was filed by OCA-Asian Pacific American Advocates, OCA-San Mateo, OCA-Sacramento, Common Cause, ACLU of Northern California, ACLU of Southern California, Asian Americans Advancing Justice – AAJC, and Asian Americans Advancing Justice Southern California (AJSOCAL), represented by the ACLU Voting Rights Project.

Since August 2026, USCIS has run what it calls an “Unlawful Voter Initiative” aimed at tracking and investigating foreign-born citizens under the guise of voter eligibility checks. As part of this initiative, federal agents rely on outdated, error-prone data and questionable methods — including posing as individual voters to search private voter registration records on state election websites. As a result, thousands of fully naturalized American citizens are subjected to improper investigations, door-to-door interrogations, and potential disenfranchisement based on flawed government data.

“The Trump administration is challenging voters and threatening states based off flawed and outdated data,” said Theresa J. Lee, senior staff attorney with the ACLU’s Voting Rights Project. “These allegations are putting eligible voters — including naturalized U.S. citizens — at risk of disenfranchisement. The administration can’t keep creating political stunts to sow distrust in our elections and lay the groundwork to question results they don’t like. We’re challenging both these unlawful actions and the unreliable data behind them, and we will fight to ensure that no eligible voter is targeted or silenced because of it.”

The lawsuit aims to immediately stop the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) from continuing the Unlawful Voter Initiative. It also seeks to block the federal government from pressuring state election officials to withhold or discard valid ballots cast by individuals appearing on DHS’s unreliable lists. Additionally, the legal action demands a formal declaratory judgment establishing that the initiative violates the Civil Rights Act’s Uniform Standards Provision, the Privacy Act, and the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

“Our communities have spent generations fighting to overcome barriers to the ballot box, and we cannot allow government intimidation to become another obstacle,” said Thu Nguyen, executive director of OCA-Asian Pacific American Advocates. “Instead of helping voters participate in our elections, federal agencies are using flawed information to investigate and intimidate the very people they are supposed to serve. These actions threaten to undermine years of progress in building trust and encouraging civic participation in immigrant communities. We cannot allow fear to keep people from exercising their right to vote.”

“This administration knows its data is flawed and unreliable, but they’re using it anyway to scare eligible voters away from the polls. It’s a deliberate effort to spread unfounded lies and make people doubt our elections,” said Virginia Kase Solomon, president and CEO of Common Cause. “When even one voter is targeted, all of us are at risk. Common Cause will keep fighting in the courtroom and in our communities to make sure every single eligible voter can cast their ballot without fear of government harassment.”

“Naturalized citizens are U.S. citizens, with exactly the same right to vote as anyone born here,” said John C. Yang, president and executive director of Asian Americans Advancing Justice – AAJC. “The ‘Unlawful Voter Initiative’ was never designed to confirm citizenship, and election officials have found it erroneously flagging eligible voters. Purging or investigating voters based on their system errors punishes citizens for the government’s own mistakes. Asian American voters, many of whom are naturalized, are bearing the brunt of it. We are suing to send a message that no eligible voter should be subjected to this intimidation tactic. We urge voters to go to the polls. Do not stay home out of fear.”

“Citizenship earned through naturalization is not second-class citizenship. Yet this administration is combing through immigration records to single out naturalized Americans, many of them Asian American and Pacific Islander, and to treat their right to vote as suspect. No other voters face this scrutiny. We are proud to stand with OCA and Common Cause to insist that every eligible voter, however they became a citizen, is treated equally under the law,” said Dahni Tsuboi, CEO of Asian Americans Advancing Justice Southern California.
