text:
“60 Minutes” was aware that the married father of two it profiled on Sunday claimed he was gay on immigration documents in an apparent effort to avoid being deported, according to a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) official.

The CBS News program was informed of the seemingly fraudulent claims the deported migrant, Moussa Diawara, made about his sexuality on an asylum application a full two weeks before the segment aired, a DHS spokesperson told The Post Tuesday.

But the program made no mention of Diawara, who is married to a woman, invoking his alleged homosexuality in the documents from 2012 as a means to block deportation to his native Mali over discrimination concerns.

“60 Minutes” instead reported that Diawara insisted he couldn’t be sent back to Mali because he converted to Christianity and feared he would be religiously persecuted in the Muslim-majority country.

1/1Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE

A rep for the show did not immediately respond to The Post’s request for comment Tuesday.

Diawara was deported to Ghana in July, more than a decade after he overstayed a tourist visa and claimed refugee status that barred him from being sent back to Mali.

After the segment aired, DHS General Counsel James Percival revealed in an X post that he pulled Diawara’s immigration file and discovered “his claimed reason for fearing Mali was that he is ‘gay,’ just in case you’re wondering how bad the immigration fraud problem is.”

On his asylum application, obtained by Fox News, Diawara — who has a wife and is described as a “Texas dad” by CBS News — rejoiced that “since I came to the USA I had the possibilities to express my feelings to men without any embarrassment [and] no reserve.”

“Although I was born as a boy, but things appeared differently for me as I was already having female behaviors and feelings,” he wrote. “I was more comfortable being intimate with boys rather than with girls.”

In the segment, Diawara alleged that within days of arriving in Ghana, authorities in the West African country forced him on a flight to Mali.

He has since fled Mali and is living in an undisclosed country, according to “60 Minutes.”

title: Indiana ACLU attorneys are resigning in protest. What happens to these civil rights cases?
description:
Attorneys at the ACLU of Indiana have counseled and represented thousands of clients seeking remedies for suspected civil rights violations.
"The ACLU of Indiana stands behind, and with, our clients and will support them throughout that process," the statement said.
Several staff members expressed concerns that Oliver would allow larger policy goals and activist input to shape which cases attorneys take up, rather than the scope or severity of the civil liberty violations.
It also said that it will continue to work with national ACLU attorneys during this time.
Case: Planned Parenthood of Indiana and Kentucky, Inc. v. Commissioner, Indiana State Department of Health Attorneys: Gavin Rose, Ken Falk and attorneys from the national ACLU and Planned Parenthood.
text:
Over the next handful of months, the American Civil Liberties Union of Indiana will lose four respected attorneys who resigned in protest over the organization's direction and other leadership concerns. The shakeup has some asking what will happen to the dozens of cases the legal team is actively litigating.

By the end of the week, the ACLU's once five-person legal team will be down to three members: legal director Ken Falk, deputy legal director Gavin Rose and recently hired staff attorney Grace Wenstrom. Both Falk and Rose have submitted resignations, but they have extended timelines to leave the ACLU, citing the needs of their clients. They expect to complete their last days of work by the end of the year and mid-February.

Attorneys at the ACLU of Indiana have counseled and represented thousands of clients seeking remedies for suspected civil rights violations. That includes cases concerning the freedom of speech and religion, conditions inside prisons and jails, reproductive rights, unlawful searches and seizures, and LGBTQ issues. Cases range from ensuring city sidewalks are up to federal disability compliance to challenging the state's abortion ban on religious grounds.

It can take years for some cases to reach a final ruling, and undoubtedly, the attorneys' caseload will not wrap up in a matter of months.

Moving forward, clients have three options, according to a statement from the ACLU of Indiana. They can choose to be represented by the ACLU, which plans to rebuild its legal team. They could stay with the attorneys who are leaving the organization. Or they could choose to be represented by a third party. This is the typical procedure when an attorney leaves, the ACLU said, and the organization will continue to support its clients through this transitional period.

"The ACLU of Indiana stands behind, and with, our clients and will support them throughout that process," the statement said.

Rose said the ACLU's clients have agreements with attorneys, not the organization, to litigate their cases. He said the attorneys plan to continue representing almost all of their clients, even beyond their time at the ACLU.

In addition to four members of the legal team, multiple other staff members have resigned or been fired. As IndyStar previously reported, the exodus stems from a snowballing number of concerns over the organization's direction under its board and incoming leader, Nikkita Oliver.

Several staff members expressed concerns that Oliver would allow larger policy goals and activist input to shape which cases attorneys take up, rather than the scope or severity of the civil liberty violations. Two longtime staffers have also filed complaints against Oliver with the organization's human resources director. The complaints allege that Oliver questioned the objectivity of ACLU attorneys who are Jewish, said the ACLU is "too pure" on civil liberties, and intended to use the nonpartisan organization to turn Indiana "light red," a potential violation of the group's tax-exempt status.

The ACLU's board has said the ACLU is not changing its mission and disputed the staff complaints, characterizing them as false, misleading or contradictory. An external human resources firm is actively conducting a review of the situation.

The ACLU of Indiana is currently searching for an interim legal director, according to its statement, and multiple attorneys in Indiana and across the country have offered to collaborate and support the organization during the transition. It also said that it will continue to work with national ACLU attorneys during this time.

Here are some of the ACLU's notable active cases:

Indiana ruling could expand abortion access in red states

The ACLU is challenging Indiana's abortion ban, claiming the state is obstructing Hoosiers' rights after it implemented a near-total abortion ban with exemptions for some reasons — such as fatal fetal abnormalities, rape or incest, or if there's a serious threat to maternal health — but not for religious beliefs.

Those challenging the law leaned heavily on Indiana's Religious Freedom Restoration Act — a law once championed by then-Gov. Mike Pence amid intense discourse over whether the law gave license to discriminate against the LGBTQ community. Under the law, the state must prove a compelling interest for burdening a person's religion and that its solution is the least restrictive way of furthering that interest. A lower court previously ruled in favor of the ACLU's argument, finding that the state was enforcing an "inconsistent approach" to its goal of protecting life before birth.

Case: Anonymous Plaintiffs v. The Individual Members of the Medical Licensing Board of Indiana

Attorneys: Ken Falk, Stevie Pactor and Gavin Rose

Status: Awaiting decision from the Indiana Supreme Court

Fight over Ten Commandments monument's return to the Statehouse

About 25 years ago, a court order barred a monument with an inscription of the Ten Commandments from the Indiana Statehouse. After a shift in case law, a federal judge agreed to reopen the case in late May, setting off a renewed legal fight over whether the Ten Commandments can be returned to the Capitol's grounds.

Gov. Mike Braun and Attorney General Todd Rokita, both Republicans, want the monument restored. They argue it reflects the nation's history and traditions. The ACLU of Indiana opposes the move, saying it would violate the First Amendment's religious freedom clause.

Case: Indiana Civil Liberties Union v. O’Bannon

Attorneys: Ken Falk, Stevie Pactor, Josh Bleisch and Grace Wenstrom

Status: Awaiting decision from the U.S. District Court of Southern Indiana

Lawsuit: Prison failed to give ICE detainee meds, then pepper-sprayed him

An immigration detainee who was held at Miami Correctional Facility claims the prison's for-profit health contractor, Centurion Health, failed to provide his epilepsy medication, causing him to suffer a head injury from a seizure that left him lying in a "pool of blood." Then, later that day, guards at the facility pepper sprayed him without justification.

Grigoryan alleges in federal lawsuits that Centurion failed to provide adequate staffing to care for immigrant detainees at the prison. As a result, Grigoryan, who has been prescribed pills for epilepsy since 2020, frequently missed his anti-seizure medication.

Cases: Grigoryan v. Unknown Correctional Officers, Grigoryan v. Centurion Health

Attorneys: Ken Falk, Stevie Pactor, Gavin Rose and Josh T. Bleisch

Status: Awaiting decision from the U.S. District Court of Southern Indiana

Concerns over Bloomington jail conditions renewed in class action suit

This summer, the ACLU filed a class action lawsuit challenging conditions at the Monroe County Jail in Bloomington. A similar case in 2009 resulted in a settlement, but the ACLU renewed its complaint, alleging that the county has not found a long-term solution and that the same unconstitutional conditions remain.

Similar cases have been pursued against jails in Allen, Howard and Vigo counties.

Case: Grubb v. Monroe County Council

Attorneys: Ken Falk and Josh Bleisch

Status: Awaiting decision from the U.S. District Court of Southern Indiana

ACLU sues Ball State over punishment of student protesters

A group of student protesters and the ACLU are suing Ball State University, claiming its policies unfairly infringe on their First Amendment right to protest. The lawsuits stem from a demonstration last November where about a dozen students marched to President Geoffrey Mearns' office to demand that the university divest its assets from companies with ties to Israel — a common demand from the pro-Palestine movement. Months later, the university punished several of the students involved.

Case: Allen v. Mearns

Attorneys: Gavin Rose, Stevie Pactor and Josh Bleisch

Status: Awaiting a decision from the U.S. District Court of Southern Indiana

AG Todd Rokita attempts to probe refugee nonprofit

In September 2025, the Indiana Attorney General's Office sent Indianapolis-based Exodus Refugee Immigration Inc. a civil investigatory demand, a legal tool the attorney general can use to collect information prior to litigation. The office said it did so to discern whether the nonprofit is violating the law and interfering with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

The legal complaint argues that Rokita targeted Exodus for its mission of serving the immigrant and refugee community. The ACLU, which is representing Exodus, says its services are constitutionally protected activities and the civil subpoena is "unjustified retaliation."

Case: Exodus Immigration Inc. v. Rokita

Attorneys: Ken Falk, Gavin Rose, Stevie Pactor and Josh Bleisch

Status: Awaiting final decision in the U.S. District Court of Southern Indiana

Rokita investigator threatened Indiana man over '86' comments

The ACLU filed a lawsuit in May accusing an Indiana Attorney General investigator of violating a Bloomington man's First Amendment rights by intimidating him into not participating in protected speech.

The investigator questioned the man about his social media comments with the number "86" and the names of Attorney General Todd Rokita, Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith and U.S. Sen. Jim Banks. A doorbell camera recorded the conversation where the investigator told the man that he "crossed the line" and that officials "could easily indict you over this today," according to court documents.

Case: Lawmaster v. Spivey

Attorneys: Josh Bleisch, Ken Falk, Stevie Pactor and Gavin Rose

Status: Awaiting final decision from the U.S. District Court of Southern Indiana

Doctors who tell minors about abortion options cannot be punished

Indiana cannot prohibit doctors from telling minors, without their parents' consent, where they could receive an abortion out of state, a federal appeals court ruled on Aug. 18. The court upheld a decision finding a portion of Indiana's 2017 “aid-or-assist” law to be a violation of the First Amendment because it blocks providers from sharing information about lawful abortion procedures in other states.

Case: Planned Parenthood of Indiana and Kentucky, Inc. v. Commissioner, Indiana State Department of Health

Attorneys: Gavin Rose, Ken Falk and attorneys from the national ACLU and Planned Parenthood.

Status: Unclear if further appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court will be pursued

Rural pride fest fights city’s repeated efforts to restrict it

Since the pride festival was first held in 2023, the city of Loogootee and festival organizers have battled in court over where the annual pride festival can take place. Patoka Valley AIDS Community Action Group has fought back in court. The city has twice been found in violation of the First Amendment and was found in contempt after it ignored a court order.

Case: Patoka Valley AIDS Community Action Group, Inc. v. City of Loogootee

Attorneys: Ken Falk, Stevie Pactor and Josh Bleisch

Status: Loogootee appealing to U.S. Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals

Volunteers sue Indy animal shelter over policies limiting criticism

With the help of the ACLU, two longtime volunteers are suing the city, alleging that its animal shelter made policy changes prohibiting them from speaking out about leadership and animal safety concerns. The complaint challenges two provisions in the volunteer handbook as violations of the First Amendment.

Case: Ruiz v. City of Indianapolis

Attorney: Gavin Rose

Status: In settlement negotiations

Transgender bathroom case out of Martinsville

The ACLU is fighting a case on behalf of a then-Martinsville middle school student who is a transgender boy but was required to use the girls' bathroom or a single-person bathroom. Multiple courts have sided with the student and the ACLU.

Case: A.C. v. Metropolitan School District of Martinsville et al

Attorneys: Ken Falk, Stevie Pactor and Josh Bleisch

Status: Awaiting decision from the U.S. Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals

Indiana State pulls federal money for Pride Center

The ACLU is suing Indiana State University, alleging it violated the First Amendment rights of an LGBTQ community center after it revoked its ability to host work-study workers. The university is engaging in "punishment and retaliation against the Pride Center because of its constitutionally protected speech and association and because of the viewpoint that the Pride Center expresses," the ACLU said in its filing.

Case: Pride Center of Terre Haute, Inc. v. President, Indiana State University

Attorneys: Ken Falk, Stevie Pactor and Josh Bleisch

Status: Awaiting decision from the U.S. District Court of Southern Indiana

Several cases from inmates regarding conditions, religion, books

A significant portion of the ACLU of Indiana's workload is spent supporting prisoners. Many times, the ACLU helps those in jails and prisons without needing to file a legal complaint.

In a batch of cases, Pactor and Rose are representing three women incarcerated at the Rockville Correctional Facility in Parke County who say a contracted physical therapist sexually abused and harassed them. In a different class action case, the legal team and lawyers from Faegre Drinker Biddle & Reath LLP are seeking relief for inmates on federal death row who are being held in extreme isolation, which they argue violates the Eighth Amendment.

The attorneys have also litigated several First Amendment cases where inmates were denied books and circumstances where correctional staff did not respect the faith practices of prisoners.

Cate Charron’s role covering First Amendment issues at IndyStar is made possible by a collaboration amongFreedom Forum,Journalism Funding Partners and the USA TODAY Network. Freedom Forum does not provide editorial input.

authors: RYAN J. FOLEY Associated Press, ABC News
description:
Groups that provide legal services to immigrants filed a lawsuit Wednesday seeking to stop the Trump administration's new policy of hiding the locations of tens of thousands of detainees with final deportation orders.
The lawsuit challenges U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's decision, first reported by The Associated Press, to remove the locations of people facing final removal orders from its Online Detainee Locator System and to instruct staff not to reveal their whereabouts.
As of last month, the move affected more than 16,000 of the nearly 69,000 detainees who were in ICE custody.
ICE and its parent agency, the Department of Homeland Security, didn't immediately respond to a message seeking comment on the lawsuit.
The agencies have not publicly confirmed the change, but have said they are prioritizing people with final removal orders for deportation.
text:
Groups that provide legal services to immigrants filed a lawsuit Wednesday seeking to stop the Trump administration's new policy of hiding the locations of tens of thousands of detainees with final deportation orders.

The policy, adopted suddenly last month to expedite deportations, interferes with immigration lawyers’ rights by making it difficult, and sometimes impossible, to locate their clients, according to the lawsuit filed in federal court in Boston. It asks a judge to issue an order blocking the “unlawful and inhumane” change.

“No one should be denied a meaningful opportunity to defend their rights because the government has made it impossible for their lawyer to find them,” said Jacquelynne Bowman, executive director of Greater Boston Legal Services, one of the four groups listed as plaintiffs. “This arbitrary new administrative change leaves hundreds of thousands of people at risk of potentially life-altering consequences without essential legal help."

The lawsuit challenges U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's decision, first reported by The Associated Press, to remove the locations of people facing final removal orders from its Online Detainee Locator System and to instruct staff not to reveal their whereabouts. As of last month, the move affected more than 16,000 of the nearly 69,000 detainees who were in ICE custody.

ICE and its parent agency, the Department of Homeland Security, didn't immediately respond to a message seeking comment on the lawsuit.

The agencies have not publicly confirmed the change, but have said they are prioritizing people with final removal orders for deportation. They have also said they are facing a “historic number of injunctions” from courts blocking their efforts. The agencies have denied that they are disappearing detainees, saying they remain free to make phone calls.

Since 2010, lawyers and family members have used the online system to track detainees as they get moved from facility to facility through ICE's sprawling detention network.

Approximately 1.4 million people living in the U.S. are subject to final orders of removal, which means an immigration judge has ruled they should be deported and the decision has been upheld on appeal or not appealed.

Those individuals still have several options to challenge the conditions of their detention and looming deportations, including asking to reopen proceedings, seeking relief from removal to third countries and challenging violations of their rights. Federal judges have ruled thousands of times that detainees should be released or granted bond hearings.

Since the change went into effect, lawyers have been unable to find clients and potential clients and have spent “significantly more time” tracking down others, the lawsuit says. Calls to ICE, including to its Detention and Removal Information Line, “lead to long wait times on hold, sudden hang-ups, a general lack of information or no answer at all,” it says.

As a workaround, some lawyers have tried to find their clients through an ICE program that schedules legal calls, but only a small percentage of detention centers use it, the lawsuit says. The result has been delayed or missed legal filings and fewer cases taken, according to the organizations.

The lawsuit argues the change violates the Administrative Procedure Act because it was adopted without explanation and the First Amendment, which protects lawyers' ability to advise people of their legal rights and seek prospective clients.

text:
A group of legal services organizations today filed a lawsuit challenging the federal government’s new policy of hiding the locations of thousands of people detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The policy unlawfully interferes with communication between detainees, their families, and their lawyers.

The lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts on behalf of Greater Boston Legal Services, Rian Immigrant Center, Florence Immigrant and Refugee Rights Project, and Amica Center for Immigrant Rights. The groups argue the new policy unlawfully blocks them from locating, communicating with, and providing legal services to their clients and potential clients.

For over 16 years, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security has made the location of detained noncitizens available via its Online Detainee Locator System. In September, DHS abruptly changed course and stopped sharing the location of detained people with final orders of removal, either via the locator service or in direct response to queries from family members or attorneys. This policy of mass disappearance has thrown thousands into an administrative black box without any justification.

The new policy facilitates the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign by making it more difficult to provide detainees with access to attorneys and the judicial system — and thus more difficult to challenge unlawful detention and pursue lawful pathways to remain in the United States. Noncitizens with final orders of removal may still pursue a number of legal remedies to challenge their detention and deportation — but if they cannot access legal counsel or the courts, they may never have a chance to seek these remedies before they are deported.

The lawsuit alleges that ICE’s implementation of this new policy is arbitrary and capricious, and thus a violation of the Administrative Procedure Act. The complaint also alleges that ICE’s policy violates the plaintiffs’ First Amendment rights. Finally, the complaint alleges violations of the Freedom of Information Act because the government failed to publish details of their new policy. The plaintiffs are asking the court to vacate the new policy, and will shortly file a motion to stay the new policy while their case proceeds.

The plaintiffs are represented by the National Immigration Law Center, National Immigration Project, the American Civil Liberties Union, the ACLU of Massachusetts, and Annelise Araujo Law.

The following are statements from the plaintiffs and their legal counsel:

Attorneys representing the plaintiffs: “The Trump administration’s new policy of mass disappearance should send a chill through everybody’s spine. By choosing to hide even the most basic information about thousands of people in its custody, the government is unlawfully blocking their access to legal counsel and the courts, and keeping desperate loved ones in the dark. This shockingly malicious policy was implemented suddenly, without any legal basis or justification, and with immediate, devastating impacts for our clients and the people they serve. The government must reverse course immediately, restore the Online Detainee Locator System, and stop hiding people in its vast network of detention facilities.”

Jacquelynne J. Bowman, executive director of Greater Boston Legal Services: “No one should be denied a meaningful opportunity to defend their rights because the government has made it impossible for their lawyer to find them. Even with representation, navigating the legal system is complex for immigrants facing deportation. This arbitrary new administrative change leaves hundreds of thousands of people at risk of potentially life-altering consequences without essential legal help.”

Jackie Kelley, director of immigration legal services at the Rian Immigrant Center: “We cannot allow the United States government to indefinitely disappear human beings. If we cannot locate our clients, we cannot pursue the relief for which they are legally eligible. The law gives our clients the right to seek protection. This policy obstructs that right when our clients need it most.”

Laura St. John, legal director at the Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project: “The Trump administration is disappearing people within the immigration detention system. This should terrify every single one of us. Thousands of people are no longer being shown on the online detainee locator system, making it impossible for attorneys to locate their clients or identify people who might need emergency legal assistance. How can people in detention possibly have access to due process and safety if there is no way for their families or advocates to know where they are being held?”

Aimee Mayer-Salins, deputy program director of legal coordination at the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights: “When someone you love is in ICE custody, they shouldn’t simply disappear into a black hole. Families deserve to know where their loved ones are being held, and this lawsuit is about protecting that basic right.”

text:
Groups that provide legal services to immigrants filed a lawsuit Wednesday seeking to stop the Trump administration's new policy of hiding the locations of tens of thousands of detainees with final deportation orders.

The policy, adopted suddenly last month to expedite deportations, interferes with immigration lawyers’ rights by making it difficult, and sometimes impossible, to locate their clients, according to the lawsuit filed in federal court in Boston. It asks a judge to issue an order blocking the “unlawful and inhumane” change.

“No one should be denied a meaningful opportunity to defend their rights because the government has made it impossible for their lawyer to find them,” said Jacquelynne Bowman, executive director of Greater Boston Legal Services, one of the four groups listed as plaintiffs. “This arbitrary new administrative change leaves hundreds of thousands of people at risk of potentially life-altering consequences without essential legal help."

The lawsuit challenges U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's decision, first reported by The Associated Press, to remove the locations of people facing final removal orders from its Online Detainee Locator System and to instruct staff not to reveal their whereabouts. As of last month, the move affected more than 16,000 of the nearly 69,000 detainees who were in ICE custody.

ICE and its parent agency, the Department of Homeland Security, didn't immediately respond to a message seeking comment on the lawsuit.

The agencies have not publicly confirmed the change, but have said they are prioritizing people with final removal orders for deportation. They have also said they are facing a “historic number of injunctions” from courts blocking their efforts. The agencies have denied that they are disappearing detainees, saying they remain free to make phone calls.

Since 2010, lawyers and family members have used the online system to track detainees as they get moved from facility to facility through ICE's sprawling detention network.

Approximately 1.4 million people living in the U.S. are subject to final orders of removal, which means an immigration judge has ruled they should be deported and the decision has been upheld on appeal or not appealed.

Those individuals still have several options to challenge the conditions of their detention and looming deportations, including asking to reopen proceedings, seeking relief from removal to third countries and challenging violations of their rights. Federal judges have ruled thousands of times that detainees should be released or granted bond hearings.

Since the change went into effect, lawyers have been unable to find clients and potential clients and have spent “significantly more time” tracking down others, the lawsuit says. Calls to ICE, including to its Detention and Removal Information Line, “lead to long wait times on hold, sudden hang-ups, a general lack of information or no answer at all,” it says.

As a workaround, some lawyers have tried to find their clients through an ICE program that schedules legal calls, but only a small percentage of detention centers use it, the lawsuit says. The result has been delayed or missed legal filings and fewer cases taken, according to the organizations.

The lawsuit argues the change violates the Administrative Procedure Act because it was adopted without explanation and the First Amendment, which protects lawyers' ability to advise people of their legal rights and seek prospective clients.

text:
In Brief

Democratic senators renewed efforts to remove immigration courts from executive branch control following allegations of judicial interference.

Former immigration judge Karen Donoso Stevens claims Justice Department officials pressured her to reverse rulings and conduct improper bond hearings.

The allegations have intensified concerns about judicial independence within the immigration court system under the Trump administration.

Legislation backed by Senate Democrats would establish an independent immigration court system, though its prospects remain uncertain.

Congressional Democrats have again demanded urgent reforms to the country’s immigration court system after The Washington Post revealed a veteran judge’s allegations that she was ordered to reverse rulings and urged to conduct sham bond hearings.

Democratic Sens. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland and Dick Durbin of Illinois, both longtime critics of President Donald Trump‘s immigration policies, renewed calls this week to pass a bill that would remove immigration judges from the authority of the executive branch.

They spoke out in response to the story of Karen Donoso Stevens, a former Homeland Security prosecutor who joined the bench in 2016. After persistent interference by Justice Department officials, Donoso Stevens alleged, she was pulled from court mid-hearing, demoted and eventually fired.

Her accusations contradict repeated assertions by the Trump administration that — as required by law — immigration judges serve as independent arbiters of justice.

“Unfortunately, this Administration has shown time and time again that they have no regard for our Constitution or the rule of law — as we’ve seen in the case of Karen Donoso Stevens,” Van Hollen said in a statement. “This abuse of power must be stopped.”

Unlike federal judges who are protected from political retaliation by lifetime tenures and the constitutional separation of powers, immigration judges work for the executive branch. Since Trump retook office, his administration has dismissed more than 100 of the nation’s approximately 700 immigration judges and replaced many with what officials call “deportation judges.”

“Judges who decline to follow precedent undermine the integrity of the system and potentially engage in professional misconduct,” Kathryn Mattingly, a spokesperson for the Justice Department’s Executive Office for Immigration Review, said in a statement. “EOIR cannot tolerate judges who decline to follow the law in lieu of their own personal preferences.”

Mattingly — who provided no evidence that Donoso Stevens or any other judge fired without cause had declined to follow the law — also alleged that The Post’s investigation “contains several misleading statements or misrepresentations,” but she did not name any.

Every year, Donoso Stevens, 53, had denied asylum in more than half the applications that came before her, a record consistently in line with national averages.

“I stand with Judge Donoso Stevens and the many others like her … who have been fired for simply doing their jobs,” said Durbin, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee. “We urgently need an independent immigration court to prevent these abuses from ever happening again.”

Durbin and Van Hollen have joined other Democrats, including Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, to push a bill that would afford the court true independence. Without Republican support, though, the legislation has little chance of passage.

On Tuesday, the Supreme Court strengthened the president’s control over immigration courts, clearing the way for his administration to restrict a policy that had allowed judges to close thousands of deportation cases each year.

Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), who respectively chair the Senate and House judiciary committees, did not respond to requests for comment about whether they found Donoso Stevens’s allegations troubling or would call for an investigation.

“All illegal aliens receive full due process and have their claims heard,” Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement. “No lawbreakers in the history of human civilization have been treated better than illegal aliens. Once again, Democrats are running to the defense of illegal aliens and continue to ignore the victims of illegal alien crime.”

The Trump administration, Donoso Stevens told The Post, first violated her judicial independence in September 2025.

For decades, undocumented immigrants who weren’t apprehended until after they entered the country were allowed to request bond, leaving judges to decide whether it was safe to release them as their cases proceeded. But the Board of Immigration Appeals, stocked with members appointed under Trump, suddenly decided that anyone who came unlawfully should remain jailed, even those with clean records and family ties.

The opinion, Donoso Stevens and other judges discovered, failed to account for children who came to the United States without a parent or guardian and had since reached adulthood, a group that, in their view, fell under distinct legal guidelines. She granted bond in four such cases.

On Sept. 17, Eric Dillow, her supervisor at the Annandale (Virginia) Immigration Court, called. He wanted to discuss bond, “a hot topic,” according to her notes.

Dillow, who did not reply to a request for comment, emailed her a separate ruling that, he believed, meant she could have denied bond. Donoso Stevens told him she could see the merits of the argument, but she said Homeland Security should either file a motion asking her to reconsider or request that the appellate board intervene. He agreed, according to her notes, but called back a few minutes later.

“He said higher-ups said I had to vacate my decs sua sponte,” Donoso Stevens wrote in a note that abbreviated “decisions” and used a Latin phrase that refers to judges reversing their own rulings unprompted.

Dillow did not name the “higher-ups,” so Donoso Stevens pressed for an explanation: “Why can’t DHS file a motion to reconsider?”

“Oh no,” he replied. “They’re not going to do that.”

To Donoso Stevens, Dillow had not only told her how to rule, directly violating the executive office’s vow of judicial independence, he’d implied that Homeland Security had ordered the court system to acquiesce.

“Immigration judges — like almost all judges in the American judicial system — are required to follow precedent,” Mattingly wrote in her statement. “As the quotes from only Democratic lawmakers demonstrate, only the most tendentious and partisan advocates would view that requirement as ‘being told how to rule,’ and no serious lawyer views it as infringing a judge’s decisional independence.”

The Post described the allegation to three legal experts, and all of them condemned it as an unacceptable infringement of a judge’s decisional independence.

text:
The Venezuelan man shot by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer last month in Austin has pleaded not guilty to a federal charge of assaulting a federal officer while resisting arrest.

Wilber Rafael Garces Perez entered the not guilty plea in a court filing Tuesday, a week after a grand jury indicted him on one count of assaulting, resisting, impeding and obstructing a federal officer. He also waived his appearance at an arraignment hearing that was scheduled for Thursday.

Garces Perez could face up to 20 years in prison if convicted, the U.S. Justice Department has said.

Garces Perez entered the country legally under the Biden administration via the CBP One App, according to immigration attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch. He applied for asylum, but an immigration judge issued a deportation order after he missed a court appearance. The notice for the hearing had been sent to the wrong address, the attorney said.

He also received a work permit, which expired in December 2025, according to Lincoln-Goldfinch.

Garces Perez was shot on Sept. 20 after he had been pulled over while making a food delivery.

During a Sept. 30 hearing with U.S. Magistrate Judge Dustin M. Howell, U.S. Department of Homeland Security Special Agent Rick Bazan, who investigated what led up to the shooting, was the lone witness to testify and provided details that were not previously public.

Bazan, who filed the criminal complaint charging Garces Perez, testified that he interviewed an ICE agent, identified by the initials D.F., who had a body camera that captured the initial traffic stop but later turned it off. Bazan said he didn’t interview the ICE agent, identified as L.G., who shot Garces Perez and who was not wearing a body camera.

Bazan didn’t say why L.G. was not interviewed as part of his investigation but said there was a separate investigation into the shooting by other DHS investigators. Bazan also testified he didn’t ask D.F. why he turned off his body camera.

During the court hearing, federal prosecutors showed the body cam footage.

Two ICE agents stopped Garces Perez after he picked up a food delivery order and began driving, Bazan testified.

The footage depicted L.G., who was wearing a ski mask, identifying himself as an immigration officer and ordering Garces Perez to step out of his Toyota Corolla. The footage showed Garces Perez responding that he wanted to park his car somewhere else and wanted to call someone to pick up his vehicle before speeding off.

Bazan testified that when Garces Perez drove away, a side mirror swiped L.G. But the footage and still image presented in court did not clearly show the mirror hitting the ICE agent, Bazan testified, in part because D.F. moved away as Garces Perez took off.

The footage also showed D.F. calling a state trooper on his cell phone before the trooper told him to instead call dispatch for help. Typically, police seeking backup call dispatch for help rather than call someone on a cell phone.

Shane McMahon, a public defender for Garces Perez, asked Bazan why L.G. wasn’t equipped with a body camera.

“We haven’t spoken to him,” Bazan said.

McMahon also asked Bazan why D.F. turned off his camera.

“You would have to ask D.F.” Bazan responded. “I don’t know why he turned it off.”

McMahon followed up: “Well I haven’t talked to D.F. but I know that you have. Did you ask D.F. why he turned it off?”

“No,” Bazan said.

At the Sept. 30 hearing, the judge ruled that Garces Perez was a flight risk and ordered him to remain in federal custody.

The federal criminal case put on hold Garces Perez’s petition for release and protection against deportation, which says he wants a chance to apply for a U-visa, a type of immigration status for victims and witnesses of a crime. The Travis County district attorney’s office had also requested that federal officials not deport the man, calling him a material witness in a criminal investigation.

text:
Rwanda is reportedly set to host the European Union’s first third-country “return hub” for rejected asylum seekers, under plans developed by Germany, Austria, Denmark, Greece and the Netherlands. Unlike Britain’s abandoned Rwanda scheme, the proposed facility would not process asylum claims. However, it would accommodate people who have already received final return decisions while EU states arrange their removal to their countries of origin.

According to sources cited by RTL Nieuws, a proposal for Rwanda has been put forward and could be announced at a special migration meeting in Vienna on November 16. Neither the Rwandan government nor the five EU governments has publicly confirmed the plan, and it remains unclear whether Rwanda’s former UK-funded Hope Hostel would be used.

Earlier reporting by InfoMigrants suggests the initiative would begin as a pilot involving roughly 100 people, with each participating state sending about 20 rejected asylum seekers. The governments have said they want the first hub operational by 2027.

Officials have sought to distinguish the model from detention. Greece’s migration minister, Thanos Plevris, has described the planned facilities as "open" rather than closed centers, while saying responsibility for transferred individuals would remain with the participating EU states.

Critics argue that the practical difference may depend less on the label than on the agreement’s terms, access to lawyers, freedom of movement, healthcare and independent monitoring.

Read Also

Rwanda expected to become first host nation for EU migrant 'return hubs'

What the new EU rules change

The plan has been made possible by the EU’s new Return Regulation, which entered into force on October 16, 2026. It replaces the 2008 Return Directive and creates an EU-wide framework for returning third-country nationals who have no legal right to remain.

The regulation creates a European Return Order, making a return decision issued in one member state enforceable elsewhere in the EU without reopening the case. It also allows transfers to a third country with which an EU state has an agreement, even where the person has no prior personal connection there.

It expressly permits member states to establish return hubs in non-EU countries for people subject to return decisions, while excluding unaccompanied minors. Agreements must set out transfer procedures, conditions of stay, the parties’ obligations and the consequences of breaches. Where onward return is envisaged, independent monitoring is required.

Such agreements may only be concluded with third countries that uphold human rights, international law and non-refoulement, the prohibition on returning people to territories where they face persecution, torture or other serious harm. National authorities must also inform the European Commission and other member states before agreements take effect.

Read Also

EU Council greenlights new rules enabling more effective returns

Frontex’s proposed new role

The European Commission has proposed a further expansion of Frontex’s mandate that would make the border agency a more central actor in returns. The proposal would create a dedicated Return Coordination Center to collect and analyze operational information, support planning and coordinate EU-wide return operations.

Most consequentially, Frontex would be able to provide technical and operational support to third countries and help organize and carry out return operations from one non-EU country to another, subject to an agreement with the country concerned and compliance with fundamental rights and international standards. In practice, that could mean Frontex involvement in transfers from a return hub in Rwanda to a person’s country of origin.

The Commission says the reform would cover the full return process, from identification and voluntary return counseling to transport and reintegration assistance. It has also proposed a separate regulation to digitalize return, readmission and reintegration procedures.

Read Also

Brussels proposes turning Frontex into the EU’s central returns agency

Precedents in other countries

The reported Rwanda plan is not the first attempt to externalize migration control, but earlier models have repeatedly encountered legal, political and practical obstacles.

Denmark passed legislation in 2021 enabling asylum seekers to be transferred outside Europe while their claims were assessed and signed a memorandum of understanding with Rwanda. No asylum seeker was transferred under that scheme. The original plan was later shelved, although Denmark has continued to pursue third-country return arrangements with other European states.

Israel pursued an earlier and more opaque version of the model. Between 2013 and 2018, thousands of Eritrean and Sudanese asylum seekers left Israel for Rwanda and Uganda under arrangements Israel described as voluntary departure, although no formal public agreement was acknowledged by either African state. Amnesty International and other organizations documented people arriving without legal status or effective protection and Israel’s Supreme Court ultimately suspended parts of the forced-deportation policy.

Italy’s agreement with Albania offers the closest current EU precedent. Italy initially sought to process migrants intercepted at sea in Albanian facilities, but Italian courts blocked early transfers after questioning whether countries such as Bangladesh and Egypt could be treated as safe in all cases. Italy has since used one facility for rejected asylum seekers already subject to deportation but the scheme has handled relatively small numbers at substantial cost.

The United Kingdom’s Rwanda plan collapsed in 2024 after the UK Supreme Court found substantial grounds to believe asylum seekers transferred there could face a real risk of refoulement. The UK government spent £715 million ($951 million) on the policy, while only four people voluntarily relocated.

The EU’s new model is narrower than the UK’s: it concerns people with final return decisions rather than people whose asylum claims are still being assessed. But the earlier failures illustrate the central vulnerability, namely whether a third country can genuinely guarantee safety, legal status and protection from onward removal.

Read Also

The return of the Rwanda plan – rights concerns and past failures

Human rights and accountability

Human-rights organizations argue that return hubs risk creating a legal no-man’s-land. A person may have lost all appeal rights in the EU, yet still be unable to return safely to their country of origin. At the same time, they may have no meaningful immigration status, work rights or effective remedies in the hub country.

The UN human-rights office has warned that expansive return hubs carry grave human-rights risks. Its concerns include the risk of arbitrary detention, inadequate legal assistance, poor medical care, and indirect refoulement if people are removed onward without proper individual assessment.

In Rwanda’s case, refugee organizations have questioned whether independent monitoring can function effectively. The director of Dutch rights group, Vluchtelingenwerk, Sjoerd Warmerdam told RTL Nieuws that independent human-rights monitoring is "virtually impossible" in Rwanda and said the Dutch immigration service does not classify Rwanda as a safe third country.

Accountability is another unresolved issue. The EU governments say they will retain responsibility and finance the scheme but it is not yet clear which state would be legally responsible for harm suffered inside the hub, how complaints would be investigated, or whether affected people could challenge transfer decisions before European or national courts.

Read Also

Can the EU suspend the right to asylum?

Leverage for third countries

A return-hub arrangement would also alter the bargaining relationship between the EU and its partners. A country willing to accept non-nationals facing removal acquires immediate leverage -- it can demand funding, development assistance, visa concessions, security cooperation, trade benefits or diplomatic support in exchange for continued cooperation.

That leverage may be especially significant for Rwanda. Kigali previously received substantial UK funding under the abandoned British scheme and it retains infrastructure built for that arrangement. If the EU plan proceeds, Rwanda would be providing a service that several powerful European states consider politically essential, giving it a strong position in negotiations over money, monitoring and the scope of its obligations.

The same dynamic applies more broadly. States in Africa, the Western Balkans, the Middle East and Central Asia could become gatekeepers in Europe’s migration system. That may give them influence not only over individual returns, but also over EU foreign-policy priorities, sanctions debates, security partnerships and development funding.

Critics call this "migration diplomacy" -- the risk that third-country governments can extract concessions by threatening to suspend cooperation, restrict monitoring access, or refuse onward transfers. While the governments driving the initiative claim that formal agreements, EU financing and independent oversight can create more predictable partnerships than informal arrangements.

Read Also

Albanian Prime Minister rejects once more the idea of hosting EU migrant return hubs

What it means geopolitically

If Rwanda becomes the first host, Europe would be moving from ad hoc, often secretive bilateral experiments toward a more institutionalized system of externalized migration control. That would mark a significant shift in the EU’s relationship with partner states, making migration cooperation a core instrument of geopolitical bargaining rather than merely a humanitarian or development issue.

It could also deepen divisions inside Europe. The five governments pursuing the plan see return hubs as a way to restore credibility to deportation policy and respond to public pressure on migration. Spain and France have previously voiced opposition, while human-rights organizations argue that the policy risks exporting Europe’s legal and moral responsibilities beyond its borders.

text:
The U.S. Supreme Court declined on Tuesday to reinstate the authority of immigration judges to temporarily postpone deportation cases, keeping in place an agreement between President Donald Trump’s administration and Republican-governed Texas that bars the once-common practice.

The justices denied an emergency request by three U.S. cities including Baltimore and an immigrant legal advocacy group to halt for now the deal ending the practice, known as “administrative closure,” while litigation continues in the dispute.

The Supreme Court’s decision, issued as a brief, one-sentence order, did not offer any explanation, as is common when it handles emergency requests. None of the justices publicly dissented from the decision.

The administration and Texas filed the agreement in a federal court in Texas on June 22, the same day that the state sued to challenge the immigration court procedure. A federal judge swiftly approved the agreement on the same day.

Baltimore and the other litigants said the federal government improperly colluded with Texas to secure the rule’s invalidation. In a statement, the litigants and the lawyers representing them from the liberal legal group Democracy Forward expressed disappointment in Tuesday’s decision.

“Eliminating these protections puts vulnerable people at greater risk of deportation and undermines public safety in communities across the country,” they said in the statement.

“This dangerous abuse of the judicial process threatens the rule of law and sets a troubling precedent for dismantling federal policies without meaningful public participation or judicial scrutiny,” they added.

Immigration judges relied on administrative closure for decades to clear certain deportation cases off their busy dockets, including when separate proceedings involving the same person are pending that could prevent removal, such as on a visa petition or an appeal of a criminal conviction.

Critics including Texas and the Trump administration have said administrative closure has allowed immigrants who lack legal status to remain indefinitely in the United States, acting in effect like an amnesty.

Administrative closure has been applied over the years in hundreds of thousands of deportation cases. Ending the practice is part of Trump’s hardline approach toward immigrants.

In 2024, Biden’s administration adopted a regulation that formally codified administrative closure procedures, concluding that it lets judges efficiently manage their caseloads and promote the fair treatment of immigrants.

OTAY MESA (KGTV)- A man who died in ICE custody at the Otay Mesa Detention Center over the weekend has now been identified, and two San Diego County supervisors are demanding answers.

ICE has confirmed that 43-year-old Roberto Jimenez Gutierrez, from Guatemala, was found unresponsive inside his cell at the Otay Mesa Detention Center on October 24th.

Just days after the death, county leaders say they've been raising concerns about health and safety inside the facility for months. Now, they're calling for answers about this death and guaranteed access for inspections moving forward.

"When our government takes someone into custody, it takes responsibility for their life, their health, and their safety. No one should lose their basic human rights just because they're behind bars," San Diego County Supervisor Terra Lawson-Remer said.

On Tuesday, San Diego County Supervisors Lawson-Remer and Paloma Aguirre called on ICE, the Trump administration and CoreCivic — the company that runs the facility — to cooperate with investigators and turn over records and video.

"Provide a timeline of this person's care from intake to death, including any health conditions noted at intake, requests for medical help, medical visits, and when staff last checked on them," Aguirre said.

ICE says when staff found Gutierrez, they called for medical help and began life-saving measures but were unsuccessful. The cause of death has not been determined.

Gutierrez's death comes after ongoing concerns over conditions inside and the court battle to get access.

"We should not have to sue the federal government every time a public health officer needs to walk inside an ICE detention facility," Lawson-Remer said.

Following a county inspection in June, the county public health officer found problems with tuberculosis reporting and delays in getting medical equipment. ICE says it provides medical screenings, access to medical appointments and emergency care to people in its custody.

In a statement Corecivic said, "We are deeply saddened by the loss of anyone in our care. Our government partners at U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) were notified immediately. All deaths in ICE custody are reviewed by ICE."

The supervisors sent a letter to ICE and DHS demanding access and information on whether anything has been fixed.

As Nicole said, it is also an important tool for attorneys who are going to court.

text:
According to a new rigorously validated dataset, ICE has detained at least 500 U.S. since the start of this administration — and the true number is likely many times higher. Nicole Foy, Ruth Talbot, and Cengiz Yar of ProPublica spent an hour with us talking about the database they recently published that sought to quantify these cases. They walked us through why this work is so important and what they learned, how they defined what counted as being detained, how they verified that the people in the videos and other stories were in fact US citizens, and why the dataset only scratches the surface. Nicole called it “the absolute minimum” number of citizens actually detained, arrested, or otherwise stopped and held by immigration authorities.

With advances in technology, it's easier than ever to build online dashboards of varying quality, and more important than ever to understand what separates them from quality datasets that require committed journalism and careful attention to the ethics of documenting violent events. That's why I think their database is one of the best examples of this kind of work in a fast-moving multimedia environment, where it's easier to flip through emotional videos that hook us than to validate and organize what we're looking at. Cengiz told us that “no single line here was just reliant on the visual material.” What the team has done is remarkable.

They also acknowledged the many other reporters who worked on this beyond the three of them, and the reporters who covered these stories first, including local journalists, which helps vet the information. The mix of skills on the team, from a reporter to a visuals editor to a coder, shows how this work really gets done.

A dataset like this is not just important for public understanding. As Nicole said, it is also an important tool for attorneys who are going to court. It shows that these aren't a few one-off cases. This is a much larger pattern, and what that calls for, in my view, isn't fixing a couple of mistakes by a couple of officers — it calls for systemic change, oversight, and accountability. Unfortunately, the agency itself is not doing this, and neither is Congress right now. So I'm glad this team stepped up. In Nicole's words, “we're documenting this because the government isn't, and the government still isn't, so here we are.”

Huge “thank you” to Nicole, Ruth, and Cengiz. Please watch or listen to the video. I think it's really informative and a good behind-the-scenes look at how this work gets done.

Immigrant rights advocates are voicing concerns about voter intimidation after ICE agents were seen near a polling center in Yuba City last week, though DHS says the agents were there for an unrelated case.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) stated that the agents were not targeting polling places and had permission from a representative of the center to park outside while waiting for a man to exit a courthouse.

“When voters think or know that there's going to be ICE at the polls, that is discouraging, especially for Latino voters,” said Angélica Salceda of the ACLU. “And again, generally because we've had some of these laws in the books in California, where we limit any law enforcement at or near polling locations, we know that it does play a factor into whether people feel comfortable, or feel like they're able to go into a polling place safely.”

The incident has raised questions about the presence of law enforcement near voting centers and the rules governing election observers.

“Just like anyone can observe the processes here, anyone can observe a voting center, but we do have rules,” said Ken Casparis of the Sacramento County Elections Office. “Anytime an observer crosses the line—if they're intimidating voters, they will be asked to leave.”

In-person voting is currently underway in 30 counties, including Sacramento. Election officials are monitoring individuals observing and filming election workers, as well as law enforcement near polling places.

“There are state rules in place for where law enforcement can be really relevant to vote centers, so if people are out of vote centers and they think that something's off, if there's a little something that makes them feel uneasy, they're encouraged to go up to the election workers at the particular vote center,” Casparis said.

Election officials are also training staff to handle potential disruptions.

“If there's any voter intimidation, whether it's electioneering or perceived, like law enforcement interference, voters are encouraged to go check in with election workers at the vote center, and the election workers are trained on how to deal with those situations,” Casparis said.

The ACLU also emphasized that voters have options if they feel unsafe or intimidated, including voting by mail or dropping off their ballots instead of voting in person at a polling center.

text:
In Florida, ICE arrests reached new highs this summer, mirroring a national trend as the Trump administration seeks to achieve its mass deportation goals.

While arrests have climbed steadily since President Donald Trump returned to office, this summer, the numbers shot up dramatically amid a quieter surge.

The Trump Administration has shifted away from the previous shows of force that took place in cities like Los Angeles, Minneapolis and Chicago. Instead, federal authorities are scaling back on large operations and relying more on local law enforcement agencies.

Florida, which is home to one of the nation's largest immigrant populations and some of the harshest immigration policies, saw around 29,000 arrests this year, placing it second only to Texas.

The arrests are through Aug. 6 of this year, the most recent data made available by the Deportation Data Project, which obtains the information through Freedom of Information Act requests.

Florida's summer surge saw, on average, more than 200 arrests per day, nearly double the rate compared to the earlier part of the year. And, more than half of those detained had no criminal charge or conviction.

The Trump Administration frequently says it is targeting the "worst of the worst," but data shows immigrants without a criminal record make up a growing share of arrests.

ICE does not publish the underlying charge or conviction associated with each arrest.

ALSO READ: There were 20,000+ ICE arrests in Florida last year. Here's a closer look

However, independent analyses have found that a majority of those booked by ICE are not violent offenders.

A Cato Institute analysis of Oct. 2025 data that was leaked to the nonpartisan think tank, found 5% of people detained by ICE had violent convictions.

A New York Times analysis also found 7% of those arrested by ICE between Jan. and Oct. last year, had violent convictions.

Partnerships between state and local law enforcement and federal immigration agents are driving even more arrests.

State law requires state agencies and county sheriff's offices to sign 287(g) agreements, which deputizes officers to perform certain immigration tasks. Many local police departments have signed on as well.

ALSO READ: Immigration arrests are up nationwide. Here's a look at Florida's numbers

WUSF has covered multiple stories involving immigrants who were stopped initially by state or local officers for traffic violations then transferred to ICE custody. That includes a story about women struggling to support their family after their partners were detained or deported; a young Sarasota woman who chose voluntary departure to start a new life in Mexico; and a Hillsborough father who was beaten during a traffic stop before being detained.

For most, civil traffic violations were their most serious charge.

"It would be impossible for ICE to do their job without help from local law enforcement," said Joseph Nohava, an organizer with the grassroots group Tampa Immigrants Rights Committee.

Nohava said the heightened immigration enforcement has led to fear among immigrant communities. He said, many people won't leave their homes "unless they absolutely have to."

The group holds monthly "barrio walks" where volunteers go door-to-door to homes and businesses to distribute know-your-rights information and immigrant resources. Nohava said, sometimes, people will share their experiences with immigration enforcement.

text:
A federal judge has issued a temporary pause on the Trump administration accelerating refugee status revocations. Federal immigration authorities tried to cut the amount of time that refugees have to contest decisions issued to remove their legal status from 30 days to 10.

District of Massachusetts Judge Julia Kobick enjoined the federal government on Tuesday. In particular, she said the Trump administration must stop enforcing any notices to terminate immigration statuses issued between the date the most recent policy went into effect on Oct. 14, to Oct 27, the date of this decision.

“The individuals to whom such notices to terminate were issued shall not be required to respond. … Defendants are prohibited from terminating those individuals’ refugee status based on failure to respond to any notice to respond issued during that time,” she wrote.

The lawsuit was filed on Monday in the Boston federal court. The resettlement groups and several impacted refugees sued to stop the Trump administration from using three policies to stop refugees from obtaining green cards, re-assessing their status with new court hearings and speeding up the process of ending their legal immigration status. The final one has been enjoined.

The 30-day response period has been the norm for more than four decades.

“This temporary ruling provides immediate relief to thousands of refugees across the country,” said Jeff Thielman, executive director of International Institute of New England, one of the plaintiffs.

“We are seeking to permanently invalidate the rule, alongside two other policies that indefinitely freeze green card applications and subject lawfully admitted refugees to mass re-vetting,” he said.

The impact of these policies has resulted in people being blocked on their path to citizenship after years in the U.S. despite extensive, years-long vetting. It has also caused termination of work authorization. People put into removal proceedings face indefinite detention and deportation.

“This lawsuit is yet another frivolous attempt to disrupt the Trump administration’s commitment to enforce our country’s immigration laws as intended by Congress,” said U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services spokesman Zach Kahler. The agency is one of the defendants, along with its larger organization, the Department of Homeland Security.

“U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services found an alarming erosion of screening and vetting measures under the Biden Administration in order to rush processing and maximize the number of refugees admitted to the United States,” he said.

Two of the Massachusetts refugee organizations that GBH News spoke to on Monday represented at least 2,000 impacted individuals. According to the federal government’s own figures, about 113,000 refugees have pending applications for permanent residency, and the new termination rule could affect as many as 186,000 refugee cases.

In August, however, three cities with large immigrant populations — Baltimore, Maryland; New Haven, Connecticut; and Columbus, Ohio — joined with Centro Legal de la Raza, an immigrant legal advocacy group, in an effort to intervene in the case and defend the Biden-era rule on appeal.

text:
MINNEAPOLIS — A former federal immigration judge says Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., who is under investigation, could face both criminal charges and denaturalization.

There are two federal probes ongoing into the congresswoman — the first into alleged immigration fraud and the second involving her financial disclosures and a sharp discrepancy reported just one year apart.

"If somebody who's a naturalized citizen — which I believe Ilhan Omar is — is convicted of a crime, that doesn't automatically mean that they face denaturalization or anything like that," Nathan Hansen, an attorney of 23 years, told Fox News Digital. "They would be handled by any type of other normal punishment that would come from the court."

Hansen was appointed by former Attorney General Pam Bondi to serve as an immigration judge earlier this year. He served in the role for four months.

GREGG JARRETT: ILHAN OMAR COULD FACE INDICTMENT, DENATURALIZATION AND DEPORTATION

Denaturalization proceedings are separate from any criminal case that could arise from the federal investigation into Omar, whose "real name," according to sources familiar with the investigation, is Ilhan Nur Said Elmi. Omar is under investigation for alleged immigration fraud related to the way she or her late father filled out her citizenship paperwork.

"A denaturalization proceeding, or somebody to strip somebody of their naturalization, is another proceeding, which would be a civil proceeding brought by the Department of Justice, presumably maybe on behalf of the Department for Homeland Security, who handles most of these things," said Hansen.

HOMAN SAYS ILHAN OMAR COULD BE STRIPPED OF NATURALIZATION, DEPORTED IF IMMIGRATION FRAUD IS PROVEN

"If there was some sort of nexus between the criminal conviction and somebody's citizenship, it might be more likely that the Department of Justice would bring a denaturalization proceeding," Hansen continued. "But I think it would be a discretionary matter within the people who are running the Justice Department."

Omar's Washington, D.C., home was raided by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the principal investigative arm of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), in the early morning hours of Oct. 12.

During the raid, investigators reportedly seized the congresswoman's phone, passport and computer. Fox News later confirmed that authorities are in possession of her DNA.

Regarding the case, observers have speculated that if indeed Omar has broken the law, statutes of limitations could hinder a prosecution. Hansen has seen those claims but doesn't believe them to be valid.

"My view of that is generally that fraud stops any statute of limitations. In other words, if something isn't disclosed or something's hidden, then it would be unfair to the other party to toll a statute of limitations against them," said Hansen. "That's just sort of a general principle of law."

FEDERAL AGENTS SEIZE PHONE OF REP ILHAN OMAR IN RAID TIED TO IMMIGRATION FRAUD PROBE

Asked about the prevalence of immigration fraud in general, Hansen pointed to the sheer number of pending immigration and removal cases across the country and in Minnesota.

"I think I would take it from a 30,000-foot view of just the amount of cases that the United States is facing right now of people coming here," he said. "It's got to be in the tens of millions of people coming here, I think, but certainly millions."

He said that in Minnesota alone, there are 20,000 to 30,000 removal cases pending that do not have a scheduled court date, due to a massive backlog of immigration-related cases.

"Whether you want to call it fraud or whatever, it's like an overwhelming of the system and the system is not being used in the way in which it was intended," he explained.

Bogus asylum claims are also contributing to the backlog, Hansen explained.

ILHAN OMAR'S TURBULENT WEEK EXPLAINED: THE DUELING PROBES THAT THREW THE SOMALI-BORN PROGRESSIVE INTO CHAOS

"Asylum relief has to do with protected grounds," he said. "The most common ones are that, 'I was persecuted at the acquiescence or directly at the behest at the government I am fleeing from based upon my race, my religion, my ethnicity [or] my political views.' These are common claims."

Hansen said that during the time when he was an immigration judge, he frequently saw claims that "just totally didn't add up," or documents provided by the applicant were "clearly fake."

"I mean, people would — I've seen cases where people would say, 'Well, people insulted me in my country.'
